#6664. The National Black Theatre Raised a Glass—and $1 Million—at Its Inaugural Fall Fête

“Ordinary People” might be the title of a Grammy-winning song by John Legend. Yet Legend’s persona and career trajectory have proven to be anything but ordinary—as exemplified by his attendance and performance at The National Black Theatre’s inaugural Fall Fête.

The benefit gala recently welcomed Legend alongside Mickalene Thomas, Lena Waithe, Mike Jackson, Cyndi Lauper, and Donna Murphy to Current—a private event space within Pier 59 at Chelsea Piers. Inside the venue, a crowd gathered for a cocktail reception as the Kotchegna Dance Company helped kick off the evening with their powerful rhythmic processional while Reverend Rhonda Akanaké McLean-Nur poured libations to set the tone.

Television personality Bevy Smith, who was on hosting duty for the evening, fielded well wishes from the crowd, having just celebrated her 60th birthday. “The room is so full—full of hope, love, laughter, and impact. And tonight is a firm reminder that Black enterprise and artistry stem from community,” celebrity hairstylist Vernon Francois told Vogue as they took their seat. Sharing a similar sentiment was Pose star and NBT alum, Ryan Jamal Swain: “Honestly, this is a full-circle moment for me. Walking through the door tonight and seeing a large photo of myself on the wall takes me back to the beginning of my career—I’d just graduated from Howard and moved to New York, and Sade [Lythcott] welcomed me with open arms.”

In the dining room, linen-draped banquet tables topped with roses, mini orchids, and calla lily arrangements provided a colorful setting for warm plates of grilled artichoke, artisan steakhouse beef, steamed halibut, and Caesar salad. “Tonight is a call to action,” Smith said as she headed toward the podium. “This gala is further proof that Black people must continue to show up and show out. At the election booths, at special events, and all across the globe, because the world needs your talent and your energy.”

As the night progressed, event co-chairs Andi Bernstein and Sonja Warfield joined Smith onstage and spoke of the importance of NBT’s legacy. Esteemed industry creatives including Michael F. Lythcott (NBT board chair), Thelma Golden, Charles Randolph Wright, Debra Martin Chase, and Nina Shaw presented special awards to gala honorees Margaret Anadu, Sanford Biggers, Nona Hendryx, and Get Lifted Film Co.’s Mike Jackson, as well as Legend.

Accepting the Excellence in Creative Producing Award with his business partner Jackson, Legend stated: “It’s a blessing to be a Black storyteller, and I’m so grateful that the National Black Theater exists for times such as these.” Shortly after his acceptance speech, Legend serenaded the crowd with a medley of hits, including the soul-stirring “Ordinary People,” along with a new song from his upcoming NBT-backed musical Imitation of Life—a reimagining of the 1959 film.

Additional stage presentations saw Liza Jessie Peterson perform a spoken word poem, while jazz singer Somi Kakoma provided a moving vocal selection. Describing the program, actress Murphy said it was “an honor to witness and experience, because the arts can transform every single human being, and NBT does it so well.”

The fundraising total of almost $1 million was powered by Subyn Novelle’s boisterous paddle-raising expertise. Afterwards, a disco-fueled dessert reception closed out the evening with porcelain trays of raspberry macarons, brownies, and coconut cream bites doing the rounds. DJ Stormin’ Norman spun upbeat R&B tunes from Stevie Wonder and Chaka Khan to Earth, Wind & Fire as guests flooded the dance floor to celebrate.

Holding court next to the espresso café station was NBT’s chief executive officer Sade Lythcott, who reflected on the night’s success: “When Black culture takes center stage, it’s a reminder that anything is possible for all people. And tonight’s fundraising—which partly benefits The Theatre of the Future—is a long-awaited dedication to the extraordinary vision and original building plans of my mother,” she told Vogue.

NBT’s executive artistic director Jonathan McCrory echoed the sentiment. “Tonight, we celebrate 58 years of Black artistic excellence and deep-rooted Harlem legacy founded by Dr. Barbara Ann Teer in 1968. And as we near completion of our new world-class cultural arts complex, we’re reminded of how far we’ve come—but we’re also inspired by how much further we can abundantly support our community.”

#6661. David Duchovny on Books, Band and ‘The X-Files’

David Duchovny has been famous for as long as I have been alive. From 1993 to 2002, The X-Files made government conspiracies a staple of primetime television. Duchovny’s FBI special agent Fox Mulder, with his skeptical counterpart, Gillian Anderson’s agent Dana Scully, personified the imminent breakdown of consensus reality in the coming century, delivering the paranoid fringe into 20 million American living rooms. The show belongs to a world of monoculture that no longer exists, and it launched Duchovny into a realm of visibility that’s hard to imagine now, when famous people are produced and consumed at an industrial rate. A few weeks ago, as my boyfriend shopped for a suit jacket at Crowley Vintage in Brooklyn and I edited this story on my phone, I watched a college-age boy put on a long, gray trench coat and announce to his girlfriend: “Mulder mode.”

Duchovny went on to star in Californication, a raunchy dramedy about a divorced novelist navigating the sexually and professionally parasitic Hollywood studio system of the 2000s. Many viewers interpreted Californication as a kind of autofiction, although Duchovny did not write for the show. The actor has written a number of novels, but it’s apparent to anyone who has spent 30 seconds with him that this soft-spoken, reluctant celebrity has nothing to do with the character Hank Moody. Still, Californication did anticipate something about art, celebrity, and self-commodification: Anybody who writes today must contend with marketing an artistic persona for a public that does not, as a rule, read.

In addition to his six books, Duchovny has released four records, and written and directed a number of feature films. He greets the degraded state of American arts with a charming blend of rigor and self-deprecation. “I’m not Jonathan Franzen,” he says of his fiction-writing process. “But if I work on something every day, it deepens. And eventually, hopefully, I can achieve one tenth of what Jonathan Franzen achieves.” But he has an aversion to the sort of publicity that might make his various artistic ventures more lucrative. He tells me he finds it “spiritually impoverishing.”

I meet Duchovny with his band—millennial slackers half his age—at their practice space in Carroll Gardens, where they’re preparing to tour their fourth LP, Prince of Pieces. He wears a white Hanes T-shirt, tight underneath his athletic arms, and he has a tattoo on his ankle—a compass pointing west, something he got when his daughter, West, was hospitalized as an infant. (She’s 27 now, an accomplished actor. “She wanted to be a doctor,” he says. “I was so happy when she told me she was going to pursue acting. Thank God.”)

The albums are composed of subdued, easy-to-listen-to folk-rock tracks, not dissimilar from early Kurt Vile. It’s the band’s first rehearsal in ages, and one of their only chances to prepare in advance of a European tour. In person, they play the songs harder and heavier, sprinkling in crowd-pleasing covers: “Godzilla” by Blue Öyster Cult, “The One I Love” by REM, and—“sadly only one time,” Duchovny says—“Hotline Bling.” The energy in the room is high. These men like one another. Duchovny’s manager offers me a beer from the cooler I’m perched on. I gesture to the tallboy in my purse. He looks disappointed. “You didn’t trust us,” he says. Duchovny steps aside to take a sip of water and picks up the microphone.

“You can sing along,” his keyboardist, Colin Lee, says.

At 66, David Duchovny remains a sex symbol. He’s in better shape than he was on The X-Files. He’s in better shape than the boys in the band. The night after practice, during a Q&A for a screening of his 2023 film Reverse the Curse, he mentions that the wardrobe department had to fashion a “BDSM harness” for him to wear under his clothes to remind him to hunch like an old man. He plays a Red Sox fan who bonds with his estranged son over baseball, marijuana, and their shared lust for a beautiful, young death doula. Duchovny’s character has terminal cancer. “I’m in my dying era,” he tells the crowd. “I die in every film. ”

For the most part, the audience at Westchester County’s Irvington Theater is old enough to have watched The X-Files as it aired. At least two esoteric-looking old men carry David’s poetry collection like a prayer book. There are a handful of young people. A college-aged girl in a KN95 mask raises her hand to ask about Bucky Fucking Dent, the novel adaptation of the Reverse the Curse screenplay, which Duchovny wrote while the movie was in production purgatory. “In the book, Ted and Marty’s last name is Fullilove. In the movie you change it to Fullaker. Why did you do that?”

“Good question,” Duchovny says, stalling. “Full of love. Full of shit. It’s all the same.”

Inevitably, someone asks about the new X-Files. Ryan Coogler is rebooting the show for Hulu. Duchovny will later suggest to me that Chris Carter, the show’s original writer, has designs on a reboot of his own—“He has plans, and wants to end with the original show.” As for Coogler’s version, he says, “I know he said he wants me to come do something, but we haven’t figured out what yet.” During the audience Q&A, Duchovny seems to have misheard the question, and spoils the ending for The Exiles, his forthcoming Taiwanese crime film: “I die in that one too.”

Duchovny’s latest book, About Time, a collection of poems published last year by Akashic, is also largely about dying: the death of his father, the death of his first marriage, the ambient death that hung in the air at the beginning of the decade. He started writing the poems when his therapist encouraged him to talk to dead people. “He was talking about Rudolph Steiner’s belief that you can talk to the dead. And he said: You can talk to your father and you should. My dad and I didn’t connect like we might have,” Duchovny says. “When you’re younger, you think you have all the time in the world to get the relationship you want. But the relationship doesn’t end.” In conversation, he is cerebral without being annoying. “There’s a power struggle when you read a really good novel,” he says. “Somebody’s mind is taking over your mind. I think about language a lot and how we take it for granted as being an accurate signifier. When I was younger I thought communication was possible. I’m not so sure now. But it’s fun to try.”

Duchovny’s humility complicates the sexual charisma that still lives at the center of his public persona. His introduction to About Time begins, “I know what you’re thinking: Just what the world needs now—a bunch of poems from an actor.” There’s a sense that he wants to get ahead of the reader’s skepticism. But there’s also plenty of perceptive lines in the poems themselves: “You dreamt you wrote something so good, / so ambivalent and destructive, so creative, / so lacking in morals, decency, or instruction, / so sad and so funny, / so useless and old, / so familiar and new, / so full of theft and power / that they had to name a god after it.” I ask him if good writing is necessarily amoral. He says, “Probably. Which is why any politically correct work of art is usually super successful and really bad. Usually artists are difficult people, and I have no problem separating the art from the artist. But people do now.”

In college, Duchovny wanted to be a poet. “I thought it was an actual occupation you could have,” he says. When an underclassman turned up in his workshop who was better than him, he quit writing poems on the spot. “It was actually Walter Kirn,” he says. “He showed up at 16-years-old. He was a genius. I was like okay—I’m not a poet.”

The two men have become close in the last decade. Kirn, who wrote Up in the Air and founded the newspaper County Highway, tells me what Duchovny was like at Princeton: “He was golden. He had an aura. I was a little starstruck by him.” Duchovny has agreed to play paranormal radio host Art Bell in American Nights, a biopic that Kirn is developing alongside director Alex Lee Moyer. Bell’s Coast to Coast, a cult AM show during the ’80s and ’90s, was beloved by long-haul truckers and compound preppers alike, who called in to report UFO sightings, cattle mutilations, and crop circles. “I, like the rest of my generation, grew up on The X-Files,” Moyer tells me. “It made a massive impression on me, and I’ve been a fan of David ever since. The synchronicity of him being a part of this is not lost on me.”

I ask Duchovny if he always needed to be the best. “I at least needed to be the best in my class,” he says.

In LA, I meet Duchovny in a quiet restaurant to talk about his books. He describes his first novel as “an act of cowardice.” Holy Cow is narrated by an anthropomorphized barnyard animal who uncovers the conspiracy theory that is factory farming. “I thought: Well, they’re not gonna cut me off at the knees on this. Because I’m clearly not that serious. It was calculated. I didn’t want to try for the great American novel the first time as an actor.” The books that followed are more ambitious, each one better than the last. By the time he was promoting his fourth book, 2021’s Truly Like Lightning, he made his ambition plain. “I want to be taken seriously,” he said on Marc Maron’s podcast. “That’s my weakness. I want that book to be taken seriously.”

“You don’t want people to be like the guy from The X-Files wrote a book,” Maron said.

“That’s what they’re gonna say,” Duchovny said, “but I hope and I believe that eventually people will see that I mean business.”

Truly Like Lightning centers on a Mormon polygamist family forced to enter the godless world of Los Angeles when their homestead is upended. “When I started to read about Mormonism, it struck me as super optimistic. Everyone’s gonna get their own planet and everyone’s gonna be able to propagate souls. As opposed to a European perspective, which was always about the end of something, being 2,000 years removed from this thing. The Mormons said no, this is still happening.” The novel takes cues from the literary critic Harold Bloom, who wrote that Mormonism was an “American original” and called its founder a “religious genius.” Duchovny studied under Bloom at Yale, where he earned some of an English PhD. “Everything goes back to Bloom,” he says. “And you never really leave grad school. I’m not sure I’ve left grad school. They might still be waiting for my dissertation.”

But Duchovny did leave grad school. He signed with a talent agent one summer to try to earn some money acting in commercials. His agent told him that if he wanted to go out for theater or film roles, he’d have to get into an acting class. “I said: I’m not doing anything. When I stepped into acting class, something happened. I wasn’t a demonstrative person—I was an intellectual person. So it was like: Yeah, be unreasonable. Be irrational. It opened up a different world, a world of fiction, a world without consequences. I’m doing a scene, and I’m yelling at this person and I’m going to murder them, but I don’t have to go to jail.”

For someone with half a dozen good books and an enormous public profile, it’s surprising there haven’t been more reviews. Johnny Temple, who published Duchovny’s two most recent books on Akashic, tells me, “It’s certainly frustrating that there hasn't been more review coverage of David’s books. For any well-known actor, musician, or other type of public figure, there’s always going to be obstacles to being taken seriously in a different medium.” Kirn tells me, “That makes writing fiction a much purer achievement in my mind. You’re doing this because you love it, and you know that two thirds of your fans will only remember you as a TV character. It’s a brilliant, Sisyphean task. Also, he’s a superb writer.”

I ask Duchovny whether he still thinks about being the best. “I think now I can acknowledge that it’s a hollow designation,” he says. “Especially in the arts. Even though we give awards, which is silly. Holy Cow made the Times bestseller list. Ever since, everything I write sells less and less.”

“It’s hard for someone to champion it,” he adds. “If I wrote a memoir, I’m sure it would get reviewed in the Times.”

Talking to Duchovny, one is reminded that wanting to be taken seriously and being in on the joke aren’t mutually exclusive. As band practice winds down in Brooklyn, the guys are excited to cover Lou Reed’s “Perfect Day.” Duchovny crosses his arms in front of his lap like a schoolboy as he sings. To my ear it sounds just fine, but Lee, the keyboardist, asks the mixer to lower the reverb on David’s voice.

“Maybe lower David’s mic in general?” the bassist, Mitchell Stewart asks.

“Lower than zero,” Duchovny says. “Less than zero.”

A few days later, he texts me. He just screened an early cut of Soapbox, a Hollywood satire he wrote and stars in opposite Laverne Cox. At first, he’s bummed that the test audience has decided that his character shouldn’t get killed in the final moments of the movie. But a couple hours later, he writes me again: “People don’t want me to die. I guess I should be flattered.”

#6658. A Quick and Dirty History of Honey Traps, From Mata Hari to Mozhno Girls

The honeypot—or honey trap—has re-entered the zeitgeist.

Ever since Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang became public, the term has been everywhere, calling to mind KGB sleeper agent Elizabeth Jennings (and her wide variety of wigs) on The Americans, Ingrid Bergman fraternizing with Nazi collaborators in Notorious, and Eva Marie Saint’s slick Eve Kendall in North by Northwest. (Espionage fiction author John le Carré is widely credited with coining the phrase “honey trap” in his 1974 novel Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, later defining it for the BBC as when you “put a girl in a chap’s way. It’s a sexual enticement operation.”) But the real-life phenomenon has far deeper and more interesting roots.

Below, a roundup of some of the most famous honey traps in world history:

Dancer and espionage agent Mata Hari in 1906.

This Dutch exotic dancer and courtesan—who was born Margaretha Geertruida MacLeod in 1876— helped typify the concept of the femme fatale by seducing a wide variety of high-ranking military officers, including Prussian Crown Prince Wilhelm, German Major Arnold Kalle, Russian Captain Vadim Maslov, and former French Minister of War General Adolphe-Pierre Messimy. Hari was ultimately executed by a French firing squad in 1917 after a military court convicted her of spying for Germany during World War I, allegedly saying in her own defense: “A harlot? Yes, but a traitoress, never!”

Thorpe, also known as Betty Pack, Betty Thorpe, Elizabeth Pack, and Amy Brousse, was an Anglo-American spy who worked for MI6 (the British Secret Intelligence Service) and whose targets included the Polish foreign minister’s chief of staff Count Michał Łubieński, Italian naval attaché Admiral Alberto Lais, and Vichy French Embassy press attaché Charles Brousse. When a biographer asked Thorpe if she felt ashamed of using seduction as a means of gathering military intelligence, Thorpe responded: “Ashamed? Not in the least. My superiors told me that the results of my work saved thousands of British and American lives... It involved me in situations from which ‘respectable’ women draw back... [but] wars are not won by respectable methods.”

During the Cold War, the Soviet KGB deployed what it called “Mozhno girls” to befriend or seduce foreign targets in Moscow in order to gather intelligence. (Their name came from the Russian word mozhno, meaning “it is allowed”—a reference to the women’s special dispensation to break Soviet rules about intimate contact with foreigners; Jennifer Lawrence played one such figure in the 2018 spy thriller Red Sparrow.) Mozhno girls like Violetta Seina—the double agent who seduced Marine Security Guard Clayton Lonetree at the annual Marine Corps Ball in 1985—were most active under Joseph Stalin.

Actors Winfried Glatzeder and Erika Skrotzki in Schlüsselblumen, a 1987 German television program about a Romeo agent.

As it turns out, men can be honey traps too. The East German Stasi (or secret police and intelligence agency) proved as much when spymaster Markus Wolf masterminded the system of training select male agents between the ages of 25 and 35 to target lonely or vulnerable West German women—particularly secretaries, clerks, and translators—who worked in sensitive positions inside West German government. A CIA history notes that Wolf’s “Romeo” operation successfully compromised dozens of West German targets over four decades.

Earlier this year, newly declassified FBI documents provided additional information about former California Democratic Rep. Eric Swalwell’s relationship with Christine Fang, a suspected Chinese intelligence operative also known as “Fang Fang.” Not only was Fang involved with fundraising for Swalwell’s 2014 re-election campaign, but the two also engaged in an affair before Fang fled the United States in 2015.

#6657. Poulet Basquaise

Rich tomatoes, stewed onions and peppers, and tender bone-in chicken make this Spanish- and French-inspired poulet Basquaise recipe extremely flavorful while still being surprisingly easy to make. Savory and rustic, it’s a stew that’s ideal for making ahead and enjoying all week long. The key ingredient? Piment d’Espelette—the regional spice known for its peppery, smoky essence. If you’re looking to master a classic dish or simply want a reliable, cozy weeknight dinner, then this recipe won’t let you down.

Heat a large skillet with oil and season the chicken with salt. Working in batches, add the chicken pieces and sear until the skin is golden in color, which should take 5 to 7 minutes. Remove the chicken to a heatproof plate.

Then reduce the heat and add the onion, bell peppers, garlic, piment d’Espelette, and salt. You’ll want to stir this once in a while so it doesn’t stick, but also let the vegetables soften. This should take 8 to 10 minutes.

At this point, increase the heat again and add the wine. Scrape up any bits on the bottom and allow those peppers and onions to absorb the wine. The liquid should reduce.

Add the tomatoes and broth and bring to a simmer. Be careful of splattering sauce and adjust the heat as needed. Place the chicken back into the skillet, skin side up, and cook until the chicken is tender and nearly falling off the bone. The sauce should also be thicker and fragrant. This should take about 30 to 40 minutes.

Stir in the chorizo and cook until it’s warmed through. Top it off with thyme and serve!

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. It’s certainly a great meal-prep dish. Make this on a Sunday night for lunch Monday and Tuesday.

#6655. Robert Pattinson Might Be the Most Fashion-Forward Bond Yet

From Sean Connery’s immaculately tailored suits in Dr. No to Daniel Craig’s thigh-bearing trunks in Casino Royale, each man who has played James Bond has brought a new aesthetic sensibility to the role. For Connery, this meant soft-shouldered Savile Row tailoring, polo shirts, and knit ties to suit the era of Ivy Style, while Roger Moore’s wardrobe of safari jackets and nylon ski suits embodied the sporty hedonism of the 1970s. In the 21st century, Daniel Craig’s Bond was built around a timely blend of Brioni, Tom Ford, and stalwart British brands that complemented the contemporary #menswear scene. Today’s news that Robert Pattinson—a longtime Dior ambassador and one of the most consistently thrilling dressers in Hollywood—has been cast as 007 suggests Bond’s most fashionable era may be yet to come.

Daniel Craig is no slouch in the clothing department, but before donning the tux for Casino Royale, he was primarily known as a stage actor with a penchant for distressed jeans and Chuck Taylor high-tops. Pattinson, meanwhile, has been the face of Dior’s menswear for a decade, during which he’s established his impeccable taste and a willingness to take big swings with his outfits—not to mention a reputation for wearing the absolute heck out of a gray suit. Now, with fellow Brit Jonathan Anderson (who cast Craig in Loewe’s quirked-up fall 2024 campaign and posted this heartwarming pic today) running the show at Dior, the stage is set for a Bond with a taste for capital-F fashion.

Tradition dictates a vibe shift whenever a new Bond is chosen, but whatever James Bond wears has an outsized impact on menswear. Pierce Brosnan’s era had structured Brioni suits and made the Omega Seamaster a star, while Daniel Craig helped cement Tom Ford’s tailoring as a red-carpet staple and juiced sales of N.Peal ribbed Army sweaters and Drake’s suede chukkas. As GQ’s Cam Wolf noted in a 2018 article about Skyfall, Daniel Craig’s Barbour jacket, sweater, jeans, and brogue boots from that film—a classic but fairly unremarkable outfit—became the aspirational template for untold numbers of men on r/malefashionadvice. A few years later, when Craig wore a Rag & Bone slim-fit henley in No Time to Die, the brand sold out of the unassuming undershirt in a matter of days.

It’s been five years since No Time to Die’s release, and it will likely be at least a couple more before Pattinson’s first outing as 007 hits screens. That’s a long wait to see how the next Bond era aesthetic comes together, but given Pattinson’s distinctive approach to fashion, it should be well worth it for the clothes alone.

#6653. Whole Wheat vs. Sourdough: Which Bread Is Healthier?

How to pick the loaf that fits your life.

Whole wheat bread used to be the gold standard of quick, healthy carbs. Unlike white bread, it uses flour milled from the entire wheat kernel, providing extra fiber and vitamins. But sourdough has exploded in popularity over the past decade, offering a seemingly more natural option made from just sourdough starter, flour, and water. Is this ancient breadmaking method healthier than whole wheat, even if it uses white flour?

As a dietitian, I see this showdown between whole wheat and sourdough all the time. People wonder if the rustic, tangy charm of sourdough beats the wholesome, fiber-packed power of whole wheat. Let’s slice into the details and figure out which loaf deserves a spot on your counter.

Whole wheat is exactly what it sounds like. This bread is made using flour from the entire wheat kernel—the bran, germ, and endosperm. Here’s what that means:

Because it includes all parts of the kernel, 100% whole wheat bread delivers fiber, essential vitamins like folate and niacin, and important minerals such as iron and magnesium. That fiber helps you feel satisfied after eating, supports digestion, and can support blood sugar management and heart health. This combination makes this particular bread a smart, nutrient-dense choice for everyday eating.

It’s a reliable, widely available, research-backed whole grain—and most Americans don’t eat the recommended servings of whole grains every day, which the USDA suggests is more than half of the grains we eat. So, choosing whole-grain bread can help people meet this recommendation.

It seems like everyone and their mother got into baking sourdough a few years ago. We all know it’s delicious, but what makes it special from a health perspective isn't just its ingredients—it’s how it is made.

Sourdough isn’t defined by a specific type of flour. You can make it with all-purpose, rye, or whole-wheat flour; some loaves use enriched/fortified flour for an extra boost of iron and B vitamins. And its magic lies in the fermentation process. Instead of commercial yeast, sourdough relies on a “starter,” which is a living mix of wild yeast and beneficial bacteria (specifically, lactobacilli).

This fermentation process does some pretty amazing things:

In a side-by-side battle, let's see which bread comes out on top:

If your primary goal is to maximize your fiber intake and get a consistent, nutrient-packed loaf, 100% whole wheat is an excellent choice.

If you're looking for a bread that’s easier to digest and offers enhanced mineral absorption, deliciously tangy sourdough is your go-to.

But it is possible to have the best of both worlds. Grab (or bake) a sourdough bread made with 100% whole wheat flour for fiber, nutrient density, and fermentation perks.

Whether you’re Team Sourdough or Team Whole Wheat, there’s one universal truth: your body, and let’s be honest, your soul, will thank you. Because we all know that carbs are good for the soul.

#6651. Princess Kate Pulls Off Two Fresh Monochrome Suits in Mumbai

Before slipping into a fabulous gown for her big night

Princess Catherine can always pull off a pristine monochrome suit, and for her tour of Mumbai, India, she brought along at least two fresh, polished sets.

This morning, Kate slipped on a bright white suit to meet the 2026 Earthshot Prize Finalists along the Arabian Sea and Mahim Bay, at the famed Bandra Worli Sea Link Promenade.

Some hours later, to attend the Children’s Earthshot Awards, Kate changed into a more colorful number: an Easter-blue suit from Gabriella Hearst. The linen set was made up of an elongated double-breasted blazer and wide-leg trousers.

The color popped on Kate, who accessorized simply with dangly Van Cleef & Arpels vintage Alhambra earrings and slipped on her same suede heels.

William also changed looks throughout the day, choosing a very nautical light-blue striped blazer paired with a white button-down for the morning, and a dark gray blazer with a sky-blue button-down for the afternoon. The bottom half of his look—dark trousers and brown shoes—remained the same.

The Prince and Princess of Wales are one day two of their official tour of Mumbai. They made the trip to attend the sixth annual Earthshot Prize Summit, which took place today.

For the big night, Kate wowed in a custom vermilion-red Anarkali gown by Indian designer Mahima, which she accessorized with Queen Elizabeth II’s fabulous emerald tassel suite—specifically the diamond-and-emerald tassel necklace and its matching drop earrings.

William, meanwhile, was dapper in a monochrome black look that included a traditional velvet Bandhgala jacket by Indian designer Manish Malhotra.

#6650. Is Jeremy Allen White Playing Wolverine? His Mutton Chops Say Yes

Marvel has filled most of the seats for its new X-Men film. Sadie Sink is Jean Grey, Kit Connor is Cyclops, Christopher Abbott is Professor X, Samara Weaving is Emma Frost, Inde Navarrette is Rogue, and Maya Boyd is Storm. But there’s still one grizzly gap in the line-up: Wolverine.

Earlier this month, Jeremy Allen White was linked with the role after insider Jeff Sneider reported that he had met with Marvel about a small part that could become much bigger later on. Nobody has confirmed that the part is Wolverine (and Sneider has since stressed that White isn’t officially in talks) but the internet did the math pretty quickly. And now there’s a smoking gun: facial hair.

While walking around the Studio City Farmers Market over the weekend (because, of course), The Social Reckoning star was spotted carrying a bouquet of flowers bigger than his torso and wearing some extremely Wolverine-y mutton chops. Normally, growing out your sideburns wouldn’t count as casting news. But when you’ve just been linked with Logan and suddenly look ready to join the X-Men, people are going to ask questions.

White would make a lot of sense. He’s 5’7”, which puts him much closer to the comic book Wolverine’s famously stocky 5’3” frame than Hugh Jackman ever was. He also spent months getting absolutely massive for The Iron Claw, so the muscle is already there. And after years of watching him play Carmy in The Bear, we know he can do angry and exhausted and permanently one minor inconvenience away from losing it. That’s basically three quarters of the Wolverine job description.

Jackman has owned the role since the first X-Men film landed in 2000. He’s played Wolverine across 10 movies, most recently returning for 2024’s Deadpool & Wolverine. His version became so definitive that it’s difficult to picture anyone else with the claws (other than the time Troye Sivan briefly had them in 2009’s X-Men Origins: Wolverine), even though the 6’2" actor looked very different from the shorter character drawn in the OG comics.

Maybe White just fancied some giant sideburns. Maybe the flowers are covering three adamantium claws. Either way, Marvel should probably give him a call—assuming it hasn’t already.

#6647. The Real Story Behind ‘Drawing Prada’

Ferdinando Verderi has long kept a London pied-à-terre as a quiet spot to rest his head while traveling between jobs, shaping campaigns for companies including Louis Vuitton, Versace, Adidas and, most prominently, Prada. Some time ago, however, his London sanctuary was invaded by a now-regular uninvited guest: a fox. “When I walk into the garden, I realize the fox doesn’t care I’m there,” he says. “I had this idea in my mind of this fox that was completely nonchalant, indifferent.”

Verderi’s garden visitor became an inspiration for one of the animated animal characters in Prada’s Holiday 2026 campaign, Drawing Prada: Animated by Hand. Created under the creative direction of Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons, with Verderi as campaign creative director, it combines live-action photography by Glen Luchford with the work of a team of traditional animators led by John Pomeroy, whose credits include Disney’s Pocahontas and Fantasia 2000. In it, Maya Hawke, Sadie Sink, Kelvin Harrison Jr., Luther Ford and Chen Haoyu encounter an assortment of illustrated creatures, from foxes and mice to bats, which covet Prada’s clothes and accessories.

The resulting films are charmingly familiar, with a fireside glow and old-school sweetness. Since their release, they have also been placed at the center of a sharply antagonistic debate about contemporary image-making. At a moment when generative artificial intelligence is transforming commercial image production, Prada foregrounded the human hand, releasing documentary footage of Pomeroy and his fellow animators at work alongside the finished campaign.

The campaign has become a reference point in the increasingly charged discussion about AI both inside and outside the fashion industry. That discussion intensified following the release of another luxury holiday animation, Dior’s Christian Dior’s Night in Color, directed by French animator Sylvain Chomet. Some viewers alleged that the film contained AI-generated imagery, pointing to apparent inconsistencies in individual frames. Chomet and producer Aton Soumache have denied using generative AI, explaining that the film was produced using traditional 2D animation, alongside automated interpolation to smooth some transitions.

On YouTube, the Prada campaign had yesterday attracted more than 3.6 million views and 57,000 likes. The comments suggest that its appeal extends beyond Prada’s core audience. “Did I just voluntarily watch an ad for a luxury brand I neither have any interest for nor can afford just because it’s art made by actual artists while we are drowning in a sea of AI? Yes, yes I did,” wrote @fruitspunchsamurai1763, in a comment that has so far been liked 6,800 times. Another viewer, @mollie1927, proposed: “Handmade art and animation is gonna become a luxury status symbol in this time of AI slop.”

When we connect on Teams to discuss the campaign, Verderi is in London with no fox visible in the garden behind him. “What’s been missing really is the why: how this came about,” he says.

Drawing Prada was first discussed in April and May, with Pomeroy brought into the process in early June to meet a demanding schedule involving thousands of individual drawings. From the outset, Verderi envisaged a campaign whose method of creation would be central to its meaning. “Can a process be emotional? Can not just the look of something, but the way it’s made, create emotion?”

The Christmas holiday season presented an appropriate setting for an experiment in storytelling using familiar, increasingly anachronistic techniques to generate feelings of warmth and childhood nostalgia. Verderi wanted to work with the tools and methods that had originally created that visual language in order to answer a question: “Can we create emotion by showing this very human, very imperfect, very inefficient, but very charming process?” He adds: “When I presented this idea, I was determined that it had to be handmade: and Mrs Prada and Raf loved the idea, completely understood the intentions, and rallied behind it.”

That decision introduced a degree of inflexibility that is alien, Verderi says, to much contemporary image production. Verderi and Luchford wrote numerous stories, repeatedly refined through Pomeroy’s assessment of what could be communicated in just 13 seconds of animation.

The campaign’s fluidity also depends on the work of specialists known as inbetweeners, who produce the drawings between the principal poses established by the lead animators. Verderi became fascinated by smear frames, deliberately distorted drawings that convey movement. “You would have a cat with five eyes, one on top of each other,” he says. Seen in isolation, such drawings might appear bizarre, but viewed in sequence, they are an expression of the animator’s craft.

The human work involved, Verderi says, gives the process its contemporary significance. Techniques once commonplace in commercial analog animation now seem extravagant in an industry accustomed to digital efficiency. “I think it’s very interesting, the idea that inefficiencies have become so rare as to have acquired a romantic feel,” he says. This decadence of labor is especially evocative in a business where human craft is a core selling point of its end product.

Verderi is reluctant to frame Drawing Prada as an anti-AI statement. “I think this is a very innovative piece that reframes an old technology for a new world,” he says. “I don’t have an ounce of nostalgic feeling toward this project that contradicts a progressive attitude of Prada.”

The documentary footage, original sketches and subsequent public discussion form part of a larger digital experience. “This project would have been very different if done 20 years ago. It wouldn’t have had the same charge. It wouldn’t have benefited from the same ecosystem around it.”

That interest in the relationship between a fashion image and its wider cultural context has long characterized Verderi’s work. As creative director of Vogue Italia from 2019 to 2021, he challenged conventions of fashion publishing with an entirely illustrated issue, a blank white cover during the pandemic and a September 2020 edition featuring 100 different covers. For Prada, one of his earliest campaigns saw advertisements printed on the paper used to wrap flowers in florists’ shops, transforming an everyday commercial material into a new advertising medium.

“The contemporary world is made of items that push it forward, and items that look back. They are equally contemporary,” he says. Something borrowed from the past can, he adds, become newly relevant when introduced into a different cultural environment.

Verderi also oversaw Prada’s Spring/Summer 2026 campaign, I, I, I, I AM PRADA, with artist Jordan Wolfson, whose uncanny digitally constructed creatures prompted discussion about the role of AI in fashion imagery. Prada said AI was used in post-production. The two campaigns offer contrasting expressions of Verderi’s interest in pushing the possibilities of a fashion image: one involving a contemporary digital aesthetic, while the other deliberately revives a traditional animation. “I like to use the word anachronistic because I don’t like the word obsolete,” he says of the older techniques. Their relevance, he adds, can be renewed through the contemporary context in which they are employed.

The current debate about AI-generated imagery demonstrates that audiences increasingly regard the provenance of an image as an integral part of its meaning — and that they are keen to debate both provenance and meaning on digital forums. Here, transparency becomes critical. Asked about the appearance of dishonesty in complex production processes, Verderi suggests the difficulty may lie in maintaining oversight. “I think more than dishonesty, it’s probably lack of control,” he says. “There are so many layers in each of these ideas that, ourselves, when we started to hear about this controversy, we just went back to every single vendor or partner and triple-checked that they were true to the premises. And they were.”

Speaking to Charlie Porter in Interview in September 2025, Miuccia Prada attributed the house’s commercial success in part to the maintenance of trust. “It’s not about performing culture, it’s about intellectual honesty,” she said. In the same conversation, Simons spoke about the designers’ desire to make clothes that are “real”, intended for human beings to wear rather than merely to admire as spectacle. More recently, backstage at Prada’s Fall/Winter 2026 show, Simons argued that in the age of AI, creative decisions must originate “from the heart, from the mind, from feeling, from our knowledge, from our respect for history and our interest in the future”.

Verderi sees these principles as central to the emotional relationship between brands and consumers. “People respond to human traits when they look at brands. They respond to traits that they can see in people,” he says.

As we chat, I wonder whether the fashion debate surrounding AI might eventually fade away in the manner of earlier controversies over initially unfamiliar technologies such as digital retouching, Photoshop, and even digital photography itself. Verderi agrees that those precedents offer comparisons, but adds: “The linear progression of technology has always seen technology as a tool,” he says. “I think what we’re talking about now is the risk of this tool becoming more than a tool, becoming really an agent of intention.”

For Verderi, the argument is unlikely to disappear as the technology becomes more familiar. “A big conversation like this, which basically is humanity versus machine, I don’t think it’s an ephemeral topic. It’s eternal.”

#6645. 40 More Million-Dollar Watches Just Sold at Auction

This is an edition of the newsletter Box + Papers, Cam Wolf’s weekly deep dive into the world of watches. Sign up here.

Back in June, I reported on the bonanza of watches crossing the million-dollar-plus mark at auction. What once felt like a unicorn price for watchmakers, auction houses, and the industry as a whole no longer feels so magical. “I joke with people that $1 million is like the new $250,000 of five years ago,” Paul Boutros of Phillips auction house said over the summer.

In just the first half of 2026, the number of million-dollar watches sold nearly eclipsed the total from all of 2025. Now, after a raft of high-profile auctions in Geneva a couple of weeks ago, the industry has set yet another record. In just the last month alone (including Monaco Legend Group, which kicked things off in late October), 40 million-dollar watches hammered, according to numbers provided by EveryWatch. That’s more sold than in any entire year before 2020.

If you’re keeping score at home, we’ve seen 133 watches sell at or above seven figures this year. And we’ve still got plenty of year left.

The question is: How much steam does the auction world have left? And what’s driving this radical spike in big-ticket timepieces?

A $10 million Patek Philippe Perpetual Calendar Chronograph ref. 2499

Mike Nouveau, WatchTok King and dealer, has told me that if more kids knew how much growth potential there is in the vintage market, they’d put down the creator-style tiny microphones and start studying reference numbers. The vintage market spiked in the middle of the pandemic, when prices on sport watch grails like the Patek Philippe Nautilus and Rolex Daytona went crypto-mode as a new wave of speculators flooded the high-end collecting scene.

But while the steel sport watch craze has cooled—or at least leveled off—the market has continued riding a remarkably durable wave, helped in part by the arrival of a previously quiet category: the insiders-only independent brands. “For many years at auction, we always said, ‘You have Patek Philippe and Rolex. What’s the third brand that can compete?’” Alexandre Ghotbi, a deputy chairman at Phillips auction house, told me in 2024 for a story on the beloved watchmaker Rexhep Rexhepi. “Today’s third brand is not a brand—it’s a genre: independent artisanal watchmakers.”

Think F.P. Journe, Berneron, Phillipe Dufour, Rexhepi’s Atelier Akrivia—companies helmed by watchmaking auteurs turning out hyper-limited runs, most of which sell out long before a perfectly-lit product photo ever hits the web. Oftentimes, the only way to get your hands on one of their wares—if you haven’t yet achieved friend-of-the-brand status—is by raising a paddle at auction.

When I asked dealer Eric Wind if he thought the indie insanity would remain strong, he was unequivocal: “At the top end, yes.” The dealer Zoe Abelson, of Graal Watches, actually believes we haven’t reached the peak yet. “I do think there's still room for the pieces that are actually rare to continue to grow in value with a continuance in new interest in collecting watches and the yearning to build the most impressive collection,” she said.

Two weekends ago, a new independent brand joined the list of million-dollar watchmakers. Sylvain Pinaud cut his teeth restoring antique watches and established his eponymous brand in 2018. He’s known for showing his work—the instrumental components of his watches are often highlighted on the dial. A unique version of his Origine, a model that only launched in 2022, sold for 1,011,200 Swiss francs (roughly $1,211,500).

Pinaud’s success is indicative of what happens to the elite independent brands that hit the big time. Compared to many of the heavyweight Swiss makers working at scale, independent watchmakers are seen as artisans who hand-produce their designs in extremely limited quantities. It’s why a watchmaker like Kari Voutilainen, considered a master of his craft, has sold more million-dollar pieces this year than many of the big fellas getting rap lyric shoutouts. “There's a growing appreciation for what these watchmakers are producing,” said Ben Horesh, EveryWatch’s CEO. “It’s great to see more independents challenging the old guard."

Look at that list above. Voutilainen ranks just after Rolex and Patek Philippe but ahead of Cartier for the most million-dollar watches sold at auction in 2026. The list is heavy on independents, including Rexhepi’s Akrivia, George Daniels, Philippe Dufour, and Vianney Halter. The real headline, though, is seeing F.P. Journe—the godfather of the indie scene—at the very top. If one area of the market doesn’t feel entirely sustainable, it’s the inferno around FPJ’s pieces. For deep-pocketed newcomers to the “hobby” of catching big-ticket whales, the Geneva-based maker has come to represent the grailiest of grails. Nearly every Journe piece that comes to auction sells for multiples of its estimate. And I mean everything: an empty watch box made for a set of FPJs sold for $230,000 at Christie’s! “The less rare—or in Journe's case, current production—pieces that get swept up in the overall market growth will slow down soon,” Abelson said. “I don't think it's sustainable; at a certain point the values will price out enough people that there should be a correction.”

A $13 million F.P. Journe Chronomètre à Résonance "Régence”

If six-figure watches were once rare, 10-million-plus pieces were true spectacles. Between 2020 and 2023, not a single watch crossed that threshold. In the last decade, from 2015 to 2025, there were just seven 10-million watches total. But with some time still on the clock, seven watches have already topped that threshold in 2026. A solid chunk of that is thanks to the wild one-of-one Daytonas that Rolex made for a charity auction—three out of the four sold for seven figures—but it’s still an astounding feat. The rest of the list is filled out by:

These days, it’s hard to find a category of watches that isn’t doing well at auction. Cartier hasn’t fallen off—in fact, the brand keeps setting records: a very cool clock known as Portico No. 4 hammered for approximately $5,768,400 at Phillips the weekend before last, becoming the most expensive Cartier ever sold in the process. Breguet is, rightfully and finally, on the rise. And after relaunching just last summer, Urban Jürgensen’s vintage pieces are hotter than ever. A super sexy pink-gold version of the brand’s Reference 2 went for 358,400 Swiss francs (about $430,000) at Sotheby’s.

To put a fine point on all this, just look at how overall sales are soaring. Last year, Phillips set the record with $83,018,538 worth of timepieces sold in a single auction. It only took 12 months to shatter that number. This month saw Phillips reset the record with a $112.3 million auction. I would say 2026 is an inflection point for the industry…if I didn’t anticipate that we’ll be back here talking about even more record-setting sales every year for the foreseeable future.

#6642. How Tecovas Is Taking Western Mainstream

For CEO David Lafitte, Tecovas can outlast cowboycore. In fact, he believes Westernwear isn’t a trend at all.

“There is this cultural zeitgeist going on, and I think we’re kind of in the bullseye of it, so that’s a good thing,” Lafitte says. Cowboycore peaked in 2024 on the heels of Beyoncé’s Cowboy Carter album, Pharrell Williams’s Western-inspired Fall/Winter 2024 Louis Vuitton collection and the series finale of Yellowstone. Tecovas, which specializes in cowboy boots and was founded in 2015 by Paul Hedrick in Austin, benefited from the boom.

Now, Tecovas has surpassed $400 million in trailing 12-month revenue, marking almost 40% year-over-year growth — one of the strongest stretches in the company’s history. When Lafitte joined the company in 2022, revenue was around $150 million. The brand now has 69 stores across the US, from Austin to cities like Boston, New York, Miami, and LA.

“We want to make sure that we stay authentically Western, and we can’t worry about the trends. If we try to move around too much, we’re going to lose our DNA and our anchor. There are a lot of people in the middle of the country for whom this is their lifestyle. It’s not a fad or a trend.”

Eleven years in, Tecovas has cowboy boots down pat. Now, the brand is looking at how to grow its Westernwear offering without falling into the traps of fleeting trends or diluting its original USP: well-made, authentic Western footwear at an accessible price point. Though the brand intends to remain footwear-led, as Lafitte puts it, it’s also investing more in men’s shirting, womenswear and accessories. Belts and wallets have been doing especially well, he notes. Still, the brand’s boots — most of which sit in the $300-400 range — remain the entry point to the brand. “People are still coming in for the boot,” he says.

11 years in, Tecovas is taking the western aesthetic mainstream.

Tecovas’s ethos is best expressed in-store, Lafitte argues. Physical retail accounts for 60% of the brand’s revenue. “It’s a product that I think is important for people to see, touch and smell as soon as you walk in our doors,” he says. It’s also where shoppers then encounter the brand’s wider range. “We’ve got a lot of traffic in our stores, so when we come up with compelling products, we’re able to showcase that and don’t need to necessarily spend a lot of marketing dollars on shirts or other things — because we have that audience coming into our doors,” Lafitte says. He points to the Monterrey slip-on loafer: not traditionally Western, not necessarily what you think of when you think of Tecovas, but the style still does $7 million in annual revenue. And many buyers likely already have a pair of Tecovas boots at home.

Tecovas sits at an interesting intersection in the US fashion ecosystem. As European luxury brands are scrambling to increase their presence in the country’s southern and southwestern states, Tecovas is going in the opposite direction. States like Texas, Colorado, and Tennessee are Tecovas’s strongholds. Now, the brand is pushing into fast-growing regions including the Southeast, Midwest, and West Coast.

With four funding rounds totaling $130 million, Tecovas is well positioned for growth. Here’s how the brand is making the cowboy aesthetic mainstream — without falling into the trappings of the often derided “concrete cowboy”.

Lafitte is conscious that, even as the brand grows, authenticity is key to sustained growth and success. That the Western aesthetic has become more mainstream has cleared the way. “People are seeing that to have a pair of cowboy boots in their closet doesn’t mean that ‘I’m just going to a costume party’. You can wear it with other things that may not be Western,” the CEO says. “We need to make sure we stay in our lane, and we need to make it cool. That’s part of what our job is as a steward of this genre: to make sure it’s cool and authentic.”

This logic has informed Tecovas’s approach to retail. The brand held off on branching out into wholesale until 2024, almost 10 years into its founding. But it was a priority for Lafitte. “If you’re not in a multi-brand format and your product’s not there, you’re going to be out of sight, out of mind,” he says.

But the approach was careful, and started with independent Western stores. “They cater to a very authentic Western consumer,” Lafitte says. “Our goal is to create an ecosystem. We almost want to drive traffic to their stores, so we’ll do joint billboards and do some marketing tactics that drive consumers to their stores to look for Tecovas products.” The goal isn’t necessarily to then bring them to Tecovas directly, he says, though this would be the dream. “I don’t think that’s going to happen,” he concedes. “These consumers have been shopping with their favorite Western retailer for many, many years. So that’s not the point.”

The brand keep close ties with independent western retailers.

The point, instead, is to stay in step with the brand’s beginnings while expanding beyond specialty Western retailers. The brand entered 20 additional Nordstrom locations in the spring, and is now in a total of 35 doors. It’s intentionally measured, the CEO says — he doesn’t want Tecovas to be everywhere, lest the brand risk overdistribution. “We want to go with a little bit of a scarcity model, so you can’t find us on every corner of every city and get overexposed.” The goal of these select fashion accounts, he adds, is to reach a customer they may not otherwise; and to establish a presence in regions where opening a store might not make sense due to limited traffic.

“The traditional Western retailers give us that authenticity, the authentic consumers that are buying the brand,” Lafitte says. “And places like Nordstrom that are a little bit more fashion, that may be expanding the tent a little bit more, but they too want us to make sure we’re authentic, the real deal — and not some concrete cowboy, or whatever you want to call it.”

To meet these consumers where they are, Tecovas is tapping into the modern brand-collab playbook, with other brands, sports teams, and musical artists. To Lafitte, anybody can be a Tecovas customer, because anyone can integrate a cowboy boot into their wider wardrobe. He’s banking on a high proportion of music and F1 fans being fans of his brand, too. But, Lafitte insists, its approach is reserved. “I’d rather have very good partners that sort of align with our craftsmanship and ethos and then do them very well and not try and rush them.”

The latest launch is a tie-up with Los Angeles-based Anine Bing that includes shoes, belts and cowboy hats. A single weekend delivered the sales and unit movement originally forecast for the month, according to the brand, with several styles selling out. Still, the goal for these collabs isn’t to drive revenue so much as awareness, the CEO notes. “It’s more a brand heat moment and awareness gain,” he says. “We’re getting exposed to a consumer base that might not otherwise know Tecovas.”

The brand takes a similar approach to the sports it taps into; recent partnerships include NASCAR and PGA golf. Neither are the most obvious picks for a Westernwear brand, but there’s a method to the madness. “We’ll test with some upper funnel work, and when we see a pretty good return on that ad spend, then we know that’s an area that we’ve got consumers in that demographic,” Lafitte says. NASCAR driver Ryan Blaney was already a fan, which made him a good fit, he adds. “Consumers are very smart, so we make sure we’re partnering with people who would be wearing the brand regardless of whether we’re giving them product or writing them a check.”

The Anine Bing collab outperformed expectations.

Tecovas is choosey about which brands it collaborates with, and when.

Music works in the same vein. Tecovas has partnered with country music stars including Ella Langley (it sponsored her “Choosin’ Texas” music video) and Ryan Bingham (it sponsored his, as well as Langley’s, tours earlier this year). But country ties aren’t the only marker of a good partnership. Lafitte points to Noah Kahan, who he met when the singer came into the South Congress store. “He loves Tecovas and brought his team in there,” he says. “When you see him at his Dallas concert, I think probably 80% of that crowd was wearing boots,” he adds. This combo made the partnership a no-brainer.

“The interesting thing is that Western is resonating across a lot of these different areas, whether it’s music, food, race car driving — F1,” he says. “The drivers love coming to Austin, and that’s been a fun thing to partner with a lot of their drivers.”

Tecovas’s sports and music activations thus far may have centered on the US, but the brand has international ambitions. For Fall 2026, Tecovas sold its first international stock to German multibrand retailer Zalando. When we speak, Lafitte has just returned from Paris, where he met with a handful of retailers including Le Bon Marché. He first met their team when they visited the brand’s Soho, New York store. The plan is to lean on local European distributors, rather than rush to open a European HQ, the CEO adds. “We’ll choose distribution partners and do it in an asset-light manner. We’ll start with wholesale, and then, over time, open a couple of doors with a partner over there.”

Down the line, the goal is to go public, Lafitte says, though he doesn’t have a set timeline for this. (It won’t be in the near-term, he adds, since everything is AI-focused at the minute.) “We want to work toward that knowing that we need to lay the groundwork to be an independent company,” he says. “I don’t want to skimp on, say, ‘we don’t need a distribution center because it’s likely we'll get bought by X, Y, or Z’. We’ve got to make sure that, operationally, we’re laying the groundwork to keep up with the demand.”

“The brand’s got broad shoulders,” he says. “I think we can be the steward of the West, but we can also, I think, launch a lot of Western-adjacent type products.”

#6641. Best Harrington Jackets 2026: Preppy, Punk, and Ultra-Functional

Few jackets have managed to cross as many style tribes—and decades—as the Harrington. In fact, if you were to enroll in Classic Menswear 101, the Harrington jacket would be a prerequisite. The transitional season staple—a favorite of Elvis, James Dean, Steve McQueen, and every member of The Clash—is constantly found across lookbooks and style Instagram accounts, because it does so many things so well.

For one, it's incredibly practical: Water-resistant, pocket-forward, lightly insulating, and ever-adaptable to the day's conditions thanks to its full-zip and collar. But the almost-cropped length—and popped collar, if you so dare—is also a style swerve that makes every wearer feel one dose cooler than they did before. No wonder it’s been embraced over the decades by everyone from golfers to preppies to A-Listers and punks.

The original Harrington—a Baracuta G9—is still available almost a century on from its release, and still excellent. But if you’re looking to broaden your horizons, today’s Harrington jackets aren’t resting on their laurels. Below, the standout versions worth adding to your rotation before we’re into parka territory.

The classic Baracuta G9 golf jacket is as British as beans on toast. This is the original tartan-lined, ribbed-cuff Harrington, the jacket you picture when you think of Steve McQueen or Paul Newman, and the brand that insider-y menswear favorites like Engineered Garments and Noah have collaborated with when they wanted to make Harringtons of their own. Baracuta got its start making raincoats for other brands—Burberry included—before branching out with its own designs, and the G9 is still made in England today. Crafted from a water-resistant cotton-poly blend, and featuring the signature Fraser tartan lining and iconic umbrella back yoke (which keeps rain off your back while letting air circulate) it really doesn't get any better than this.

Uniqlo delivers a whole Harrington jacket without sacrificing anything, and in fact saves you some precious dollars along the way. We’re talking a slightly cropped, slightly relaxed silhouette, a touch of stretch, classic slant pockets and even a genre-affirming plaid lining. And while it’s not water-resistant like some other options, it makes up for it with a durable cotton fabric that’ll dry off in no time, and still keep you protected from a few unforeseen raindrops. If you’re after the workaday Harrington aesthetic without spending a lot, this one gets the job done and then some.

If you're looking to purchase a Harrington jacket that'll serve you for seasons to come, but don't particularly want to spend half your rent check on it, J.Crew's faithful take on the Harrington is as true as it gets. And this is no compromise pick: It still comes with plenty of details to get excited about, from the handsome, buttoned interior chest pocket to the warming full lining, leather zip tag, and 10-ounce cotton twill that's already been washed a few times by the brand to make it feel lived-in and well-loved from the jump. It also comes in multiple colors, partly because J.Crew is confident you'll be back for more. Oh, and if you want a winterized Harrington, check out the corduroy iteration, which also has a quilted, Primaloft-stuffed lining.

A pared-down, easygoing take on the classics, Quince’s Harrington strikes a smart balance of polished and sporty, without even the faintest fuss. Offered in khaki, navy and black, this one is the modern minimalist’s Harrington—a clean, contemporary style that does what a staple should do: make you look good without causing a scene. Oh, and that twill outer will break in wonderfully over time, in case you were wondering.

One of the best parts about a Harrington Jacket is that the idea is fully formed. As such, it can be a hard style to riff on, mostly because the source material is so dialed in that it’s often best to leave well enough alone. Ernest W. Baker designers Reid Baker and Inês Amorim, however, couldn’t care less about that tradition and went nuclear with this one: it’s a true-blue Harrington complete with a cropped fit, ribbing at the waist, barrel cuffs and a point collar. But then the inclusion of a leather collar and Western-inspired yoke details in lieu of the classic back vent turns it into something else entirely, without changing the fit one bit. And they nailed it. It’s transformative without being performative, utterly distinct and eminently familiar and, most improbably, contradiction free.

This has most of the trappings of your classic Harrington—stand collar, cool back vent, functional cuffs—but it also eschews the classic ribbed hem for a cinched waist, which adds a little bit of drama to the notoriously no-drama silhouette.

Todd Snyder often plays it straight—Ivy-ish classics with just the right details. Here, they’ve ditched part of the trad playbook and leaned into the modern with water-resistant tech cotton-nylon blend, but it's also a bit cropped and fits very much like you'd remember. And now, it's also on sale.

A Harrington is already pretty pared down, but Barbour trimmed every ounce of fat on this one, leaving us with a slightly longer silhouette, all the *essential* bells and whistles and a brown cotton outer that gets to take center stage.

We could get into the buttery leather collar or the insane Italian wool serge fabric that Wanze deployed on this stunner, or even lock in on that two-way RiRi zipper, but that'd be burying the lede because you're not going to get a red like this anywhere else.

We wouldn't typically include different versions of the same style in one guide, but when our Best Overall version also comes in a buttery suede, exceptions are made.

Stone Island traffics in the unexpected, so, in a way, it should come as no surprise that the Italian label's take on the classic is a Gonzo, teched-out one—one made with a garment-dyed fabric that's been treated with an "anti-drop" finish.

The Harrington is an icon of preppy style, so of course Ralph Lauren has blessed us with its lightweight cotton take, complete with the signature Polo pony on the chest. It’s preppy, American, and exactly the kind of jacket your kids will proudly say “This used to be my Dad’s” about.

You might not think of a Harrington as a "winter jacket," but hear us out: it can be. This Percival joint, for instance, is made out of a hardy birdseye wool blend that will hold up to some chilly weather and layer up nicely when calling things "chilly" is understatement.

The funniest thing about the Harrington? It wasn’t originally called a Harrington at all. The original—and, as you've read above, our favorite—was called the “G9.” It was cooked up by Baracuta in 1937 in rainy old Manchester, England, as a golf jacket—the “G” stands for “golf.” (The idea was to make a garment that could take a beating from British weather without cramping your backswing.) But the jacket earned its now-iconic name thanks to Rodney Harrington, a character from the 1960s TV show Peyton Place, who wore one so often that the name just stuck.

The traditional Harrington jacket fits close to the shoulders and chest, but still has enough room for a full range of arm motion—it is a golfing style, after all. The hem then typically sits either at the waist, or for a more stylized look, just above the belt line. It should be easy to spot from product shots whether the designer in question has stuck to this traditional shape, or elongated the style a touch. From that point, the only thing left to consider is whether you plan to wear it over thick sweaters, or lighter T-shirts and shirts. If it's the former, you may want to consider sizing up.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6640. From Nike to Selfridges: GTA VI Is Coming for Fashion

On a chilly morning last week outside Selfridges, gamers formed a line under the pink glow of a huge neon sign decorating the exterior: I <3 VC.

Vice City is the fictional, Miami-inspired setting for Grand Theft Auto VI, but its impact in the real world is already astronomical. Billed as the most anticipated entertainment launch in history, the video game finally goes on sale this Thursday, with pre-order sales already shooting past $1 billion, breaking records for PlayStation and Xbox.

The London department store is capitalizing on that energy with a GTA VI-themed pop-up, featuring a 60-piece merchandise collection that includes £8 Vice City keychains, £50 hot pink logo tees, and a patch-covered varsity jacket for £2,500. Sounds pricey, until you spot the sky-blue supercar, modeled after the in-game Grotti Cheetah, parked on the ground floor: yours for £1 million.

Charles Hambro, co-founder and CEO of Geeiq, a data platform that has worked with brands including Gucci and L’Oréal to build strategies in the gaming world, says that now that video games are downloadable, the physical aspect of the activation takes on a new charm. “It’s a fantastic moment for GTA fans to come together and meet in real life and celebrate the title and the game and the launch,” he says. “Now that everything’s digital, it’s wise for Rockstar [the publisher behind the game] to hold onto that physicality.”

The partnership is a win for the department store, too. “The response has been extraordinary,” says Rebecca Warburton, Selfridges’s marketing and experiences director, who worked with GTA’s publisher Rockstar Games on the launch. “[There’s] a real sense of excitement for the collaboration. It’s been fantastic to see the GTA community join us to experience it for themselves, bringing a new audience and energy to our stores.”

The pop-up is part of a raft of major retail activations that Rockstar is rolling out for the launch, which include a Nike collaboration with Travis Scott on a GTA VI-themed Air Force sneaker, and a pair of matte black sunglasses with reflective blue lenses by Oakley that are part of a merchandise box sold on Rockstar’s website.

Emy Cies, Women in Games ambassador and projects administrator at the Fashion Innovation Agency at London College of Fashion, says that these kinds of physical products help widen the appeal of both the game and the brands or platforms that get involved. “Because GTA is so huge, it has that pull between consumers that are absolutely going to play the game and then consumers who are in it for the cultural wave,” she says.

For Adam Cheung, style writer at British GQ, the overlap between gamers and fashion fans may mean a more engaged consumer base, but the product itself still needs to stand up. “A collaboration gives them a way to bring those interests together, but they’ll still have opinions about the product,” he says. “The association with GTA might get their attention, but the design and price will help determine whether they actually buy it.”

When images from the game were released in the run-up to the launch, netizens quickly pointed out similarities between real-life brands and the clothes characters were wearing in-game. The list includes a white Birkin-like handbag, Rolex and Audemars Piguet watches, monogrammed Gucci-esque sweatpants, Chrome Hearts jeans, and a hoodie that recalls Versace’s black-and-gold Barocco print.

The GTA franchise has long parodied fashion. Jokey-sounding brands like Güffy (a nod to Stüssy), Le Chien (perfume that bears a resemblance to Chanel No. 5) and Ferruccio Tucci (its logo similar to Massimo Dutti) have appeared in previous titles in the series. “GTA has always excelled at satire and social commentary, and fashion and style is part of that,” says Jian DeLeon, men’s fashion director at Nordstrom. “It does a good job of fleshing out a world and giving players who care about style the option to express themselves accordingly.”

Julie Zerbo, a New York-based lawyer and founder of The Fashion Law, says these spoofs highlight an interesting tension at the heart of luxury marketing. “Luxury brands work to maintain exclusivity, but their cultural influence depends, in part, on widespread recognition,” she says. “The more recognizable a brand becomes, the easier it is for others to reference, imitate, or parody. That visibility can be commercially valuable, even when the brand has no control over how it is being represented.”

This lack of control is not necessarily a negative thing. “Appearing in a game this big could introduce them to people who haven’t paid much attention before, especially with labels that are more familiar within fashion circles,” says Cheung.

Zerbo says that inclusion in the game, even as a parody, is a measure of a brand’s real-world relevance. “[These brands] communicate certain qualities to consumers, which makes them obvious subjects for a game that draws heavily on popular culture and consumerism,” she says. “In some cases, being recognizable enough to be referenced without permission is itself evidence of the value of the brand.” Neither Rockstar nor the parodied brands replied to a request for comment.

With the in-game fashion representing its own socioeconomic system that ranges from thrift stores to luxury boutiques, players graduate from tank tops and cargo pants to Italian suiting and loafers as they expand their influence in the city’s criminal underworld. GTA VI also introduces the franchise’s first female protagonist in the form of Lucia Caminos, meaning we can expect to see plenty of options for in-game womenswear. “It opens up the game a lot more [in terms of fashion], so I think that will be massive,” says Cies.

Though there is precedent for in-game brand collaborations (GTA Online featured clothes by the Polish brand MISBHV back in 2021), product placement is rare in Rockstar’s games. But in the same way that GTA borrows the language of fashion to create in-game parodies, brands can also co-opt the aesthetic of GTA. Gucci, for instance, released a campaign in February that featured AI imagery of a couple sitting on a car bonnet in front of a neon pink Gucci sign. The visuals were unmistakably Vice City, and a neat way for the brand to tap into the zeitgeist.

Social teaser campaign ahead of the Gucci Primavera campaign in February 2026.

Hambro also references recent images posted to BMW’s Instagram that feature illustrations that draw on the pink, palm tree-heavy aesthetic of the game. “That’s a brand that has sort of managed to circumnavigate; they’re involved without getting involved,” he says. “The core point is that there’s going to be a lot of people playing this game, and a lot of those people are going to be firmly within the target market of a lot of these companies. The question is, how are you going to engage with them?”

Dazed saw the game’s potential early. For its Fall 2026 issue, the magazine collaborated with Rockstar to put GTA VI’s dual protagonists on the cover. “The anticipation surrounding GTA VI was unlike anything we’d seen in gaming or entertainment,” says Danil Boparai, Dazed’s content strategy director. “We knew how hungry the game’s fanbase was for new information. We wanted to create something that would reward that anticipation while introducing the game to audiences who might not traditionally engage with gaming media.” When the story went live, it became the most-read article on the Dazed website in a decade.

As gaming has become more mainstream, perceptions of its audience have shifted. “The cultural relevance of gaming is something that no longer needs explaining to brands,” says Hambro. “The preconception of who the gamer was in 2007 probably would’ve been an acne-ridden young boy in their mother’s basement. And now it’s Travis Scott.”

Though GTA VI will be limited to single-player at release, it is expected that it will eventually expand into a multiplayer online experience. GTA Online, the multiplayer component of GTA V, reportedly earns over $1 million in daily revenue with 10 million weekly active users. “For Gen Z and Gen Alpha, their version of socializing is going into a game together and chatting and playing and hanging out,” says Hambro. “They just might happen to be doing it in Gucci Town in Roblox, or on GTA Online.”

For many players, gaming is also becoming less about playing as a ready-made character and more about creating one that reflects their own taste and identity. According to a recent report by Dentsu, 65–70% of Gen Z and millennials who play games say they can express themselves more easily in games than in real life. With games like GTA VI offering increasingly sophisticated options for customization, clothing becomes a way for players to construct and communicate who they are. “It’s [about] creating a world where identity isn’t just something you select, but something you actively shape through your choices,” says Boparai.

Will the aesthetics we see in the game translate IRL? DeLeon is skeptical. “I don’t really think there will be a huge effect on how people dress in the real world, but I’m sure there will be parallels with the kind of brands and clothes that are glorified today and the kinds of things we’ll see available in-game,” he says.

Cheung has budgeted a full eight hours to play the game as soon as it launches at midnight. “I’ll probably spend much longer choosing the clothes than I need to,” he says.
