#6639. Loaded Mashed Potatoes

Mashed potatoes are a classic side dish that can make almost any meal better. They’re creamy, fluffy, and nearly perfect…nearly. When thinking of how to improve on a dish already so close to perfection, I decided to go back to the basics. What’s the best kind of potato? A loaded baked potato. With this in mind, I combined the two superstar spuds into one glorious dish. In it, light, airy mashed potatoes are topped with all of the classic baked potato fillings—cheddar cheese, chives, bacon, and sour cream—for a dish that truly embodies the best of both worlds.

The beauty of these potatoes is that they can go with any number of dinners. Serve them alongside your favorite protein—chicken, steak, pork chops, the world is your oyster—or alongside a few lighter sides like any of our green salads, caramelized Brussels sprouts, or roasted green beans.

Any leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for 3 to 4 days. If you haven’t already added the toppings, store them separately. Whatever you do, don’t let leftovers go to waste. We’ve got plenty of leftover mashed potato recipes to make sure you get the most out of the special spuds.

#6637. John Mulaney Wore Joe DiMaggio’s Watch to Host 'Saturday Night Live'

Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.

Between sniffing out paternal autism and perfecting his Robert F. Kennedy impression, you may have noticed that John Mulaney was wearing an extraordinary watch while hosting Saturday Night Live this weekend. It’s a beauty—a gold vintage Patek Philippe with swoopy Breguet numerals—but its backstory is even more impressive. On December 12, 1948, New York Yankees legend Joe DiMaggio purchased this timepiece and owned it until his death in 1999.

The Patek Philippe, a ref. 130 circa 1947, is already a rare bird before you add in its Joltin’ Joe provenance. The model is one of just 180 made in yellow gold with Breguet numerals, and only 55 with this same combination have ever reached the secondary market. In late October, dealer Eric Wind of Wind Vintage put this specific watch up for sale with a $1.2 million asking price. “I think it’s the greatest Patek that’s known and tied to any athlete,” Wind told Robb Report last month.

For his seventh time hosting SNL, Mulaney came to Wind in search of “an important watch,” the dealer explains now. After surveying Wind’s entire catalog, the comedian landed on this piece, whose ties to a legendary New Yorker felt right for helming one of the city’s most hallowed institutions. To be clear, Mulaney only borrowed the watch for the show, which means its legend will have only grown by the time it reaches an eventual buyer. Talk about an illustrious provenance: A DiMaggio-owned Patek that also appeared on Saturday Night Live. “It was a very special moment and another cool moment of history for this important Patek Philippe,” Wind says.

As a known history buff and devoted baseball fan, the watch likely appealed to Mulaney on several levels. But its eggshell-hued dial also happened to go perfectly with the brown suit Mulaney sported during his opening monologue. “John has classic styling,” Wind says, “and the Joe DiMaggio Patek Philippe was the chef’s kiss on his wrist.”

Over the past several years, Mulaney has emerged as one of Hollywood’s most prolific and tasteful watch collectors. He is an eager and omnivorous admirer, bouncing between his beloved Rolex Air-King, loud Chopard chronographs, and glamorous Grand Seikos.

Mulaney, styled by Michael Fisher, wearing Cavour

During our watch-focused interview last May, Mulaney told me that he steers away from more obvious models like your garden-variety Rolex Submariner. “I don’t ask any questions about it, I know what it is,” he explained. “And I’m just more interested in watches that [are a little more] mysterious.” As an example, Mulaney specifically referenced a Patek Philippe Calatrava his wife Olivia Munn bought him.

The DiMaggio Patek is full of intrigue. The watch obviously has important provenance, but it’s historic on its own accord, too. The ref. 130 is named for the movement inside, known as the Calibre 130. That engine was the basis for Patek’s 1518, the first serially produced watch to combine a perpetual calendar and chronograph.

Funnily enough, this isn’t the first Mulaney, DiMaggio, and SNL crossover. In his 2018 special Kid Gorgeous at Radio City, the comedian explained what it was like working with famous SNL hosts during his time as a staff writer. “It’d be like if you went into your childhood bedroom and Joe DiMaggio was sitting there,” Mulaney quipped. “Yeah, he’s Joe DiMaggio, he’s a legend, he had sex with Marilyn Monroe, but only you know where the bathroom is.” And only Mulaney has had DiMaggio’s watch on his wrist, for now.

#6636. Holiday Campaigns: Can Luxury’s Hand-Drawn Holiday Campaigns Really Rebuff AI?

That’s the message brands are sending this holiday season, as luxury turns to hand-drawn illustrations and stop-motion animation for its batch of festive holiday campaigns.

As audiences filled theaters to watch animation studio Laika’s Wildwood, which ended with close-up clips of (literal) human hands crafting the puppets featured in the film, a host of luxury brands released holiday campaigns in step with this emphasis on human craftsmanship.

Prada got in first before Halloween with a holiday campaign for which the brand commissioned a group of artists led by cinematic animator John Pomeroy (known for his work at Walt Disney Animation Studios and Sullivan Bluth Studios, which he co-founded). Dior followed suit with a holiday film directed by Oscar-nominated animator Sylvain Chomet. Loewe released a collection in partnership with Tim Burton, an interpretation of his seminal The Nightmare Before Christmas, with a documentary about Burton’s work accompanying. Rimowa created miniature worlds inside its suitcases, all done by hand.

All of the campaigns placed emphasis on human touch — as did the communication surrounding them. “A Prada fantasy, created by hand,” Prada’s release read, citing inspiration “from the human core of storytelling at the heart of the holiday season”, celebrating hand-drawn illustration for its anachronism and romanticism. Loewe emphasized the film’s handmade puppets and handcrafted sets, and likened this to the brand’s own relationship to craft. It’s trickled down the fashion funnel, with brands from Pamela Anderson’s skincare brand Sonsie to Barbour tapping this technique.

Prada tapped animator John Pomeroy to lead its “Drawing Prada: Animated by Hand” campaign.

This was Rimowa’s fifth year collaborating with artists for its holiday campaign, most of which have been 2D animations. This year, the brand wanted to level up, introducing handcrafted miniature worlds from clay, paper, felt and wood. “From a technical point of view, it was quite challenging to go from a 2D animation to creating a full 3D world with puppets,” says CMO Mathieu Plenier: over 30 artists, about 200 hours of work that went into its creation, plus a week filming across two film stages to make the films. Many of this year’s campaigns cite similarly lengthy production processes.

For Prada, this process was part of the draw. “The idea was to celebrate and display a creative process that would in itself create a sense of wonder,” a Prada spokesperson tells Vogue Business, noting that hand-drawn animation felt like the best way to do so because of its sense of touch and association with craft. Pomeroy was a no-brainer because of his deep understanding of “old school” 2D animation, they add. “John has described animation as a collaborative art form that takes many hands and many hours to complete, and it is because of that collaboration that animation is a marvelous endeavor.”

“It’s a universally beloved, nostalgic approach to signaling ‘we’re human, we believe in human creativity’ and to position the brand as anti-AI,” says Michael Scanlon, chief creative officer at creative studio Chandelier Creative, of the influx of illustrated and animated campaigns this season.

To Ariella Starkman, founder and creative director of creative production company Starkman & Associates, it’s less a response to AI itself than the anxiety the tech induces. “They are a response to a larger cultural anxiety about what AI represents: the coldness, the automation, the one-size-fits-all approach, mixed with a very real fear of losing our jobs and feeling replaceable,” she says. “Deeply spooky.”

Rimowa’s holiday films were made in collaboration with animation studio Studio Linguini.

The campaign showcases the journeys toward whatever destination its characters are heading.

These fears aren’t without basis. This year, brands have leaned into ‘effort signaling’ with their marketing, from edible art to hand-drawn illustrations, to indicate to their consumers that they are putting time and care into their creative. While appealing to shoppers’ emotions, effort signaling fails to alleviate these very real concerns Starkman highlights, about the state of the world they’re living and shopping in. One anonymous creative director, who runs the account Dank Art Director Memes, leveled a similar critique at this year’s crafty holiday campaigns, flagging the disjuncture between campaigns designed to “humanwash” their image after a year of layoffs and high-speed AI adoption.

As a marketing mechanism, these crafty campaigns are effective — when done right. But the state of the world into which luxury brands are releasing this content places an onus on these businesses to foster and embrace creativity behind the scenes as they do in their communications.

Brands positioning themselves as meticulous about craft by commissioning artists is nothing new, notes Quentin Jones, illustrator and founder of House of Quentin Jones. “People have been drawn to tactile, handmade imagery online for a long time. When I graduated in 2012, brands were already commissioning me to make beauty campaigns for digital platforms rather than working with traditional photographers, because they knew people would stop and look at something where they could feel the human touch,” she says. But, she observes, the prevalence of overly polished AI work has heightened the instinct toward the artist’s hand.

“It’s a reaction to the sameness of digital worlds,” Scanlon agrees. “Hand-drawn and stop motion animation have a certain kind of imperfection that makes you feel. It triggers an emotion, and I think a lot of brands are struggling to emotionally connect right now.”

For Starkman, this offering of nostalgia — “like cartoons on a Sunday morning when you have no school the next day” — is telling. “The holiday season is one of the most commercially significant periods of the year for many brands, so it’s very interesting — and telling — that they’re leading with feeling rather than product,” she says. “Brands are realizing that making people feel something is just as important as getting them to buy something.” Starkman recently wrapped a campaign for a major luxury brand where one of the main requests was to create something that made you feel something, she says.

Tim Burton illustrating his original Nightmare Before Christmas characters.

Loewe licensed Tim Burton’s original illustrations for the collection.

“There’s something very special about animation, particularly at Christmas. It connects us to childhood and a shared imagination,” says Elisa Valenzuela, illustrator and founder of motion studio Studio Convergences. “It allows even the most serious and demanding luxury houses to embrace fantasy, humor and a certain lightness.”

This was at the core of Rimowa’s campaign, Plenier says. “With this campaign, we wanted to connect the holiday with human emotions, thinking about a more enjoyable, struggle-free life. Blending the tangible with the imaginative, the campaign invites viewers to celebrate life’s simple daily pleasures.” The idea then is that gifting a Rimowa suitcase will “feel like gifting an invitation to travel and explore new worlds”, he adds.

For its holiday campaign, Scottish handbag brand Strathberry tapped stop-motion artist Alina Golovlova for the fifth time; and her second holiday campaign. “Making by hand is at the core of our brand, so partnering with artists and craftspeople is hugely important to us in any creative project,” says co-founder Leeanne Hundleby, who was especially drawn to felt stop motion for how highly specialized it is. “We wanted to champion the patience and skill it takes to make something truly by hand.”

A still from Strathberry’s three-part series with stop motion artist Alina Golovlova.

Over the past year, Valenzuela has noted growing enthusiasm for animation, craft, stop motion and images that, she says, embrace imperfection. “What’s slightly paradoxical is that so many brands seem to be embracing these techniques at the same time,” she says. “A desire for individuality is becoming a collective trend.” It’s not necessarily a bad thing, she says, noting that this is often how creative movements evolve.

Still, Scanlon hopes to see brands venture into an array of hand-crafted techniques, not solely animation. “Anti-AI approaches don’t need to be so obvious. Animation is an incredible, timeless craft, but it also feels like an easy route for a brand. You can see the strategy on the sleeve,” he says. “The world needs more and other kinds of practical magic. Stagecraft, surrealism, handmade spectacle.”

For all the brand comms about the time and effort that go into these campaigns, they’re not without scrutiny at a moment when audiences are hyper-aware of the potential for AI augmentation.

Dior’s film, for one, was not met with the reception the brand might have hoped for. Audiences fast pointed out flaws in the film they believed to stem from AI use: a sixth finger on a character’s hand; glitches between frames. Commentators were quick to hop on their soapboxes to drag Dior for promoting the film as hand-drawn. Chomet told Variety that the film did not use generative AI, but used automated interpolation in a “very small part” of the process. Dior did not respond to requests for comment.

For all of the online warriors’ grievances, some illustrators are unconvinced by the uproar. “I find this debate interesting, but also rather sad, because it risks overshadowing the work and talent of the artist involved,” Valenzuela says. Traditional animation involves production time that can’t be compressed, she says, noting that the time it takes to draw, build sets or animate objects frame by frame doesn’t always align with commercial production schedules. “I think it’s a shame if the occasional use of AI is enough to call an entire artistic project into question.”

Jones doesn’t believe it’s a matter of handmade versus AI. “I see nothing wrong with an image-maker using AI as one of their tools, much as we use Photoshop, After Effects or Premiere. It’s another way of getting an idea out of your head and into the world,” she says. The key is not to use the tech in the creation of the artwork itself. “So much of the magic happens in the process of making.”

For Prada, though the starting point was “the human core of storytelling”, the brand is under no illusions about the context into which the campaign was released. “We can understand why people are looking closely at this concept with AI in mind, particularly given the wider conversation around AI and creative work at the moment. What is interesting for us is the degree of attention people are paying to craft and the creative process, and we think that’s a positive conversation to be having,” the spokesperson says, adding that Prada didn’t use the tech in the campaign’s creation. “We are very comfortable being transparent about that process.”

Anyone working with handmade elements today does also need to be digitally fluent — especially when the work is ultimately going to be consumed digitally, Jones argues. “It’s about having the taste and skill to use everything at your disposal without letting the technology dictate the aesthetic,” she says. “What people are craving isn’t necessarily the absence of technology, but the presence of a human being. We need to preserve both the human touch and the human intention behind the work.”

Looking ahead, Starkman is acutely aware of how “terrifyingly good” AI will get at replicating craft, human imperfection, and all the visual cues we currently associate with ‘authentic’ creative expression, she says. “What happens when we can no longer tell the difference? If something looks handmade and makes us feel something, does it matter whether a human actually made it?” she asks. “I think it does, but I also think we’re going to have to get much better at explaining why.”

Perhaps the why comes down to what’s going on behind the scenes, beyond the holidays: not just the painstaking hours of crafting a stop-motion animation, but at the brands commissioning these artistic works in the first place. “It all has to come from a truth in their product, their organization, and how the brand approaches creativity,” Scanlon says.

Take Hermès, which was Valenzuela’s first-ever animation client back in 2018 — back when AI was, to the average person, more of a lofty sci-fi trope than a sweeping threat to one’s livelihood. “They gave me my start in this field, and I think they’ve demonstrated for years how collaborating with artists and their distinctive creative worlds can beautifully express a house’s values,” she says. “It’s essential today to preserve our ability to dream, experiment, make mistakes and surprise ourselves. Whether we’re fashion designers or image-makers, perhaps our role is simply to keep bringing poetry and humanity into the world.”

#6634. The OG 'Thomas Crown Affair' Is an Essential Menswear Movie. How Will the Reboot Stack Up?

Between a stacked roster of Hollywood icons in their prime (Newman, Poitier, Redford) and a cadre of auteur directors on the come-up (Kubrick, Peckinpah, Coppola), the late 1960s produced some of the 20th century’s most stylish movies. Right up there with the best of them is The Thomas Crown Affair, a 1968 caper film directed by Norman Jewison and starring Steve McQueen and Faye Dunaway. Fast-forward a few days and the same could be said about the 1999 remake starring Bond-era Pierce Brosnan, which is worth watching for the suits alone.

Now, in other news of a formerly Brosnan-led, menswear-centric franchise being rebooted: Oscar winner Michael B. Jordan is the producer, director, and star of a third riff on The Thomas Crown Affair, as he announced at CinemaCon back in April. Judging by the first trailer that dropped last week, the film aims to uphold the sartorial reputation of its forebears.

Hitting theaters in March 2027, Jordan’s The Thomas Crown Affair remake follows the same premise as the 1968 and 1999 versions: a wealthy playboy businessman plots art heists for fun while being pursued by a sexy insurance investigator, played in this iteration by potential future Wonder Woman Adria Arjona. There’s crime, there’s glamour, there’s sexual tension—but most of all, in the spirit of the Thomas Crowns before him, there appears to be plenty of high-octane menswear. The movie’s style credit is bolstered by Ruth E. Carter, the two-time Oscar-winning costume designer of the Black Panther movies, who also dressed Jordan for his Oscar-winning turn in Sinners.

But how will MBJ’s high-fashion Thomas Crown land? In the trailer, he can be seen wearing a stiff gray shirt with a matching tie and trousers by Bottega Veneta. The shirt, marked by the luxury brand’s signature triangle pocket detail, had an odd fit: taut around the torso yet puffy around the biceps. Here’s hoping we’ll see some sharper tailoring in the next preview.

Still, to understand Thomas Crown’s legacy as one of the best-dressed guys in film, and why the forthcoming reboot will likely be a smorgasbord of big-time menswear, it’s worth looking back at what made the original such a gem of classic American style. Beyond Jewison’s use of Mondrian-esque split-screen and a very cool soundtrack by French composer Michel Legrand, McQueen’s wardrobe is a perfect embodiment of late 1960s cool, and a how-to for anyone looking to capture it.

Equal parts finely tailored and adventurous, Crown is the ultimate man’s man: He closes million-dollar deals by day, but also flies planes, plays polo, and does donuts on the beach in a juiced-up dune buggy. Likewise, his wardrobe is split between incredible tailoring and a supremely dialed-in lineup of casual pieces. Crown’s suits are a primer on old-school Savile Row: structured, traditional, and precisely tailored, and his shirts, ties, and pocket squares are equally on point. Crown’s double-Albert style watch chain (attached to a Patek Philippe pocket watch, naturally) is a decidedly advanced swerve, but his Cartier Tank Cintrée looks as good in 2026 as it did in 1968 (or 1928, for that matter).

Steve McQueen and Faye Dunaway in The Thomas Crown Affair (1968).

Off-duty Crown’s casual looks include a parade of hall-of-fame menswear pieces like the Baracuta G9 Harrington jacket (classic navy blue with a red tartan lining), brown suede desert boots, and Persol aviators he wears while piloting his glider (gliders—also extremely cool). Club rules be damned, he plays golf in a non-regulation long-sleeved tee, whacks polo balls in an outfit straight out of a Ralph Lauren campaign, and later dons an Aran sweater for a romantic evening clambake at his beach house. It’s often said that Steve McQueen could look good in anything, and that might be true, but the clothes in this movie hit hard enough to make anyone look several orders of magnitude cooler.

Set to the funky bars of Fela Kuti’s “Gentleman,” the trailer for Jordan’s forthcoming Thomas Crown Affair offers several tantalizing tidbits of what’s in store, including a Ferrari F40, several razor-sharp tuxes, and a glimpse at a watch that’s almost certainly a vintage Piaget. That monochrome Bottega look aside, between Jordan’s leading man chops and Carter’s knack for high-concept menswear, we’re assuredly in good hands.

#6632. What’s It Like to Be Tennis’s World Number One? Daniil Medvedev Lets Us Into the Club

The ATP Finals—the most important men’s tournament on the tennis calendar outside of the Grand Slams—kicked off on Sunday in Torino. Founded in 1970 as a season-ending competition pitting the highest-ranked players against each other, the current iteration features the world’s top eight men—Alexander Zverev, Carlos Alcaraz, Ben Shelton, Daniil Medvedev, Flavio Cobolli, Arthur Fils, Frances Tiafoe, and Rafael Jodar—facing each other first in a round-robin group format and then in elimination stages. (It’s similar in format to the women’s WTA Finals, which concluded Sunday in Indian Wells, with Mirra Andreeva taking home the big trophy.)

Ranking, of course, is everything—it’s what gets you invited to the finals—and the summa achievement of the world’s top ranking is the subject of a new book, ATP No. 1 Club: Icons of Men’s Tennis, just out from Phaidon. It features iconic photos of each number-one player since 1973—the men’s game has seen only 30, including Alcaraz, Zverev, and Medvedev—along with text by the late award-winning tennis writer Mark Hodgkinson.

We sat down with one of those iconic players—Medvedev, one of the five current or former number-ones still competing—to ask him, you know, what it’s like to do something better than anyone else in the world.

Vogue: Do you remember, from your earliest years playing tennis, who was number one at the time?

Daniil Medvedev: I started playing tennis when I was six, in 2002, but I was not yet a tennis fan, let’s say. By the time I started to understand tennis a bit more, Roger [Federer] was there already, and I think for most of my childhood it was Roger at number one, and then Rafa, who from time to time took the top spot. And then came Novak—who, as we know now, took the leading spot for a longer period of time. One time, years later, I made a game of it—I think I named, not all of them, probably 27 of them.

Did you have a tennis hero when you were a kid?

So I have to be honest here: I’m still probably a bit like this, but when I was young, whoever was winning too much—doesn’t matter which sport—I stopped liking them. I’m like, Okay, he’s only winning. So at one point I was supporting anyone against Roger—I don’t say it in a bad way, it’s just how I am. At one moment it was Barcelona with [their former coach] Pep Guardiola and they were beating everyone, and I was like, Okay—give us something new.

But it changed from tournament to tournament: I supported Marat [Safin in 2005] when he won the Australian Open. This was incredible—we, as kids in Russia, were waking up early in the morning to watch his matches. Andy Roddick—I loved his serve; sometimes I was copying it. Novak as well, when he just came in, before he started beating everyone and I was cheering for the underdog. I never had one hero.

When you were dreaming kid dreams, was it about winning Wimbledon or another tournament? Was being the world number one ever part of that?

I never was thinking about number one or a Grand Slam. Of course, when I grew up and started playing better tennis, those kind of goals came into place. But when I was really young, I remember hitting against the wall, and because the wall never misses, I was thinking that I’m playing against Roger, Rafa, Novak. I was trying to beat them, but of course you cannot beat the wall. Those were fun memories—and I think, probably, in the back of my mind, I knew that if I’m playing them, it means that I’m somewhere in the top rankings.

My dream was to become a great tennis player, and I feel like I achieved it. I’m happy about it: Every day you go to practice, you work hard, you fight for the matches, and you don’t think about it. But when I talk to someone like you and put myself back there, I’m like, I actually achieved my dream. It’s just that the dream constantly changes, because you want more.

Did you feel different when you first became the ATP number one player in 2022?

Yes and no. Maybe there’s a tiny bit more pressure and attention paid to you, but it’s also just such a nice feeling. I mean, you are the best in the whole world, and everyone else is just trying. And it was not easy, but I made it. [Medvedev became the first player outside the so-called Big Four—Djokovic, Federer, Nadal, and Murray—to hold the top ranking in 18 years.]

Did that put a kind of target on you that hadn’t been there before?

For sure, especially in the world we live in now, that happens. Whenever you lose: “Oh, he’s not good enough to be world number one.” But I didn’t care, because I’m like, “I’m number one,” and it felt so good. People would ask me after a loss, “Maybe the ranking put more pressure on you? Maybe that’s why you didn’t perform.” I’d just say, “Maybe yes,” but I didn’t care. It was such a good feeling. Anyone who has been there, I think, will tell you the same: It’s a nice feeling. I want to try to be there again, of course—it’s going to be super tough, especially with Carlos and Jannik [Sinner] winning so much.

Did people—either inside or outside of tennis—treat you differently when you were number one? Did things come to you more easily?

For sure, when I was the world number one—I was on a big stretch of winning the 2021 US Open, playing some Masters finals, winning some Masters—I got some, whatever you call it, invitations. I remember going to Los Angeles before Indian Wells after I became world number one, and I went to some restaurants and I would ask for the bill and they’re like, “Yes—someone took care of it.” So stuff like this—when you are world number one, people talk a bit more about you; you’re on TV more. These are things which come with, let’s call it fame, which also can have a downside: Some people do this kind of thing just for pleasure, but maybe someone else pays and thinks that you’re going to sit and talk to him for 30 minutes. And I don’t want to be obliged to do something because someone did something for me—that’s just how I live. Especially if I’m rushing somewhere, you know: I’m okay to pay, man. As I say, there are some upsides, some downsides. If you get invited to a football match and you meet some players, or a baseball match: fun.

Ah, game. Okay. I didn’t know this. In any case: I just enjoy life. I’m number one, I enjoy life. I’m number 10, I enjoy life.

This conversation has been edited and condensed.

#6630. Exclusive: The World’s Top Players Look Back on a Wild Year in Men’s Tennis

It was Friday the 13th, and Turin, Italy, the site of the Nitto ATP Finals, glowed with cobalt light as a fingernail moon hung in the air. It looked almost like a Tintoretto painting.

At the Piazza San Carlo, a blue carpet had been laid out lengthwise for the world’s eight best (and currently active) men’s tennis players as fans called out for autographs and selfies. Carlos Alcaraz in Louis Vuitton and Ben Shelton in Ralph Lauren walked among them; missing was the home favorite, Jannik Sinner, who qualified for the field but is sidelined with a knee injury. The scene delivered a surreal, Hollywood-esque half-hour of public stagecraft—paparazzi flashbulbs, police escorts—with all of it designed to celebrate the end of a very notable, and sometimes odd, year in men’s pro tennis.

Speaking of the dreamlike: the evening included an ATP-commissioned portrait session with the photographer Szilveszter Makó, a man who has skyrocketed to industry prominence for having shot multiple covers this year—including for the American, British and Italian editions of Vogue. Makó’s aesthetic itself is rather painterly; photographs as aged frescoes, both cerebral and unusual. Within Turin’s Inalpi Arena, he forged two vignettes with his signature box sets. We stepped in to take a look as Arthur Fils, wearing Balenciaga, was instructed to stand tall and lift his right foot, balancing it on the heel. (“It’s kind of weird, no?” Fils asked, before leaning in.) Makó lensed seven of the eight athletes; due to extenuating circumstances, Alcaraz was unable to stop by the makeshift studio.

But, no matter. In a mad dash between the Principi di Piemonte Hotel, the Piazza San Carlo, a jam-packed van ride across gridlocked roads, and, finally, the Arena, we caught up with all eight players, who together offer an apt representation of the deep and diverse present state of the world’s elite-most men’s tennis. What was discussed: everything from self-reflections to coaching change-ups to cellys to the popularity of the Maldives.

2026 was the biggest year of Zverev’s career: he won his maiden Slam at Roland-Garros, then followed it up with a victory at the US Open. The German also reached the world number 1 spot for the first time (it’s worth noting here that Zverev also holds a super-rare tennis title: an Olympic gold medal, from Tokyo). At 29, he is a half-generation older than the sport’s current dominant duopoly of Sinner and Alcaraz, but if he keeps his current level of play up, he’ll make a strong case for another “Big Three”(the nickname assigned to Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic during their long run of supremacy). Despite the settlement of a domestic abuse lawsuit involving his ex-partner Brenda Patea, a new case was brought to light just a few days ago: the tennis writer Ben Rothenberg reported that Patea has sued Zverev for public misrepresentations. It’s been a career year, but it has to be said that Zverev remains a polarizing figure.

The finest Canadian tuxedo I’ve ever seen.

When you wear head-to-toe denim, yes. You’ve had an incredible year. What worked—and is working—best for you mentally, looking back on it now?

I made a decision with my team last year to change my game style—changing the way we play. I think it was quite a bold move at the age of 29. But we said: it had been working, I’ve had a great career, but it wasn’t working at the final stage of Grand Slams. It hadn’t worked to achieve the dreams and the goals we had. So, sticking to the new game plan, I think that was the biggest thing. Sticking to it and being brave enough to accept it. I think, in the end, it paid off.

Definitely. Two Slams this year, the number one ranking. Are you happy with your game right now, or is there anything you want to improve in 2027?

No, I don’t think I’m complete at all. There are always things you have to improve—and at the end of the day, everybody else is improving, too, so you have to keep with it to stay relevant.

You had some frustration a few weeks ago in Paris in having to defend your number one ranking. Are you still reckoning with that?

I think in Paris it was all just quite new, and I was mentally a little bit tired. There were a lot of new things. And of course, it’s a different kind of pressure. But, I think it’s all settled down, and I’m very happy to be here among the best in the world. It’s an honor.

What’s your vacation plan once the season ends?

Alcaraz—men’s tennis’s brightest star—nicely bookended an otherwise turbulent 2026. The Spaniard, 23, won his first Australian Open all the way back in January, and has enjoyed a surge of recent title wins (in Vienna, Tokyo, and Paris) after returning to the tour from a bout with wrist tenosynovitis that kept him offline for nearly five months. His return at the US Open—where he reached the quarterfinals—brought with it a much-hyped collaboration with Nike’s Cactus Jack line and a tousled new hairstyle. One interesting note going into Turin: Alcaraz has not yet won an ATP Finals, and will be hungry to add that to his resume.

What’s your best 2026 memory off of the court?

Oh, well, I have a couple, to be honest. One of the highlights I had this year was attending the World Cup final. Seeing Spain win the World Cup was unbelievable. So yeah, I’m going to say that! Ferran Torres’s goal, that was the turning point of his career. From that, I would say his stock is really high.

You’ve come back from injury, and you’ve had a strong tail-end of the year, winning Tokyo and Paris. After being hurt, did your mentality change at all? Any hesitation?

I knew that, coming back, I needed matches. I needed competition. I need to feel I was back in the rhythm of competing, and I’m still [building that back]. I need to go out there and feel those nerves of competition. I’m still working on being strong for these difficulties.

With the season ending, what will you try to do in the offseason?

Well, I am not allowed to play golf yet, because my team [won’t let me]. Probably the first thing I’m going to do after the season is over is play golf.

Shelton, 24, had two standout moments on the court in 2026: he defended his Canadian Open title and reached his first Major final at the US Open. Though he lost to Zverev there, it was still a considerable level-up for the Florida-born phenom. Shelton made recent industry news by tapping Juan Carlos Ferrero—Alcaraz’s former coach—to join his team in 2027 (Shelton’s father, Bryan, will remain his coach as well).

You’re bringing on Juan Carlos Ferrero as a coach. Talk us through that decision.

Yeah. Even in the early stages, I think we’ve done a good job of putting together a schedule where I will have two coaches. I don’t want either of them to have to travel 40 weeks a year. So I think we’re putting together a really good formula where they’re both traveling about half the weeks. That’s the ideal scenario for us.

What’s the strongest, most resonant moment you’re taking with you from 2026?

Defending my title in Canada is one. I thought that was the best tennis I’ve played in my career. I didn’t drop a set all week. I was clinical. It was fun for me to see that I can play at that level. But, I have to say, walking out on court for a US Open final and feeling the energy of that stadium on that day, even though I took an L, was pretty special.

I’m just going to play it by ear. I might go on vacation with Arthur Fils, but we’ll see.

The tennis world is happy to see Medvedev, 30, back in elite form. After a less-than-stellar 2025, the lanky Russian has been playing significantly better in 2026, having won four titles and returned to the top 10. Yes, he still has outbursts, and yes, crowds will either go with him on them or boo relentlessly. But that’s just part of the Medvedev Experience. What’s helped on a deeper level: coaching change-ups, and a newfound self-assurance. Don’t forget: Medvedev is a Slam winner (US Open, 2021), a former world number one, and an ATP Finals winner (2020).

Looking back at 2026, what’s the most significant thing you fixed?

What I was looking for was probably finding confidence in myself. Sometimes that requires changing things, and I wanted to take a bit more responsibility. That was probably the biggest fix I managed to make, closer to the end of the year.

Was that rediscovering your old confidence, or was it something new?

Rediscovering in terms of tennis, yes. But more in terms of… I want to say, it’s more like confidence in a tennis life path. I was listening to my old coaches a lot rather than trusting myself fully. So there was always a bit of back-and-forth. Where do I trust them? Where do I trust myself? And now it’s more about trusting myself fully, and then discussing that trust with the team, if that makes sense.

You’re known for your heated interactions with crowds. At this stage in your career, how much of that is just a reaction versus a choice?

It’s never a choice. It’s always a natural reaction.

Any indulgences you’re looking forward to after the season ends?

I have a photo shoot with Lacoste, and then I’m in the Maldives the next day. I would love to go to Hawaii, I don’t know, or wherever. But it’s way too far from where I live.

Cobolli, 24, had the best year of his young career in 2026. His breakthrough: reaching the final of the French Open, where he lost to Zverev in five sets. In Turin, the Italian naturally received the loudest cheers on the blue carpet. With Sinner absent, he’s the home favorite. Cobolli is well-liked on social media, too; the ATP sometimes jokingly calls him their “admin.” He’s had some struggles with fatigue as the season nears its conclusion, but here’s hoping the Florentine can turn on the jets in Piedmont.

At Wimbledon this year, you made some headlines for doing Matheus Cunha’s “surfing” celebration. Should tennis have more cellys?

No, you know why? Two weeks ago, Cunha beat AS Roma. He beat my team, so I’m really pissed with him. [Laughs] But no… I think [for celebrations] if I have something on my mind, I just do it.

You’re the home favorite in Turin. What does that feel like?

It means a lot to me to play here and to win in front of the Italian crowd. Of course, we miss Jannik a lot. He deserves to be here. So I play for him, for the country, for my team, for myself, and for my family. I just want to play for everybody!

Fils, the 22-year-old Frenchman, struggled in the beginning of the year with a back injury that forced him out of the Australian and French Opens. But he had a strong enough summer to qualify for the year-end tournament, winning his first Masters 1000-level title at the Cincinnati Open. In tennis circles, many believe Fils has the natural talent to eventually challenge the Tour’s stalwart top three Sinner, Alcaraz and Zverev. But he’s already matched them if not exceeded them in aura: in Turin, Fils stepped out on the blue carpet in a full Balenciaga look—he has a deal with the brand—and space-like sunglasses. Audiences went wild.

What are you most happy with regarding your play this year?

I’m serving better, moving better. I mean, I knew I was a great competitor. But I didn’t know I could be that good in competitive moments.

When the season is said and done, what’s going to be your first indulgence?

I’m going on holiday in the States, so I think I’m going to go with… having some ribs.

Tell us a little about working with Balenciaga.

They’re changing [internally] now, I know. But I love the brand. It was kind of a dream when I was a kid to sign one day with a huge fashion label. I feel very comfortable wearing them. It’s a new world for me, but I enjoy it.

Tiafoe, 28, has reached the ATP Finals for the first time. It’s testament to his grit and commitment—what he calls a re-established sense of “showing up” day in and day out. “Big Foe,” as he’s endearingly called, has had a productive year; he won his first 500-level tournament in Halle, reached the semis at the US Open, and recorded the fourth-most match wins of any man on Tour. He was all smiles in an expertly tailored Giorgio Armani double-breasted suit on the blue carpet, too.

You’re having a great season. What are you most happy with, not necessarily numbers wise, but in terms of your play?

I think I just found a flow state. I found this peace, and I’m showing up every day. I think sometimes you try to figure out this whole thing of how to get to X to Y to Z, or how to do X, Y and Z together. And it’s kind of just: you show up, man.

Every day looks different, but you just go out there and give your best and be okay with the result. Every time I’ve been able to lay it out there and lost, I was cool with it, rather than having regret that I could have done a little more. I was also focused on my preparation, and once preparation meets opportunity, you get the results.

During the long season, what was a favorite memory away from the court?

I saw the Chris Brown and Usher concert in D.C. and it was out of control. One of the biggest things was getting to meet Matthew McConaughey at the US Open. He’s a special individual.

What are you looking forward to during the break?

Jodar, the youngest man in the Turin field, has been lightning in a bottle this year. He broke men’s tennis’s record for the quickness of his ascent: from his tour debut to hitting the top 10, Jodar needed only 296 days. With that in mind, the Spaniard can be forgiven for speed bumps along the way: a highly publicized outburst at a ball kid during the Shanghai Masters, and a gamesmanship debate around equipment changes. He’s among the youngest of tennis’s new guard—a quarter-generation behind Alcaraz and Sinner, even—and his future feels bright.

So much has been said about the speed of your year, and how quickly you’ve risen. Is there anything you wish would slow down?

Well, I think how it works is that if you do well on Tour, you’re going to have more expectations. That’s something you just have to deal with when you’re doing well. Not every day you’re going to be in a happy mood. But at the end of the day, you just have to handle the situation in the best way possible, and keep focusing on and trying to get better at the game.

What do you do with your limited free time?

I think I’d say spending some time at home and doing some activities in Madrid. Probably, the thing I want to do most is go to the Bernabéu to watch Real Madrid. That’s when I disconnect completely from tennis, and focus on the football game.

#6629. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6628. Is Zalando’s New AI Agent a Blueprint for the Future of Retail?

What happens when a multibrand fashion retailer starts selling products it doesn’t stock? European e-commerce giant Zalando is joining the AI shopping agent race with plans to let shoppers buy from other retailers through its platform. Its new offering, Zalando Extended, will use AI agents to complete purchases on customers’ behalf, potentially transforming Zalando into a shopping gateway beyond its own catalog.

Zalando is testing the service with premium home and living retailer Westwing. Its products already appear in Zalando’s search and browsing results, but shoppers currently have to click through to Westwing’s website to buy them. From 2027, Zalando’s AI agent will handle those purchases on customers’ behalf, allowing them to check out without leaving the Zalando app.

Retailers can join through a relatively simple integration, providing something similar to an affiliate product feed and entering into an additional agreement with Zalando. The company has not disclosed what commission or fee, if any, it will earn from these transactions. It's a notable move for a retailer that has spent years building its own assortment and relationships with thousands of brands, from Gucci to Burberry and Jacquemus. But as the likes of OpenAI, Google and Meta race to make general-purpose personal AI agents, the battle is increasingly over who controls the customer relationship, rather than simply who stocks the product.

Zalando’s AI assistant currently helps shoppers purchase from the multibrand retailer’s product catalogue. Photo: Courtesy of Zalando.

Zalando’s response is to position itself on both sides of that coin. Its three-pronged strategy aims to make its own platform the first stop for fashion discovery, expand its assortment through external retailers and also reach shoppers through third-party AI agents. It plans to offer checkout within Google’s AI Mode and Gemini app when its agentic commerce launches in Europe, and has tested advertising inside ChatGPT in the UK.

This also places Zalando in competition with specialist AI shopping platforms such as Daydream, which also launched a new AI shopping agent this week. Both are betting that fashion requires expertise beyond that of general-purpose AI agents. While Daydream operates in the US and Zalando in Europe, the latter enters the race with a significant advantage in scale.

But for rival luxury and multibrand fashion retailers, Zalando’s AI strategy raises a bigger question: is the future of fashion e-commerce about selling your own assortment, or becoming the gateway to everyone else’s?

At the Web Summit conference in Lisbon, Vogue Business sat down with chief technology officer Graeme Smith to discuss the company’s ambitions and who stands to own the customer relationship in the age of AI agents.

Vogue: Why allow Zalando customers to buy products from other retailers through Zalando Extended?

Smith: We’ve got over 63 million active customers at Zalando, and through our Lifestyle AI [Zalando’s umbrella term for its AI-powered personalization technology], we’ve really got to know their preferences — the brands they like, the price points they shop at, the brand values like sustainability they look for, and how their needs change over time. We can use all this to create a personalized experience that can even become proactive.

So we thought, why limit ourselves? We already have our wholesale and partner platforms, but with AI agents, we’ve found a really lightweight way to bring in other retailers whose products you wouldn’t normally find on Zalando.

Our first partner is Westwing. Today, you can discover its products on Zalando and click through to buy them on Westwing. But early next year, you’ll be able to buy that sofa or lamp directly on Zalando, using your existing account and payment details, without leaving the app. We’ll buy it on your behalf.

Imagine how much more assortment across fashion and lifestyle we could offer this way, without stocking it ourselves. We can then build that into our personalization, learning more about customers’ interests beyond our existing catalog and helping them discover more products.

Vogue: With general-purpose AI agents increasingly capable of shopping on consumers’ behalf, are you competing directly with the likes of OpenAI, Google and Meta? Why would shoppers choose Zalando instead?

People are going to use a variety of agents, but our mission is always to make Zalando the best place to start the fashion and lifestyle shopping journey. That comes down to the customer experience we can provide that others can’t, which starts with data.

We’ve been using AI for over 15 years, including for personalized shopping recommendations, and we’ve invested heavily in size and fit. We get tens of thousands of body measurements a week, and we have so much data from customer returns about which items run small or large. So we’ve got over 10,000 size charts, and we’ve put AI on top of that. No third-party agent has got that. So if you care about getting the fit right the first time, Zalando’s agent will be the place to come.

We’ve also invested in recommending whole outfits based on our understanding of trends, how people shop for different occasions and years of customer behavior at scale.

Vogue: How quickly do you expect Zalando Extended to grow? Are you planning to onboard lots more retailers in the coming months, or is this more of a test-and-learn phase?

It’s a little bit of both. We’re testing and learning, but it’s not a particularly complex thing we’re doing, and we’re very excited by what we’ve seen so far. Assuming it’s successful, this has the potential to scale very fast because the integration is so lightweight.

Most of these retailers already produce an affiliate feed, which is essentially what we need. We can make the sign-up and operations very simple for them, and it’s very light for us too. So there’s potential to scale this massively.

Vogue: Trust is fundamental to AI agent adoption, and attitudes vary between markets. Why would consumers trust Zalando Assistant more than a general-purpose AI agent?

Zalando is a brand that people trust, and we’ve worked very hard to earn that trust. The company has just turned 18, and we’ve built that trust through how we look after the customer experience, including how we handle their data. We’re a European company, so the data we hold is subject to high European standards for data protection.

We’ve seen customers enthusiastically adopt Zalando Assistant. Interestingly, questions about what we know about them haven’t been a big part of the conversation — people have just started using it. We’ve had 22 million customers engage with Zalando Assistant this year, including 13 million in the last quarter.

Customers are twice as likely to buy something in a session where they use Zalando Assistant compared with one where they don’t. And of course, we have all the consent mechanisms required in Europe. Customers can also request that their data be deleted.

Graeme Smith, Zalando’s CTO. Photo: Courtesy of Zalando.

Vogue: Is there a risk that Zalando could lose its direct relationship with customers by bringing other retailers onto its platform?

No, we don’t think of it like that. We want people to come to Zalando more and more, and for it to be the place where they start their shopping journey. We’ve got 70% organic traffic, which is very high, and we work hard to maintain that.

We think we can do that by building really great experiences tailored to fashion and lifestyle shopping. Bringing in more retailers actually gives people more reasons to come to Zalando, because they know they can access a wider variety of products. They can buy a sofa on Zalando, as well as everything else. So we think this could actually drive more traffic.

Now, could someone go directly to Westwing to buy their next sofa? Of course, and that’s fine. We don’t sell sofas on Zalando. What matters is that we’re the best place to discover fashion and lifestyle products, wherever they come from.

Vogue: You’re also piloting advertising in ChatGPT and preparing to participate in Google’s Universal Commerce Protocol. How does that fit with your ambition to make Zalando the starting point for shopping?

There are three strands to our strategy. The first is getting people to keep coming back to Zalando as the best place to start their shopping journey. The second is what we call inbound agentic commerce, and the third is Zalando Extended, which allows us to massively expand the assortment available through outbound agentic commerce.

Inbound agentic commerce is what most people talk about when they discuss AI shopping agents. People are using ChatGPT, Google’s AI-powered search and other platforms. We had to decide early on how we felt about that, and we saw it as an opportunity. Our customers are going to use these services anyway, so we want Zalando to be there and meet them where they are. We also want to reach new customers.

We’ve become very good at generative engine optimisation (GEO) — we’re the number one fashion destination in Europe referred to by AI agents. But we haven’t stopped at organic visibility. We’ve also piloted advertising inside ChatGPT in the UK, and we’re now looking at the results and deciding where to go next.

With Google, it’s even more interesting. When Google launches agentic commerce in Europe, Zalando will be there from the start. Customers will be able to discover Zalando products and even check out within Google if they want to.

But they’ll still need a Zalando account. That’s very important to us. We want to engage with these AI platforms on our own terms and maintain the customer relationship.

Vogue: Fashion shopping is often emotional and highly considered. Do you think consumers will really want to complete purchases through AI agents, rather than visiting a retailer’s website?

We don’t know how this is going to play out. I’m very excited by it, but fashion is very personal and emotional.

What we see is that when customers arrive at Zalando from another channel, whether that’s an AI agent, Instagram or TikTok, they often don’t buy the item they landed on. They explore three or four more products, look at similar items and browse around before making a purchase.

It’s another signal that fashion is different, it’s a high-consideration purchase. So if I had to bet — and it’s always difficult to make predictions — I think people will use agents to research products, but they’ll still want to click through to the retailer, like Zalando, to ask: is this item quite right for me? What more can I learn about it? What similar products are available? And then maybe they’ll buy from there, but let’s see.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#6626. Robert Pattinson’s Hair Is Already 007 Material

Whether you like it or not (or placed bets on Kalshi), Robert Pattinson is our next James Bond. During the years-long process in casting 007, we used our best detective skills to narrow down the field to who would join His Majesty’s Secret Service. And if you were going by hair type alone, well, Pattinson makes a rather compelling case.

Let’s review the canon for a moment. In the 1957 novel From Russia, with Love, Bond creator Ian Fleming describes the spy’s mane thusly: “The hair was black, parted on the left, and carelessly brushed so that a thick black comma fell down over the right eyebrow.”

Pattinson’s hair might be naturally light brown, but a darker ‘do is hardly out of the question for the actor’s upcoming transformation. For his turn as Bruce Wayne in The Batman, he dyed his hair to a darker, almost pitch-black hue. The rest of Fleming’s description fits the actor nicely, particularly the bit about being “carelessly brushed.” In real life, the actor’s hair is rarely anything approaching immaculate. Even at more formal engagements, it tends to retain a certain studied dishevelment, with stray strands escaping an otherwise respectable comb-through. Fleming’s famous “comma,” after all, isn’t a carefully sculpted curl. It’s simply a lock of hair allowed to fall where it pleases, which just so happens to be very on trend in 2026.

We got our first glimpse of the 40-year-old actor taking on the role in a video posted by the official James Bond X account where he’s seen stepping out of the shadows pointing a gun at something (or someone) just outside the frame. It’s hard to tell whether the golden lighting is playing tricks on his hair color, but the accompanying promotional image certainly seems to suggest a shade of black. Plus, his hair’s parted on the correct side.

It’s worth noting that Daniel Craig’s casting as Bond was initially met with considerable resistance, much of it centered on one detail: He’s blonde. Fleming’s Bond, after all, was famously dark-haired, and Craig represented a departure from the physical template established by the novels and previous screen incarnations. We know how that turned out. Craig went on to deliver one of the most celebrated interpretations of 007, proving that a little deviation from the source material needn’t be a deal-breaker.

Pattinson will still need to prove himself to be agile in a tuxedo, nimble behind the wheel, and thirsty for a martini or two, but one thing’s sure: He's got the hair down pat.

#6625. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6623. Daydream’s New AI Agent Can Shop for You While You Sleep

Daydream wants to become a personal stylist in your pocket. The AI-powered fashion discovery platform, launched in 2025 by former Stitch Fix executive Julie Bornstein, is introducing a 24/7 AI shopping agent that can learn consumers’ tastes, assemble outfits and purchase products on their behalf — even while they sleep.

The new agent, which shoppers can chat with through Daydream’s app or by texting it directly via SMS, marks an evolution from the conversational fashion search engine the company launched just over a year ago. It can remember previous exchanges, put together complete outfits, offer virtual try-ons using an uploaded photograph and handle the steps leading up to checkout.

During an exclusive preview, co-founder and chief brand officer Lisa Yamner asks the agent to resume shopping for an upcoming trip to Mexico. Remembering her plans, it asks a few questions before assembling looks for beachfront dinners, complete with dresses, shoes and bags. Yamner swaps between pieces, tries them on using a virtual version of herself and uploads an influencer’s Instagram image to find similar items.

“Once you express a need or an interest, it can shop while you sleep,” Yamner explains. Shoppers can leave the agent to monitor products for price drops or continue working on a shopping request in the background, rather than repeatedly checking themselves. Any purchase still requires their approval. “We firmly believe that shopping doesn’t have to be a task, but there are parts of it that become that.” The aim is to take the drudgery out of shopping without losing the pleasure of discovery, she says.

At launch, the agent can shop across Daydream’s existing network of roughly 350 brand and retail partners, spanning more than 10,000 brands and three million products. Shoppers can ask it to purchase an item on their behalf, or check out directly with the retailer.

It comes as OpenAI, Instinct and Meta double down on shopping as a core use case and revenue stream for their newly launched ‘always on’ agents, and fashion retailers are now racing to build their own agents. Last week, Zalando announced plans for an AI agent that will purchase products on customers’ behalf from other retailers as well as its own catalog, from 2027. Meanwhile, brands including Ralph Lauren and J.Crew are building out their own branded AI shopping assistants, with J.Crew partnering with Anthropic on its new AI “Style Advisor”. Last month, Prada became the first luxury brand to launch an official plugin within OpenAI’s ChatGPT.

Daydream's answer is to sell its fashion expertise. The company has developed an internal “fashion knowledge graph” to enrich the information attached to products in its catalog, while human stylists help shape the agent’s recommendations. It recently appointed Francesca Sully as its first “stylist in residence”, tasked with teaching the technology to think more like a stylist and keep pace with trends.

Daydream recently appointed Francesca Sully as its first “stylist in residence”, tasked with teaching the AI agent to think more like a human stylist and keep pace with trends. Photo: Courtesy of Daydream.

Its founders believe a general-purpose AI agent, however sophisticated, will struggle to replicate the nuances of personal style. It comes back to the central question haunting fashion AI: can it mimic taste?

“We feel like a generalized agent is just not going to get fashion right,” Bornstein tells Vogue Business in an exclusive interview alongside co-founder Lisa Yamner. “Style is so nuanced. It relates to some very specific things that matter. So we need to know the right questions to ask, but also understand the product catalog of every brand out there — not just the price points, but also what the aesthetic of a brand world is, and how to connect that to other brands that align with that aesthetic and may be of interest.”

That expertise is also intended to help shoppers discover unfamiliar labels: approximately 97% of searches on Daydream contain no brand name, according to Bornstein. But in an increasingly crowded market, can that fashion expertise stand up as an independent AI shopping offering against the mass convenience of frontier AI agents and trusted retailers’ owned product catalogs?

When Daydream debuted last year, its proposition was to solve one of fashion e-commerce’s enduring frustrations: finding the right product across a fragmented universe of brands and retailers. Its conversational search engine allowed shoppers to describe what they wanted in natural language, rather than relying on conventional keywords and filters, encouraging users to “say more” about what they sought.

Although Daydream had already positioned itself around the idea of an AI agent, what it lacked was the ability to deliver the more involved, personalized service its founders envisaged — agents in their current form didn’t actually exist.

“We’ve been wanting to build from day one, but it took us a while to get there for a couple of reasons: one was that the agentic technology wasn’t yet there, and two is that the first version of the platform helped us really understand what consumers were looking for and what they wanted from an AI shopping assistant,” Bornstein says, explaining that Daydream was finding its original product couldn’t deliver the level of assistance shoppers wanted. Shoppers were asking very specific questions to find products for a need that included an occasion and their body type, and Daydream was showing them a page of search results, “when what they really wanted was more tailored help,” Bornstein adds. Conversational search might make finding fashion products easier, but it doesn’t necessarily solve the more subjective problem of deciding what to wear.

Bornstein recalls a similar challenge at her previous company, The Yes, where shoppers struggled to move beyond the conventions of traditional search. “We tried to get people to search by telling us a need and they would say, ‘Oh, I need a red dress for a Valentine’s Day party. I want to look sexy, but age-appropriate.’ And then you’d say, ‘Great, go ahead and type it into the search part.’ But then they would type in ‘red dress’, because their trust in search working was so low, and there was no mental model of being able to give a more detailed prompt.”

ChatGPT helped change that behavior, she says, making consumers more comfortable describing their needs in detail — and helping users understand how to use a product like Daydream. “Consumer expectations have started to change and people now understand what an agent is in a way they definitely didn’t two years ago when we started and no one understood what we were talking about,” Bornstein says.

The platform says it has amassed more than 2 million users since its June 2025 launch, with millennial women its largest audience, followed by Gen X and Gen Z. Bornstein describes two overlapping groups: fashion-savvy shoppers who appreciate having thousands of brands in one place, and time-poor consumers seeking more direction. But Daydream won’t disclose how many of its 2 million shoppers return or make purchases, making it difficult to gauge whether initial curiosity is translating into increased sales.

It comes just a week after Zalando announced an adjacent offering — a new AI agent feature, Zalando Extended, that will allow shoppers to discover and buy products from other third-party retailers without leaving the Zalando app, available from 2027. The European multibrand platform has 63 million active customers, extensive brand relationships and years of purchase and sizing data — assets that a much younger shopping platform like Daydream can’t easily replicate. Yet Bornstein argues the two companies are targeting different markets — Zalando solely operates in Europe, while Daydream is focused solely on the US. She also says the US retail landscape’s department stores and multibrand retailers generally have “more curated assortments”.

“The fact Zalando is going outside its own catalog makes a lot of sense because they’ve always tried to be extremely broad and like the higher-end ‘Amazon of fashion’ in Europe,” Bornstein argues.

But geography offers only a partial defence in a market where frontier AI models like ChatGPT and Claude are developing shopping capabilities that could eventually reach consumers across multiple countries, and gain more sophisticated fashion knowledge, via direct brand plugins like ChatGPT’s recently launched Prada plugin.

Asked what Daydream can offer that a much larger retailer can’t, Bornstein points to its first-mover advantage as the first cross-brand conversational search tool that’s “properly entrenched in fashion”, and the two years of data and prompts it’s collected from fashion-savvy consumers in that time. “I would also say we are solely focused on this,” she adds. “Having worked for other larger companies before in my past, I know how hard it is to build something like this on the side.”

There is also competition from fashion brands themselves. Ralph Lauren’s Ask Ralph and the launch of J.Crew’s new AI stylist last week suggest that brands increasingly want to provide personalized guidance within their own shopping environments.

Yet Bornstein says these brand-owned stylists can sit alongside Daydream’s ambitions. “When we launched originally, many brands asked us if we could build this AI agent for their sites,” she says. “And what we said to them is our initial goal is to have one place for consumers to go and see all brands — without having 10 tabs open.”

Daydream has also expanded into providing its technology to brands. Around eight brand sites are currently using its conversational search technology, Yamner says, and the company plans to bring some of its new agentic capabilities to those partners.

“Our feeling is if you know the brand and you go straight to the brand, there’s no reason why you wouldn’t want tools to help you shop that brand as effectively as you can,” Bornstein says. “So we’ll evolve the agentic product that we provide to brand sites to map to our core product, as it’s very portable to single brands too. But we are fundamentally focused on the B2C experience — it just also happens to work for B2B.”

One of Daydream’s potentially most valuable assets is the information it gathers from the way consumers describe their shopping needs. Traditional e-commerce search data might tell a brand that shoppers are searching for dresses or shoes. Conversational search can reveal the occasion, aesthetic and practical requirements behind those searches, as well as details like whether shoppers are searching for particular past collaborations or archive pieces — valuable data for brands’ product development and merchandising decisions, Bornstein says.

“That’s been the single best thing I think we’ve done for the industry over the last year — being able to surface really valuable and different insights for them, especially catalog intent,” she says, adding that they’ve found the same shopper tends to be entering complex conversational queries on Daydream but still be searching ‘red dress’ on brands’ own DTC sites. For brands, that information could can offer a more granular understanding of what customers want and why. For Daydream, it also creates a potential advantage over competitors that lack the same volume of detailed fashion-related prompts.

But the next stage of its personalization strategy requires shoppers to share considerably more. Daydream is developing integrations with Gmail and Google Calendar so its new AI agent can access this customer data and allow it to identify upcoming occasions and learn about previous purchases and marketing email subscriptions. Shoppers will soon also be able to share Pinterest boards with the agent to communicate their style preferences.

Users can set Daydream’s new AI agent tasks, like price comparison and stock checks, that it can carry out 24/7, even while they sleep. Photo: Courtesy of Daydream.

Daydream also operates on a commission model, yet Bornstein insists that commercial relationships won’t influence what the agent recommends — and it’s not pursuing advertising within the agent, at least for now. “There are no commercial incentives that go into what shows up for the customer,” she says. “Whatever they buy, we receive the same level of commission. So we are completely agnostic in what we’re showing and it’s about the customer’s preferences.” Brands will continue to receive customer information when purchases are completed through Daydream.

While Daydream is investing in a more complex and personalized experience, it’s not disclosed the conversion or retention figures needed to assess how effectively that experience translates into repeat purchasing. But Bornstein and Yamner remain convinced that fashion requires a different approach from the general-purpose agents increasingly being developed to manage everyday tasks.

“We’re watching the direction that the tech and customers are moving in, and we’re trying to get out ahead of it,” Yamner says. “We’re trying to say we get it. We get that this is what the customer’s expectations are going to become.”

#6621. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.
