#6620. 3 Ways To Defrost Chicken Without Spreading Salmonella, According To An Expert

Your dinner plans aren't ruined just yet.

Forgetting to take chicken out of the freezer is an all-too-common occurrence that can bring your dinner plans to a screeching halt. To get things back on track, your gut instinct may be to thaw it as quickly as possible. But there are more important things to worry about than a delayed dinner.

Raw poultry can carry Salmonella, so how you handle it matters. Nothing is less appetizing than giving your whole family a foodborne illness.

But before you give up and order takeout, we’re here to help. We chatted with Ellen Steinberg, PhD, RD, LD, and food safety specialist, to find the best (and safest) methods to thaw chicken. Whether you plan ahead or need to defrost it fast, here’s what you should do.

Defrosting chicken isn’t as simple as taking it out of the freezer. Salmonella is real, y’all—according to FoodSafety.gov, roughly 4% of chicken packages at American grocery stores are contaminated with the bacteria. That bacteria can multiply rapidly in the temperature danger zone, between 40°F and 140°F. Translation: Leaving your chicken out on the counter can actually make you sick.

To prevent that, choose the right method and protect the surrounding environment from cross-contamination. Even with supposedly airtight packaging, the plastic may have holes, or chicken juice may transfer from other packages at the grocery store. It’s especially difficult to spot when the meat is frozen, so Steinberg says it’s better to be safe than sorry.

“You should put your [raw] chicken in a roasting pan or a baking sheet so the juices won’t spread,” she says. Everything that touches raw chicken should be thoroughly cleaned with hot, soapy water. If you want to take food safety even further, Steinberg suggests keeping a separate cutting board in a different color that you use exclusively for raw meat. And above all else: Wash your hands!

If you’re not in a rush, thawing chicken in the fridge yields the most consistent results. Because refrigerators should stay at 40°F and below, frozen chicken can gradually defrost without entering the temperature danger zone where bacteria multiply more rapidly.

Because of this, Steinberg says it’s the only USDA-approved thawing method that lets you refreeze raw chicken without cooking it first. “If you end up deciding that you don’t want to cook the chicken or you only want to use half of it, you can place it back in the freezer,” she says. There is a caveat, however: Once your chicken has fully thawed, you should either cook or refreeze it within one to two days.

If you opt for the refrigerator method, keep these safety measures in mind. Beyond keeping your meat contained on a plate or tray, place it on the bottom shelf. If juice drips, it’ll contaminate the fewest ingredients. Steinberg also suggests storing the chicken toward the back of your refrigerator. “The temperature is more consistent, unlike the areas closest to the door,” she says.

If you need to defrost chicken fast, one of the best ways is with cool, running water. Unlike fridge air, water conducts heat much more effectively. Keeping the water moving also helps maintain consistent thawing conditions. But you don't necessarily need to leave the faucet running: The USDA also recommends submerging chicken in cold water and changing it every 30 minutes.

So if cold water thaws meat quickly, would hot water do the job even faster? It might, but the potential food safety risks aren't worth it. "If you thaw chicken under warm or hot water, the outside of the meat can enter the temperature danger zone while the center is still frozen,” Steinberg says.

For the running-water method, place the chicken in leak-proof packaging in a bowl and run cool water (70°F or lower) over it. Thawing times depend on the size and thickness of the meat, but smaller packages may be ready in an hour or less. Once thawed, cook the chicken immediately before considering refreezing it.

The final USDA-approved method involves using your microwave’s defrost setting. While it’s certainly faster than letting meat thaw in the fridge, we suggest relying on this method only if you have no other option.

Steinberg says this technique leaves the least wiggle room for planning your dinner. “You have to cook it immediately,” she says. “You can’t defrost it and then decide to cook two hours later.”

The need to cook immediately is certainly one downside of the microwave method. However, another compelling argument against using the defrost setting is that it can make your chicken taste worse.

Microwaves heat food unevenly, especially with thicker pieces of meat. Some areas can start warming up or even cooking before the center fully thaws. It's not a big deal when reheating leftovers, but it can nearly ruin frozen proteins.

By the time the center is fully defrosted, the outer edges may already be partially cooked. Can you imagine chicken that tastes worse than unseasoned microwaved chicken? We can't.

It’s a safe and fast defrosting method when followed by immediate cooking—but at what cost? So we'd only vouch for this technique if your chicken will end up shredded or submerged in enough sauce to mask the texture.

#6618. On the Podcast: How Richard Avedon Redefined Fashion Photography

Richard Avedon spent decades shooting for magazines like Vogue, Harper’s Bazaar, and The New Yorker before his death in 2004. Now his life and work are the subjects of a new documentary, Avedon, directed by Ron Howard.

To learn more about Avedon’s legacy—and to hear what it was like to work with him as both a model and a fashion editor—Nicole Phelps invited Tonne Goodman on to The Run-Through.

Goodman was still in high school when she entered the world of fashion. “I was in 10th grade and I wanted a summer intern job,” she explains. What she got, through her friendship with Diana Vreeland’s grandson, was modeling work for Vogue. “I think that the fact that she sent me to Avedon and to Penn and to the best photographers that the magazine had at that point was really a gesture of kindness to her grandson,” Goodman says.

Her first photograph in Vogue, taken by Avedon, was published in 1971. Decades later, she would collaborate with him as an editor on a commercial shoot for Neiman Marcus starring model Nadja Auermann. “Dick was a sponge. He captured every single kind of example of a fashion photograph that you could possibly take,” she says. “I’m sure that there is not a photographer today who has not referenced his work in some way or another.”

Later in the episode, after the break, Chloe Malle sits down with the film’s director, Ron Howard. At first, he says, the Avedon Foundation was reluctant to open its archives to a documentary crew, but Howard’s 2024 film Jim Henson Idea Man persuaded them that the material would be in safe hands.

As he began the research, Howard says, “I think they could just see that I was pretty blown away. I related to him a lot more than I thought I would. I began to understand that these weren’t snapshots. He wasn’t ever counting on luck—he really was a storyteller.”

The two also discuss Avedon’s motivations, and some of the unflattering reviews he received during his career. “A lot of interesting people are paradoxes, right? He had that anger that was pushing him,” Howard posits. “We talk about how he was frustrated by the critics. And of course, they were devastating to him in a way, but I think he used that as fuel.”

In the end, Tonne believes that Avedon would have appreciated what Avedon has to say about him. “I think Ron got him,” she says, “and I think he would’ve gotten it totally.”

#6617. Denis Villeneuve on Finishing ‘Dune,’ Casting James Bond, and Why ‘Reality Is Unbeatable’

The last days of the making of the Dune trilogy take place on an unassuming Hollywood side street in September, in a dark, mostly silent room. “We were about to have a quick look at reel one because they did some adjustments, and it’s without sound,” Denis Villeneuve says, apologetically. “So it’s a way to discover the film that is a bit brutal for you.”

Villeneuve, the director and cowriter of Dune, Dune: Part Two, and Dune: Part Three, is tall, slender, and bearded, with deep-set eyes. He has a disarming effect. Many directors of Villeneuve’s stature—Christopher Nolan or James Cameron—lead their productions with a kind of remote but dazzling competency: They can do everything better than you and are used to the deference that comes with that fact. Villeneuve’s charisma is closer and more mischievous: He speaks quietly and playfully, in Quebecois-accented English, and commands loyalty via the protective instinct he inspires in nearly everyone he meets. His method is emotional; his instructions are conveyed with sincerity and praise. When presented with the results he is seeking, he will let you know with an almost childlike enthusiasm: I deeply love it. Or: Wow.

Today, Villeneuve and his cinematographer, Linus Sandgren, are at the postproduction facility Company 3, where they have been the past weeks and months, color-timing—the process of adjusting and balancing a film’s many colors and contrasts—the 150 minutes of Dune: Part Three. For my sake, and because there is still work to be done on it, they have started, once again, at the beginning of the film. “So here we could have fucked up the Warner Brothers logo if we wanted,” Villeneuve says, gesturing at the screen at the studio’s iconic WB, “but we are nice guys.”

Then he leans forward: “No, but seriously, without joking, are they too rich, the colors? A little bit? Or is it the original to your eyes?” Sandgren—a calm Swede in Birkenstocks—and Matt Wallach, the film’s colorist, chime in to agree and to tone down the blue. “Their logo is a little cartoonish,” Villeneuve says, still staring at it. “It’s not their best work, I will say. But that feels better. Thank you, Matt.”

Villeneuve and his wife, Tanya Lapointe, who is a producer and second-unit director on Dune: Part Three, disagree on how long they have been working on Dune: Villeneuve tends to say nine years, and Lapointe says 10. (It’s 10.) Frank Herbert’s Dune books, which are notoriously complex and hard to adapt, have stymied directors as talented as David Lynch and Alejandro Jodorowsky. But Villeneuve seems to have found a way. The first two Dune films—Part One came out in 2021—have grossed over a billion dollars, been nominated for 15 Academy Awards, and helped make stars of Timothée Chalamet (who plays Atreides, the film’s complicated messiah figure and main character) and Zendaya (who plays Chani, a native Fremen warrior and the lover of Atreides) while still capturing the uniquely strange and surreal texture of Herbert’s novels. (Multiple people in the Villeneuve films imbibe what one character describes as “worm piss.”)

Right now Villeneuve is feeling the last decade acutely. “I’m at that stage of the process where all my body hurts,” he says. On Dune: Part Three alone, the production shot for nearly a hundred days, in three countries: Hungary, where the film’s main stages were; Iceland; and the Liwa Desert, in the United Arab Emirates, which doubled for the sand planet of Arrakis. They wrapped last November, and Villeneuve went directly into the film’s edit and postproduction process. “It’s a feeling of some kind of deep melancholia to finally come to the conclusion of this long journey,” he says. “Because it has been nine years of my life dreaming about Arrakis, about sandworms, about the adventures of Paul Atreides. I’m pretty emotional about that.”

In the history of Hollywood, there have been only a handful of directors who have had the ability to work, again and again, at the highest level of the art form while also connecting with audiences at the widest possible scale. Villeneuve is one of them. His signature films—2015’s cartel thriller Sicario, or 2016’s science fiction film Arrival, which was nominated for eight Academy Awards—are knotty and severe and not always easy to follow; they are also beautiful and seem to play well anywhere, whether on an airplane, in an HBO rerun, or at an IMAX theater. Villeneuve’s reward for all his success is his next project: the 26th James Bond film. “It’s a blessing,” Villeneuve says. “Because to leave Arrakis, I need some kind of strong rocket, something that will grab me and pull me away from the orbit of that planet. I’m leaving a childhood dream. I need something so powerful to pull me away from it. And Bond is the one that will do it.”

In the dark screening room, Wallach lets the first minutes of the final Dune film play. We watch soldiers on a dimly lit warship prepare themselves for battle. Sandgren and Villeneuve discuss trying to bring out one of the actor’s features more concretely. “I guess what we’re fighting is we could have lit him more,” Sandgren says, “but also what Denis really wants here is the realism and the sort of incidental light—like he just happens to sit in a shitty light here, and gets what he gets, which adds to the realism, which is nice. But you still want to see him. So it’s a balance.”

“What Linus says, in a very polite way, is that it’s my fault,” Villeneuve says, smiling, while Wallach finds a little more detail in the actor’s face.

“I deeply love it,” Villeneuve pronounces, when he is done. “Thank you. The scene is at the beginning, and becomes claustrophobic. In French, we say they are chair à canon.”

“Cannon food, we call it in Sweden,” Sandgren says.

Villeneuve watches his own film as it plays on. “Wow,” he says. “Fantastic. Fantastic. That’s beautiful. Nice work on the highlights here. Thank you, guys. Wow. Great work. It looks real now. Wow.” His voice is full of emotion as he turns to Sandgren: “It’s beautiful, my dear friend.”

In the Dune movies, you can feel Villeneuve’s desire to go deeper into the desert, to shed all the big, loud machinery of his own films, and to get to the places out near the horizon. This is one of the reasons his trilogy works where others have failed: Despite Villeneuve’s talent for spectacle—his Dune is full of menacing, chromed-out oblong shapes and eerily familiar war machines—his true gift is finding the uncannily quiet spots in the worlds he creates, the lonely places where his characters are tested against themselves.

“That was the main condition when I agreed to make these movies,” Villeneuve says, about the way all three Dune films were shot in the desert, on location. “I said that it was deeply important for me to shoot it in the real environment.” The Liwa Desert was so mind-bendingly hot while shooting Dune: Part Three that the director had to incorporate a midday break into the crew’s daily schedule. Robert Pattinson, who joined the cast for the third film, has talked about the set being so intensely warm that he basically disassociated for most of shooting. But being there is one of the main things Villeneuve is after. “I love reality,” he says. “I love to be in the environment. It’s like a pleasure that I give to myself to be in the crew with a camera in the desert. I feel that there’s all these shots that we did, the realism, that I think you cannot achieve otherwise. And you cannot feel the power of the desert if you’re not there. There are some shots you can cheat sometimes. But in general, reality is unbeatable.”

Villeneuve on the set of Dune: Part Three with Timothée Chalamet.

Villeneuve and Zendaya on location in the Liwa Desert, Abu Dhabi.

Villeneuve, 59, grew up in Gentilly, Quebec, a small town right next to a river. From that place he emerged with “a relationship with horizon and silence,” he says. “I was in contact since my birth with incredible gigantic skies, very dramatic, operatic skies. And colors as well. I grew up in a world that has a black-and-white winter, which has a tremendous, beautiful, precise palette of black and white and blue and grays.”

Villeneuve likes to point out that the two main structures in his town were a church and a power plant. “I grew up melancholic, a child that was dreaming big alone in his corner and fascinated by the engineers that were working in that nuclear power plant,” he says. “I was raised as a Catholic, and I was raised going to the church, and those chants and the passion of religion [are] all that mixed together with incredibly powerful grandmothers. I think that’s the background of Dune right there.”

Villeneuve was a reader, a dreamer. It was only as an adult, when Villeneuve became a documentary filmmaker, that he began to discover a larger world outside his own mind. “I think that there’s something about Paul Atreides in the way he’s introduced at the beginning, the way he is like a kid that has been protected in a small bubble all his life and suddenly finds himself confronted to a new reality where he has to consolidate his identity in another culture,” Villeneuve says. “I think it’s something that I, at the time when I was a kid, I really connected with. And early on when I became a young adult, I traveled a lot, a lot. I went a lot to Asia and was spending a lot of time there doing small documentaries and being in contact with so many perspectives, so many points of view on reality.”

Villeneuve made his first feature, August 32nd on Earth, in Canada in 1998. He would go on to make three more films in French, before making his first English-language film, Enemy, in 2013. “I consolidated my identity as a filmmaker,” Villeneuve says about the time before he came to Hollywood “through documentaries and movies with less commercial pressure where I was free to express myself and find my own voice.” Partially, he learned by failing. “I will say that I don’t see my first feature films as...they had some clumsiness in them. I was a beginner. I learned my craft. I made mistakes and I learned from those mistakes, a lot more than from my successes.”

Villeneuve, as a young filmmaker, was wary of Hollywood, even as he was pointed at it like an arrow. “Hollywood has always had that kind of dichotomy, to be a paradise for a filmmaker and hell at the same time,” he says. “Since the birth of Hollywood there has been a struggle between the art of cinema, the idea that you want to express yourself—and for that you need a lot of money, and somebody will write the check, and you have a responsibility. Since the birth of cinema, it has been like that.”

In 2012, Villeneuve found himself facing a rare opportunity: He had two films greenlit at more or less the same time. One was Prisoners—an in-demand Hollywood script about the abduction of two children and the vigilante efforts of one father to get them back. The other was a coproduction between Spain and Canada called Enemy, about a college professor who becomes obsessed with another man with whom he appears to be physically identical. Both were English-language films, which Villeneuve had not yet done. Both films starred Jake Gyllenhaal. But to Villeneuve, they were very different propositions: Enemy was a deeply personal film about identity and the unknown nature of the self. And Prisoners, which also starred Hugh Jackman and Viola Davis and which would be largely distributed by Warner Bros. Pictures, represented Villeneuve’s first true chance to make a real Hollywood film.

Villeneuve decided to make both. But he made Enemy first. “I did convince the studio, Alcon”—the producer of Prisoners—“to wait a few months for Prisoners because first I wanted to make a first film in English in a smaller environment. And the real reason is that I wanted to make sure that I will shoot something that will be so close to me that if ever I was smashed and destroyed by Hollywood, there will be something. If people say, ‘What’s that? Oh, Denis’s there. He’s flying over there.’ Because I did feel that I was afraid.”

I remember watching Enemy in a small screening room the year it premiered, in 2013 (the movie was distributed in the United States by a then upstart studio called A24), and being increasingly unsettled and haunted by the film. Sometimes, in quiet moments, the final shot of Enemy still comes to me, unbidden. Who is this guy? I wondered then.

Enemy and Prisoners were both stylish, morally ambiguous films that showed the extremes of human behavior without ever venturing into sadism or pure spectacle, and this style of filmmaking—brutal, unresolved, lush, and heartbreaking—would become Villeneuve’s signature as he made progressively bigger, and bigger-budget, films in Hollywood: 2015’s Sicario, 2016’s Arrival, 2017’s Blade Runner 2049. “I always did projects I [felt] ready to do,” Villeneuve says. “I was ready to do Dune after Blade Runner. I would have not been ready to do Dune after Prisoners. I slowly learned my craft one step at a time—my skills with actors and then to work with more and more background action and increase the technical difficulty slowly. I just felt secure. And when I started Dune, I knew I could not go in front of people and ask them to invest $200 million [until I was ready]. I need to feel deep inside me that I can do that.”

Villeneuve says he only recently stopped feeling like a tourist in Hollywood. “I think that feeling of having the right to be here in some ways came from other filmmakers, colleagues that wanted to reach out and share thoughts about cinema with me or some friendships that began and that I accepted,” he says. He’s coy about who exactly he’s talking about. But part of it, surely, has also been the acceptance of the films, which despite their increasing size and scale and sometimes exotic source material are consistently deeply personal.

“My work is all about me,” Villeneuve says, helplessly. “If you don’t like Dune, the movies, I’m 100 percent responsible because I made every single decision. I brought them to the screen, and they are very personal films. Even for me, it’s like—scope is not something that is contradictory with the ownership of a movie. These movies have been brought to life by me, and I say that without arrogance. I mean, I’m the one who brought them to life. And yeah: It’s my Dune.”

A few weeks later, Villeneuve and Lapointe, who is shorter but equally warm and charismatic, are at the North Hollywood warehouse of Legendary, the production company behind the Dune films. The warehouse is full of costumes from past productions: Pacific Rim, Crimson Peak, Godzilla. In the back, transported from another continent entirely, is one of the ornithopters—a helicopter-like vehicle—from Dune: Part Three. Soon this prop, which is the size of an actual helicopter, will join a bunch of others in an upcoming exhibition of work from the Dune films. But right now it is here, in a parking lot under the glaring Los Angeles sun. Its paint—an homage to the specific color of a 1981 Porsche—glows in the light. “The last time I saw this vehicle, it was in a deep desert,” Villeneuve says, looking on. “We had brought it to Abu Dhabi, and it was, I remember vividly, at the top of a cliff of sand. This thing I’ve seen a lot. It’s like an old friend.”

Later in the day, Villeneuve tells me he is set to approve a final handful of effects shots. And then Dune: Part Three, and the director’s work on the trilogy, he says, will cease. “I do feel that I have to stop,” he reflects. “I don’t think I should spend another minute on it. Because I’m still curious, I’m still alive, and I do it for artistic reasons, not because I see that I’m comfortable or I see that it’s going to be good business-wise or for my career. I think it’s good for me to stop artistically.”

As Villeneuve’s star has risen, he has increasingly had to think through the question of how to remain an artist at the very high tier of the business that he’s in. “In the past 25 years, there’s a tendency to try to find the perfect formula to make a film, and to try to reproduce, reproduce, and make sequels,” Villeneuve says. “I’m responsible. I just made three Dune movies. I’m about to make James Bond 26. So I’m a sinner. But the idea is that as an artist, I feel that there’s an urgency, and you feel it in the young filmmakers, which I deeply love—the idea to bring new stories, original stories to the screen. It’s very important. And that we have to try to, at the end of the day, we need to take risks.… I want to say that we, as humans, as artists, if we want to be better than AI, we have to be unpredictable.” Only humans, he says, “can step into the unknown and go deeper into the dream. That is the strength of a human being. And I think that no computers can do that.”

It’s the end of September, and the Paramount–Warner Bros. Discovery merger is about to close. “I think that consolidation, I mean, less players in the business is never a good idea,” Villeneuve says. “Those studios are historical studios. And I hope, I truly hope, that the people in power will have the wisdom to protect the legacy of both studios. There’s a limit to profit. I mean, if the only goal is to make money, it’s really sad. Those things are historical gems of American culture and they have a duty to—I hope and I pray that they understand the responsibility that they have and that they will take care of both of these entities.”

Villeneuve, for his part, is already turning his attention toward Bond—another character, and another world, he grew up fascinated with. “I adore James Bond,” he says. “I adore Sean Connery, the Sean Connery years, the verve of James Bond, his panache, his drive, his charisma, his unapologetic way of living the strength and what it says, good and bad, about masculinity. There’s something about James Bond that deeply inspires me.” He says the previous producers of the franchise approached him with the idea of directing the film a few years ago, right as he was beginning Dune: Part Three. Villeneuve says he hung up the phone and actually screamed out loud when they offered the franchise to him. Then he told them they’d have to wait. “I said to them, ‘Yeah, I’m up for it, but I have something before called Dune: Part Three. I’m shooting in two weeks.’ And the only way I can do things in life is to fully commit to something. So I said to them, ‘If you want to work with me, you will have to wait many months because I will be entirely focused on Part Three.’ And so that’s why I’m sorry for everybody, but it took more time for the casting because I’m busy.”

Now we know: Robert Pattinson is James Bond. Villeneuve’s decision, albeit in consultation with his producers and the studio. He is incredulous that I am even asking. “I am the director!” he says. And then softens a bit: “I’m doing cinema because I love to share the creative process,” he says, about the conversations that led to Pattinson. “Otherwise, I will do ice sculpture in my basement. I love the idea to share creativity. But when it comes to casting, it’s something that—I’m doing the casting. But, of course, it will need to be accepted and approved by a ton of people, including you, the pope, my mother, my brother, who has a strong opinion about who should be James Bond.… I think Donald Trump wants to be James Bond. Everybody talks about James Bond. So yes, I will choose James Bond with my friends, producers, and hopefully everybody will.…” He pauses. “You know what? At the end of the day, the truth is, no matter who I choose, some people will be excited and others will be disappointed.”

Now Villeneuve has a gleam in his eye, talking about what he was looking for in the part. “The first quality is that I need to believe that this man is a killer, because more than a spy, Bond is an assassin,” he says. “I need that kind of anger deep in the eye. It’s not everybody who has that. I need someone who has that kind of unapologetic panache, someone that when he comes into the room, everything starts to gravitate around him, that kind of strong charisma and someone that has a lot of sensuality as well and that people are attracted to and that someone who expressed some kind of pleasure, someone who has width, sometime who has dark humor, sometimes that has pleasure into being in deep shit, someone who is not afraid to put his hand in the mud. I need someone that is strong, muscular, someone that is a force. And someone, of course, who has a deep intelligence in the eyes, someone that is always ahead of us.”

He is grinning. You can feel Lapointe, in the nicest possible way, willing him to say less. But Villeneuve, as is typical, is swept away. “Every time I’m thinking about James Bond,” he says, “there’s an electricity that goes into my vein that is the electricity of pleasure. It’s like: For me to do that is just a pure cinematic pleasure. Incredible pressure, stress, yes. But the pleasure is bigger.” ✦

#6616. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

Tip: Docking, or pressing through the pastry a few times with a fork, allows steam to release from the tiny holes, which is helpful for keeping the Joulutorttu from opening up in the oven and securing the jam in place. #6613. Netflix’s ‘The Body’ Is The Most Fun Teen Drama We’ve Had In Years

The following article contains minor spoilers for The Body.

It’s been a big few years for the teen drama, from Off Campus and Sterling Point to The Summer I Turned Pretty and Heartstopper. Nothing ever truly bad happens, but emotionally there’s always something at stake.

Quinn Shephard’s The Body, which came out on Netflix this month, is also a teen drama—but don’t confuse the latter with other iterations of the genre. The Body is winking, sapphic, and totally deranged. It has more in common with Mean Girls and Cruel Intentions, by way of Carrie and The Crucible, than the gentle high school stories of late. (Already there’s a Christian petition to cancel it that has gathered 90,000 signatures, so you know it’s good.)

Our story begins on Halloween in 2004, at a Catholic high school in a small town (we’re not told where, though filming took place around Ontario, Canada). Everyone’s in Juicy Couture, lips glossed to the nines, Chloé Paddingtons and Balenciaga Le City bags slung over their shoulders (never mind that the former was released in 2005; you’ll discover that The Body plays fast and loose with historical accuracy). In the opening episode, the school’s dance troupe, the Lions, throws a big party at an abandoned convent and everyone’s invited: even the weird outcast, Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros). But when they all take ecstasy and engage in a Satanic initiation ritual—leaving one of the dancers, Grace (Sofia Wylie) unconscious—the balance of the group is thrown into disarray.

What happens next is part mass psychogenic hysteria (when some of the girls’ hands start shaking, followed by seizures and visions, it brings to mind the 2011 story out of LeRoy, New York, in which 20 girls at a high school developed “conversion disorder”), part possible supernatural occurrence; we’re left hanging in the balance. What’s more interesting, though, is the idea of repression and religious guilt, compounded by the attitudes of the era (everything lame is described as “gay,” so extra points for accuracy there). Sapphic thoughts and feelings bubble beneath the surface, threatening to spill over. Burgeoning sexuality fizzes throughout these high schoolers’ lives. The series is an excellent portrait of girlhood; more times than once I was transported back to being 15 or 16 and acting like a girl possessed.

Yet while plenty of the themes are gritty (religious trauma, crystal meth addiction, internalized homophobia), this isn’t a serious show. The humor is dark and a little twisted (at one point, the girls are all screaming their confessions, which range from “I’m not a natural blond” to “my brother killed seven people in Afghanistan”). The fashion is a sort of Gen Z-ified version of millennial style (all J’adore Dior tank tops and bejewelled XXL shades, rather than, like, greasy side-bangs and knit hats with flames on them). The latter is fun rather than annoying or erroneous; much like in Mean Girls and Cruel Intentions, we’re given a slick and sexy version of high school. In many ways, that’s the most 2004 thing of all.

Of course, the eight-episode series is not completely flawless. There are moments when the pace sags a little, and a few plot points arise that are either hard to make sense of, or that disappear into the ether. Even so, in this era of mild-mannered and overly earnest YA shows, The Body stands out as deliciously knowing and mischievous—even a little off-color. (In the opening minutes, as the teen girls stretch each other in the grass, the brilliantly wry Elise, played by Sara Boustany, comments, “Holy fuck, you guys look like a bunch of dykes.” Again, historically accurate.) In fact, I haven’t had this much fun watching a teen drama since the first season of Yellowjackets, or early episodes of Riverdale.

As is often the case with Netflix, the ending leaves room for a second season, without there being any indication as of yet that there will be one. Reddit threads are already alight with fans stressing out over whether they’ll axe the show (my instinct is that a second season is a no-brainer, though that doesn’t really mean anything). Regardless, it’s been a truly addictive first outing. And the streamer would be possessed—nay, demonic—not to green-light another.

#6612. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6611. The Governors Awards Marked the Official Start of the 'You Can See Everything' Oscars Campaign

This is an edition of the weekly newsletter Tap In, GQ senior associate editor Frazier Tharpe’s final word on the most heated online discourse about music, movies, and TV. Sign up here to get it free.

Start your engines: the 2027 Oscars race is officially underway. Awards Season always starts in earnest with the Governor’s Awards, a ceremony held in a smaller ballroom in the same Dolby Theater complex where the main event will take place early next spring. It’s where they give out honorary Academy Awards (the Irving Thalberg Award, for the real heads) to the legends who, woefully, have yet have won a competitive Oscar—last year’s marquee honoree was Tom Cruise, this year’s were Glenn Close and Ridley Scott. But it’s also where Best Picture and the other awards narratives we will discuss endlessly for the next four months really begin to take shape.

Dune 3, Artificial, and Misty Green all had big presences in the room, which, duh. (Tim and Kylie in the cut, mostly sitting and not mingling, but it was interesting that he showed up this year but not last for the big Marty Supreme push.) But there were a few other films represented whose presence made their campaign intentions clear. Mahershala Ali presented the first award of the night to Floyd Norman (a 90-year-old trailblazing cartoonist who worked with Walt Disney and later Pete Docter) but the Your Mother 3x squad was deep, from director Bassam Tariq to John Cho. Jesse Eisenberg, Paul Giamatti and Julianne Moore put on for A24’s The Debut, Eisenberg's second directorial effort. (Watching Jesse and Andrew Garfield reconnect made for a beautiful Social Network reunion.) And Curry Barker and Inde Navarette being there would certainly imply a real push for Obsession. The duo with the most motion in the room, though, was unquestionably Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. The only time they didn’t seem like the big dogs that everyone was gassed to chat with was when they were talking to King Big Dog himself, Christopher Nolan, front and center receiving will-wishers at The Odyssey table. Nolan and Fielder is a crossover that needs to be cemented on wax, a drum I will continue to beat. But it was cool to see Zendaya talking intently with Oppenheim; her collaborator curation has been pretty elite—imagine her in whatever Oppenheim chooses to follow Primetime with?

When I asked Fielder about embarking on the campaign trail and how far the doc can actually go, he sighed and said “one day at a time,” in that Fielder monotone where you can’t quite tell if he’s being earnest or not. But he laughed off the idea of being too invested in any nominations either way.

But most importantly: the Governor’s Awards is just a really fun room in which to be an interloper or fly on the wall. I spotted Shawn Levy and my brain immediately started spamming the word “sublime.” Daniel Kaluuya started cracking up at the mention of his great airport interview with Tyriq Withers. Olivia Wilde, Seth Rogen, Penelope Cruz and Ed Norton joined ranks for a brief Invite huddle. Everywhere I turned, there was either a person so famous or certified that it startled me to see them walk by (like Zendaya breezing in right as the show started, or turning around to find myself face-to-face with personal favorite Carla Gugino. (Karen Sisco mentioned!) Unlike some stuffier award ceremonies, the Governor’s Awards is kind of like the cocktail hour before the big sit-down dinner in March.

Ambling around the room with a stiff glass of Johnnie Walker in hand—“Did you just get carded”? an exec asked me incredulously; the bartender replied that he thought I was “like, 14"—I briefly caught up with David Corenswet, who, true to form, was unfazed by the forces beyond his control as ever. When I said “weird week huh?” he didn’t even realize I was referring to James Gunn’s DC exit, then laughed when it dawned on him and said “above my pay-grade” with a genuine shrug. We should all be so blissfully unbothered.

Later, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II told me he was excited for this week’s Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth red carpet premiere, noting that this film will be the first time he only read his scenes for a project and no other part of the story. Without wanting to give too much away, Yahya said Tarantino’s script is structured in a way where he could comfortably read his parts and get enough of the gist to stay in the dark about the rest, because the only thing better than starring in a new Tarantino joint is getting to still experience it like a fan.

Other notable sightings, interactions, and crossovers: Travis Scott doubled down on what he told me at our Men of the Year party: he wants that golden statue for his original Odyssey song, and he’s willing to play the campaign game for it, dutifully sitting through the whole night (and jetting off immediately after the ceremony ended to go catch Future’s 10 pm set at Camp Flog Gnaw up at Dodger Stadium.) Speaking of Odyssey collaborators, James Blake was also in attendance—I watched him meet H.E.R. and talk about potentially collaborating. Tom Cruise was the belle of the ball at last year’s ceremony but played it super lowkey this year, to the point where I didn’t actually realize he was there until I saw him sneak out of a secret side exit after briefly talking with Tessa Thompson. Digger’s divisive reviews and reactions have evidently not knocked Tom off of his Best Actor pivot.

As for the actual awards, after Floyd, John Malkovich charmed the room with a great toast to Glenn Close, and King Storyteller Matt Damon regaled everyone with a great impression of triple-OG crank Ridley Scott from their time together on The Martian. (Matt was hesitant to do another movie about a loner astronaut right after Interstellar, to which Ridley apparently replied “No one gives a shit.”) Both tributes and subsequent speeches were expectedly emotional; Damon pointedly said that "it’s about time we see Ridley Scott with an Oscar in his hand,” but Ridley’s remarks were all about how much the late great Tony Scott would’ve deserved one too, leading to misty eyes and standing ovations. Close addressed going 0 for 8 but said the work is the real reward as her daughter tearfully watched on. But there were great moments of levity, too, like Todd Haynes presenting Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler with an award by revealing that he and Christine both slept with the same guy back in college.

Either way, a narrative of being long overdue seems to be emerging. An Awards Season where the Tom Cruises and Glenn Closes of the game finally get theirs, while upsets like You Can See Everything shake the table. What more could you ask for?

#6610. How to Reset Your Skin Care Routine After 40

Dermatologists break down the ingredients, steps, and treatments that matter most for skin over 40.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

As we age, there’s seemingly always something new to think about, including adjusting your skin care routine to meet your skin’s evolving needs. You may not need to add a bunch of new products to your current regimen, but increased dryness, changes in texture, fine lines, and enlarged pores may require ingredient swaps that your current lineup can’t deliver. The skin care products you used in your 20s and 30s may have worked then, but once you hit 40, your skin may start to need something different. Experts share how to reset your routine for 40+ skin, including the non-negotiables, new ingredients that can have the greatest impact, and what to avoid to keep your maturing skin looking and feeling its best.

Over 40, skin has already started to thin, at both the epidermis and dermis levels, explains Dr. Suzan Obagi, a board-certified dermatologist, associate professor of dermatology and plastic surgery, and director of the UPMC Cosmetic Surgery & Skin Health Center. “This means that skin will start to appear more fragile, fine lines will start to show, and skin becomes drier. For these reasons, a good skin care regimen should include a retinoid (retinol, retinaldehyde, or tretinoin) to help improve skin thickness, increase extracellular matrix proteins (collagen, elastin, and glycosaminoglycans (GAGs)), and encourage fibroblasts to make more of our Natural Moisturizing Factor (NMF),” Obagi tells ELLE.

Most skin over 40 also has some sun damage, which Obagi says can present as freckles and sun spots. Well before 40 and certainly after, there’s one daily non-negotiable for skin of any age: sunscreen. If the spots have already shown up, Obagi recommends a skin-brightening serum with tranexamic acid (TXA), antioxidants, and peptides to help correct the hyperpigmentation.

Additionally, Dr. Chris Tomassian, a California-based, board-certified dermatologist and founder of The Dermatology Collective, says a retinol at night will go a long way, as will vitamin C in the morning and aggressive moisturization.

As for ingredients, Tomassian says the key players in the post-40 reset will be retinol, SPF, and vitamin C, as already noted, along with PDRN, ectoin, ceramides, and occasionally estradiol.

If you’re not already on a daytime and nighttime routine, now’s the time to start.

Morning: Use a gentle cleanser if your skin is oily or if you didn’t get to a proper wash the night before. Tomassian suggests skipping the cleanse if your skin feels dry when you wake up. Follow with a good antioxidant like an L-ascorbic acid (vitamin C) serum or one with tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate (THD), silymarin, or phloretin. Layer on a PDRN moisturizer and SPF before any makeup.

Night: Before bed, cleanse thoroughly to remove makeup and sunscreen. Layer on a copper peptide serum, ptiox treatment, tretinoin (retinol), and a PDRN moisturizer. Obagi also suggests combining a pigment-correcting serum with a retinoid to help build the dermis extracellular matrix and target hyperpigmentation.

Bonus steps: Exfoliate one to two times each week with a combination peel pad, alpha hydroxy or beta hydroxy acids depending on your skin’s dryness level or if you’re experiencing any breakout. Tomassian warns, though, that post-40 skin should avoid over-exfoliating. “Skin gets drier with age, and breaking down your skin barrier by scrubbing or peeling too aggressively or too often can leave skin vulnerable to drying out,” he explains.

At any age, consistency is key. Even if you’re lucky enough to have minimal signs of aging, both experts agree that these steps will go a long way. “It is still important to incorporate a retinoid, an antioxidant, and a good moisturizer into your daily routine,” says Obagi.

There’s plenty you can do at home to care for your skin after 40, including adding LED light therapy to your lineup to help with fine lines and wrinkles and stimulate collagen—but Tomassian notes these are only beneficial if you use them consistently. An even greater investment is pairing your home routine with regular visits to a professional for in-office procedures like microneedling or ablative and nonablative lasers. These treatments can jump-start your skin to start producing more collagen. For chronic sun damage like redness and dark spots, Tomassian recommends Intense Pulsed Light (IPL), Picosure, or DermaV/Fraxel/CO2 lasers. These devices target pigmentation concerns that skin care does little to improve.

Obagi adds that pro visits are important since collagen production peaks at age 18 and, with each passing year, our skin makes 1 percent less collagen, elastin, and GAGs. “By our mid-30s and early 40s, we would benefit from devices that boost collagen production periodically. These can be noninvasive lasers, microneedling, and radiofrequency devices. These will boost collagen for a short time, but when combined with a well-thought-out skin care regimen, the results can be prolonged,” says Obagi.

You’ve lived with your skin for 40+ years, so you can tell when things start to change. Obagi says you have to listen to your own skin. “If you are on the dry side or have fragile skin, avoid harsh ingredients such as glycolic or lactic acid, strong retinoids, or over-exfoliating with scrubs. These can irritate the skin and drive sensitivity,” she highlights. If you have thicker skin or are oilier, she suggests exfoliating fruit acids and says your skin can tolerate stronger retinoids.

Tomassian’s rule of thumb is that after age 30, use as many ingredients as possible to bank collagen and focus on thicker moisturizers as you get older, since we produce less oil.

Key ingredients: oat-derived surfactants, plant-derived humectants, polyhydroxy acids

Key ingredients: liposomal tranexamic acid (TXA), oligopeptide-68, THD, and hydrolyzed algin to help target the various pathways driving pigmentation

Key ingredients: stabilized vitamin C, hyaluronic acid, panthenol, soothing allantoin, and green tea extract

Key ingredients: collagen, copper peptides, smoothing and brightening niacinamide, retinal, rice PDRN

Key ingredients: low-molecular PDRN, moisturizing squalane, panthenol, and ceramide, brightening niacinamide, firming rose peptide

Key ingredients: glycolic acid, lactic acid, malic acid, antioxidant-rich resveratrol, and green tea extract

Key ingredients: 10 percent Homosalate, 5 percent Octisalate, 3 percent Avobenzone, brightening niacinamide and ethyl ascorbic acid; moisturizing argan oil, squalane, and bisabolol

#6609. What Happened To Every Great British Bake Off Winner? Here’s Where They Are Now

From cookbooks to career pivots, the GBBO champs have stayed busy.

Since The Great British Bake Off premiered in 2010, countless talented contestants have shared their passion for puddings, tarts, and everything in between with the world. But only the very best dominated biscuits, perfected their pastries, and showed off their cake skills to get crowned the winner.

But where are those GBBO champs now? From authoring cookbooks to welcoming children, they have kept busy. Some made baking their full-time career, while others stepped away from their ovens. Wherever they ended up, one thing’s for sure: Once a star baker, always a star baker.

“The boy who bakes” paved the way as the first-ever winner of The Great British Bake Off, or The Great British Baking Show as it’s called in the U.S. and Canada. The former debt collector has since focused solely on his writing, cookbooks, and television appearances, often contributing to magazine columns and appearing on shows such as Sunday Brunch and Good Morning America.

Jo Wheatley is one of the few Bake Off champions to have stepped away from their cooking career. Since her season of the show, she has written two cookbooks and even run her own cooking school for a time before retiring and moving to Portugal with her husband. She still shares the occasional recipe on social media and on her blog, but for the most part, keeps it to “sunny snaps & padel in between,” according to her Instagram bio.

Since winning the show, Whaite graduated from Le Cordon Bleu and opened his own cooking school. He also started a bakery and a snack brand. He has appeared on Steph’s Packed Lunch and Strictly Come Dancing, where he finished as the runner-up. He has authored six cookbooks and a memoir, and married his longtime partner in 2024.

The winner of Season 4, Quinn continues her work as a creative consultant, food artist, and designer, and has authored a cookbook. She also holds the Guinness Book of World Records for making the largest Jaffa cake and Jammie Dodgers. She previously hosted a YouTube baking series and creates custom cakes, shares recipes online, and makes occasional media appearances.

Nancy Birtwhistle wasn’t a one-and-done after her 2014 GBBO win—she also participated in The Great British Baking Show: Holidays. Since appearing on the franchise, Birtwhistle has penned a few books on both baking and sustainable living. The GBBO alum also regularly makes appearances on TV and radio shows.

Since dominating Season 6, Nadiya Hussain has become one of the UK’s most prominent celebrity chefs. She has hosted numerous TV shows, including Nadiya’s British Food Adventure, Nadiya Bakes, and The Chronicles of Nadiya, and was even the subject of the documentary Nadiya: Anxiety and Me. The star baker also wrote over 10 cookbooks, plus fiction and children’s books, along with an autobiography.

A year after her 2015 win, Hussain was even commissioned to bake the birthday cake for Queen Elizabeth’s 90th. And in 2020, the chef received an MBE, or Most Excellent Order of the British Empire, for her work in the culinary and broadcasting industry.

Since winning Season 7, Candice Brown has opened her own pub, The Green Man, with her brother in England, as well as Margo’s, a restaurant and deli. She has also penned two cookbooks and written food columns for local newspapers. Brown has also made appearances on numerous other shows, including Dancing On Ice, Loose Women, Pointless Celebrities, and Celebrity Mastermind. She also played a role in the movie Love Sarah.

Since winning Season 8, Faldo has founded her own wedding and specialty cake business: Sophie Faldo Couture Cakes. In addition to her day job, she teaches baking classes in person and online. Plus, she returned to the Bake Off kitchens in 2023 and won The Great Christmas Bake Off.

Things have only gotten busier for Rahul Mandal after his Season 9 win. Since the show, he has released a cookbook and continues baking in his downtime and sharing his creations on social media. He also returned to the franchise and won The Great New Year Bake Off special in 2021. However, the champion still works full-time as a research scientist and engineer at the University of Sheffield. Mandal has also gotten married and had a child.

David Atherton balances his baking with everyday life. The Bake Off winner works as a practice nurse and health advisor by day, and continues his baking pursuits by night, so to speak. Since his win, he has written a series of children’s and adult cookbooks, writes a regular food column for The Guardian, and shares home cooking and baking tips on social media. Additionally, Atherton teamed up with fellow Season 10 baker Michael Chakraverty to launch the Sticky Bun Boys baking and pop culture podcast.

Peter Sawkins made history in 2020 when he became the youngest baker to win GBBO at just 20 years old—and that wasn’t the end of his time on the franchise. Sawkins returned and won The Great New Year’s Bake Off in 2025. Meanwhile, Sawkins has graduated from college and completed pastry training at the Amaury Guichon Pastry Academy. He has also published two cookbooks and frequently shares recipes and baking tutorials online. Additionally, Sawkins works part-time in sports fundraising and plays competitive badminton.

It’s been five years since Giuseppe’s Season 12 win, and he’s upped the ante on his culinary career since. In the past half-decade, Dell’Anno has authored two cookbooks and contributed to a third. He also runs a successful cake business, teaches baking classes in person and online, and frequently shares his baking insights on broadcast television and in food columns. Like some of his fellow winners, he’s also made appearances at local festivals.

Known for recipes featuring bold Malaysian flavors, Syabira Yusoff continues to feed her love of baking by sharing tutorials on social media, hosting online culinary workshops, and judging baking competitions herself. Impressively, she does all this in her free time while continuing her career as a cardiovascular researcher and bioinformatician at King’s College London. Most recently, she announced her engagement to her longtime partner just this past July.

Matty Edgell has stayed busy, both professionally and personally, since winning Season 14. The former high school teacher resigned after the show and now focuses on creating recipes on his website while also sharing baking tutorials on social media. He also tied the knot and welcomed his first child. Edgell publishes a Substack newsletter and has made appearances on TV shows and at local food festivals.

Since her 2024 win, Grasso has kept plenty busy. Not only does the winner post weekly recipes to her Instagram account, but she also released two digital cookbooks earlier this year: Cooking Therapy and Baking Therapy. She has made appearances at local food events such as the Gloucester Quays Food Festival and recently opened up about her bipolar 2 diagnosis.

As the most recent winner of GBBO, Jasmine Mitchell has only a year behind her in the culinary spotlight, but she’s exploded onto the scene with gusto. Since her time on the show, Mitchell has appeared as a guest on numerous talk shows, appeared as a judge on Danish Bake Off, and currently has a cookbook in the works. She’s doing all this while finishing medical school!

#6607. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6606. Joaquin Phoenix Wasn’t Thinking About 'Her' When He Filmed This Intelligent Eyewear Campaign

It feels like a scene out of a sci-fi movie: Joaquin Phoenix is standing across from me, instructing me to speak into his eyeglasses in a foreign language.

“Let’s see what happens,” the Oscar winner says. “It could be any language.”

The idea we’re testing here is whether the glasses Phoenix is wearing—a dark-rimmed pair from the South Korean luxury eyewear brand Gentle Monster’s new Intelligent Eyewear collection—could live-translate these words into English. This is one of the glasses’ capabilities the actor was most delighted to discover while he was shooting their campaign film directed by another Oscar winner, Jonathan Glazer. The glasses were crafted in partnership with Google and Samsung, and feature AI-powered technology.

Joaquin Phoenix in the Jonathan Glazer-directed campaign spot.

The last time Phoenix appeared in a fashion campaign, it was 1997 and he was modeling moody suits for Prada. This time around, he stars in the Glazer-directed spot that Phoenix says was partially inspired by the 1969 documentary Salesman, in which vendors travel across New England selling Bibles. In the Gentle Monster ad, Phoenix’s character—who has an intense, quasi-manic energy—ventures into an unnamed hotel, where he falls into a deep sleep and meets colorful, large creatures at the end of a hallway. (One might even call them…Gentle Monsters.) Per a press release, the “intelligent eyewear becomes his way of understanding their language and communicating with them, opening up unexpected possibilities for connection.”

Phoenix had wanted to work with Glazer for a long time. “I’ve known him for years, and when we all approached him, we came up with this really interesting and offbeat idea that just [had so] much mood. He just gets super excited and inspired,” the actor says. During the shoot, the Zone of Interest filmmaker kept the camera rolling for prolonged periods of time, encouraging Phoenix to harness different emotions. A moment in the ad might last for “30 seconds, but we shot for 15 minutes,” he explains. “A whole range of things are happening in those 15 minutes, things that we were trying.”

In an email, Glazer reiterated that he was glad to have had a reason to work with Phoenix: “The first image I had was him asleep, maybe dreaming, with the glasses all wonky across his face. The rest kind of grew from there,” the director said.

When I meet the actor last Wednesday at 23 Wall Street in Manhattan—where Gentle Monster has staged an enormous activation for the Intelligent Eyewear launch, complete with fake horses with wagging tails and huge surreal sculptures—it’s hard not to think about his turn in the 2013 film Her, one of the most prophetic AI movies of our time. In the Spike Jonze near-future drama, Phoenix’s character, Theodore Twombly, chats with and subsequently falls for an AI-powered operating system voiced by Scarlett Johansson. If 2011’s Contagion foreshadowed the COVID-19 pandemic, Her’s depiction of chatbots feels eerily similar to the world of ChatGPT dots, Meta Muses, Claude Duets, and Gemini Sparks that we’re beginning to grow accustomed to.

Phoenix and his partner, actress Rooney Mara, wearing Intelligent Eyewear at the Gentle Monster event in Manhattan.

When I ask Phoenix if filming the campaign made him think of Her, he shrugs. “I wasn’t. It seems like I should have,” he says. “It’s funny because I think that sometimes films have more of, maybe, an impact on the people that view them than for me, but I hadn’t thought about that. Somebody just made a joke about it actually, and I was like, ‘Oh yeah, you’re right.’”

Phoenix, who most recently starred in 2025’s politically tinged neo-Western Eddington, leaves on his Intelligent Eyewear glasses—which are Gemini-embedded, sleek, and thick-rimmed—while we speak.

“The thing is,” he says, “I’m not even aware that I’m wearing them.”

#6604. The Vogue Business AI Tracker

The Vogue Business AI Tracker keeps a record of the most important AI developments that will influence our industry and our world, each week. From venture capital investments and startup launches to product drops and regulatory updates, we’ll make sure you never miss a beat when it comes to the AI news that matters.

The news: J.Crew launches AI stylist built on Anthropic’s Claude.

Why it matters: J.Crew is the latest luxury brand to introduce an AI-powered shopping assistant. Built on Anthropic’s Claude, its new “Style Advisor” helps customers put together outfits based on occasions, personal preferences and specific items, drawing on the brand’s styling archives and campaign imagery.

The launch reflects a growing push among fashion retailers to make online shopping more conversational and personalized, as brands look to keep customers within their own digital ecosystems, rather than lose product discovery to third-party AI platforms. It comes a week after Prada became the first luxury brand to launch a dedicated plugin with ChatGPT, and follows Ralph Lauren’s push into branded AI personal styling last year with its “Ask Ralph” white-label AI styling tool.

The news: Natural Cycles launches its own fertility-tracking smart ring.

Why it matters: Natural Cycles is launching its first smart ring, moving beyond its existing partnership with Oura into its own wearable hardware. The new “NC Ring” measures body temperature overnight, feeding data into the company’s AI-powered fertility algorithm, which uses machine learning to calculate daily fertility status for its hormone-free contraceptive app.

The move puts Natural Cycles into competition with Oura, whose CEO Tom Hale told Vogue Business that women’s health features have been a significant driver of growth as the company moves towards a much-anticipated IPO. Unlike the Oura integration, which requires subscriptions to both services, NC Ring works with a Natural Cycles subscription alone. The company says around 80% of its active users already track their temperature using a wearable, giving it an established customer base for its own hardware.

The news: Pre-orders for Gentle Monster’s Google smart glasses are already sold out.

Why it matters: All 16 styles of Gentle Monster’s new AI smart glasses, developed with Google and Samsung, have sold out their initial pre-order allocations just days after launching, despite prices starting at $449. It’s a surprising sign that fashion-forward design could help win over consumers who might otherwise be reluctant to wear a computer on their face. Notably, most of Google’s more conventional Warby Parker styles remain available.

Gentle Monster’s sellout suggests that distinctive design could be a powerful draw, even as the surveillance debate remains unresolved. The caveat? Neither Google nor Gentle Monster has disclosed how many pairs were available to pre-order, making it difficult to gauge the scale of demand.

The news: Gentle Monster taps Joaquin Phoenix to front its Google AI Glasses.

Why it matters: Gentle Monster unveiled a campaign starring Joaquin Phoenix for its forthcoming AI-powered glasses, developed with Google and Samsung. Directed by filmmaker Jonathan Glazer, the short film will debut in mid-November, ahead of the collection’s December launch. (Pre-orders open on November 12.) The glasses, first previewed at Google I/O in May, run on Google’s Android XR platform and integrate its Gemini assistant, offering features including real-time translation, navigation and hands-free photography.

The launch marks a significant step in Google’s return to smart eyewear, adding competition to Meta’s established Ray-Ban partnership. Google has also teamed up with Warby Parker, while Kering is developing AI glasses with Google for Gucci. Gentle Monster’s decision to enlist Phoenix and Glazer is yet another sign that fashion credibility and cultural positioning are central to Big Tech rivals’ attempts to win the smart glasses race.

The news: Amazon launches SMS-based AI shopping agent after blocking Meta’s Muse.

Why it matters: Amazon has begun testing an expanded version of its AI shopping agent, Alexa for Shopping, among a small group of US customers over text. The new SMS feature lets shoppers search for and compare products, send photographs to find similar items, track prices and complete purchases without opening Amazon’s website or app.

The move reflects a broader shift toward making every consumer touchpoint shoppable, from social media and search engines to messaging. As AI agents become accessible through everyday interactions, the distinction between browsing, asking for advice and making a purchase could become increasingly blurred. For luxury brands, the challenge is not just where their products are sold, but how they appear in shopping conversations that take place beyond their own channels.

Amazon’s decision to block Meta Muse from accessing its marketplace in September also suggests that retailers want to extend their own reach without necessarily ceding control of discovery to competitors.

The news: Zalando unveils plans for AI shopping agent that can buy from other retailers.

Why it matters: Zalando has announced plans for a new AI shopping agent that will allow customers to purchase products from other retailers without leaving its app. Called Zalando Extended, the service is being piloted with homeware retailer Westwing, with AI-powered checkout scheduled to officially launch in 2027. The agent will eventually be able to complete purchases on shoppers’ behalf, expanding Zalando’s offering beyond the products it sells directly. The move builds on its existing conversational AI assistant, which has attracted more than 22 million unique users this year, according to Zalando’s Q3 earnings update.

The retailer’s plans follow a similar move by Amazon, whose Buy for Me feature allows customers to purchase products from external retailers through its shopping app. Both point to a potentially significant change in the marketplace model: rather than requiring brands and retailers to list their products on a platform, AI agents could facilitate purchases directly from their own websites.

For brands, this could open up new routes to customers without the usual marketplace integrations, while raising questions about who controls product discovery and the customer relationship. For Zalando, it offers a way to expand its assortment without holding additional stock, while keeping shoppers within its own ecosystem.

Why it matters: Prada has launched a ChatGPT plugin allowing users in the US, the UK and Italy to discover products, explore collections and find stores using information sourced directly from the brand. As AI assistants become a gateway to product discovery, the move gives Prada a more authoritative presence in conversations it might otherwise struggle to influence. “Conversational experiences represent a natural evolution of traditional e-commerce,” said Prada Group digital director Laura Campanella. “Through this pilot initiative, we are exploring a new territory for customer engagement.”

The news coincides with the launch of Prada’s Christmas campaign this week, featuring hand-drawn animation by Disney veteran John Pomeroy. These two contrasting moves reflect a broader distinction emerging in luxury: AI for product discovery, and human craftsmanship for consumer-facing brand storytelling.

The news: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals the huge costs and risks of the AI boom.

Why it matters: Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO filing offers a rare look inside the economics — and extraordinary risks — of the AI industry. As the Claude AI maker prepares for a potential $2 trillion valuation, the Financial Times reports that its revenues exceeded $33 billion in the first nine months of 2026, while its computing costs have fallen dramatically relative to sales, all suggesting a path to profitability. Yet Anthropic has also committed more than $800 billion to computing infrastructure through 2045, much of it supplied by technology giants including Amazon and Google, who are also major investors.

Crucially, the prospectus devotes 92 pages to risks, warning that future AI models could resist shutdown, manipulate information or cause harm too large for insurers to cover. For businesses embedding AI into everything from creative production to customer service, the filing exposes a central contradiction: the technology is becoming commercially indispensable even as its developers acknowledge profound uncertainty over its long-term risks.

The news: Anthropic plans European AI consultancy.

Why it matters: Anthropic is reportedly partnering with private equity firm Hg to launch a European consultancy that’ll place AI engineers and advisers in external businesses to help them integrate Anthropic’s technology, according to the Financial Times. Expected to launch by the end of 2026, hubs are currently planned in London and Berlin, with the Claude developer likely using the venture to accelerate corporate AI adoption — and even capture some of the work traditionally handled by consultancies such as Accenture and the Big Four.

Fashion and luxury businesses, many of which are still grappling with how to deploy AI, could be fertile ground for these services. But the model raises an obvious tension: while companies may welcome direct access to AI expertise, how independent can the advice be when the consultancy is backed by a company with a commercial interest in driving adoption of its own technology?

The news: Anthropic launches Claude Duet AI agent to rival OpenAI and Meta.

Why it matters: Anthropic has released Claude Duet, an AI agent rivaling Meta’s consumer-focused Muse and OpenAI’s more enterprise-oriented Dots; the Duet has both brand and consumer use cases for fashion. It can purchase products on consumers’ behalf using Shopify’s Shop Pay and Stripe Link, while merchants can instruct the agent to set up, design and manage their Shopify stores, including inventory and orders, Anthropic announced in a blog post. Meanwhile, a “richer visual editor” — which allows brands to design and preview their storefronts within the agent’s interface before anything goes live — is “coming soon”.

It was only a matter of time until Anthropic followed Meta and OpenAI in launching a personal AI assistant. Now, the battle is on between these tech companies to capture both consumer and brands’ trust, so that the integration these agents depend on across stores and payment providers is realized. The growing competition here signals a shift towards AI-mediated purchases, potentially reducing direct customer interactions for brands and making product visibility and seamless checkout across AI platforms increasingly important.

The news: Major banks and retailers block AI shopping agents like Meta Muse.

Why it matters: A growing list of US banks and retailers are blocking AI agents like Meta Muse and Instinct from acting on their websites. Amazon and Ebay have both prohibited these models from browsing or purchasing items on their respective marketplaces, while Citigroup, Bank of America, JPMorgan and Charles Schwab have each moved to prevent outside agents from logging into customer accounts and transacting on their behalf.

“We have to make sure we protect our customers in the right way [and] we’re building tools to do that,” JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week. “In the meantime, we’re not going to allow just any outside agent to come inside the company, because that’s too risky for clients and for JPMorgan.”

While much of the fashion industry runs its direct-to-consumer sites via platform providers like Shopify — which has opened its network to AI agents unless a brand explicitly opts out — the growing calls from prominent banking officials to introduce legislation point to a bigger unresolved question: when an AI agent makes a purchase that a consumer later disputes, who is responsible for putting it right? For now, experts say much of that burden may still land with the retailer.

The news: OpenAI UK employees received £2.3 million on average in pay and shares in 2025.
