#6600. More Men Are Getting Penis Filler Than You Think

In Monty Python's The Meaning of Life, Eric Idle sings, “Isn’t it awfully nice to have a penis?”

But, according to the new documentary Manhood, the feeling is not universal. In the film men look between their legs with nothing but shame, regret, and self-pity. The subjects members— particularly their perceived smallness—are problems to be solved.

Enter Bill Moore, a Dallas-based medspa operator, whose PhalloFILL penis filler procedure can supposedly add meaningful girth without surgery. The film follows his eager patients, including Ruben, an aspiring comedian and father of five, and David, a gay ex-OnlyFans star whose penis was botched by a previous filler procedure.

Director Daniel Lombroso spent years filming Moore and his patients, , slowly building trust until they opened up and (quite literally) bared all to the camera. Watching Manhood, it is clear that getting penis filler is never just about being bigger. To the patients, this procedure represents an escape from middle-aged ennui, a break from a difficult past, or a life preserver for a sinking marriage. The fast-growing, nationwide penis enlargement industry is happy to help, at $6,000 worth of filler injections per dick.

GQ sat down with Lombroso, fresh off Manhood’s breakout premiere at SXSW, to find out how he convinced a male enhancement spa to let him film inside, why the penis filler industry is booming, and who’s already getting rich off it. Manhood is available to stream on November 17.

Daniel Lombroso: That’s a great question. I think the most squeamish moment is Ruben bombing at stand-up on stage, more so than the botched penises. But, it’s funny. In real life, I am incredibly squeamish. It’s hard for me to look at surgery. It’s hard for me to look at someone using the bathroom or throwing up. There’s something about when you’re making a film, when you’re behind a lens, it gives you a level of separation. It’s sort of a mediator between you and the world. I shoot a lot of my own work, and on this project I shot some and worked with an incredible cinematographer, Vittoria Campaner. So there’s something about having that intermediary between you and the world that gave me comfort and helped me get through it. The hardest moment was the penile reconstruction, but we did not put most of that in the film.

Yeah. David, the person who gets botched, had his penis fully degloved like a banana. They had to peel back the layers and scoop out the permanent dermal filler that’s living in nodes in the shaft of his penis. That was one of the most gruesome experiences of my life. We decided to spare the audience that horror. And David is okay, thank God.

It’s tough. That was the toughest one. I also used to work at The New Yorker and I made a film on the Brazilian butt lift, which was similarly gruesome. I mean, that is one of the most gruesome cosmetic surgeries in the world. It’s a fat transfer procedure. They suck out the fat from where you don’t want it, your stomach or your arms, and stick it in where you do want it, your butt.

I filmed and watched that, and edited it on my New Yorker computer in The New Yorker newsroom for six months, and I would see David Remnick walk by and be curious and confused, and continue with his day. So it’s not my first time being in those environments, and they are hard for me personally. But something about making a film, it just gives you this level of separation that helps you get through it.

I think it’s important for people to be braced with these images. It is shocking to me how difficult it is for people to look at just a regular penis, especially straight men and older straight men. Gen X and above feel like they’re getting hit with an atomic bomb when they see a penis. Younger men, queer men, and women have always been fine, but I cannot tell you how many pitch meetings we went into where, like, the female executives love the film, the queer executives love the film. Then it gets to a straight guy at the top who is hit with one dick, and certainly one botched dick, and is out. Or he has to make sure on the record that everyone knows that he doesn’t have that problem. That happened in quite a few meetings. So I think it’s important to confront people with those images.

My business partner Kerry [Mack] joked that this is the first time I don’t have a Holocaust connection. We were looking for a penis enlargement-to-Holocaust connection, but we couldn’t find one.

I started this film three and a half years ago. At the time, we were all inundated with stories about the male loneliness epidemic. It felt almost like a cliché. I know you’ve covered it super well, and I’m sure we both grew up on Vice. It’s also something that’s really hard to show, because you don’t necessarily want to… “Condone” is the wrong word. “Platform” is also the wrong word. I hate when that word is used. But it is a cultural phenomenon that needs to be covered and discussed, and it’s very hard to do it.

I couldn’t really find a good way. Around that time, I read about the explosion in penile enhancement, and specifically, penile girth enhancement. I was less interested in penis enlargement than using that as a canvas to explore this burgeoning cultural discussion. So I called, like, every urologist in the country doing versions of it. There’s the Penuma, which is a really gnarly implant.

Yeah, Ava Kofman wrote a great story about the Penuma, which, like, pokes through and makes you bleed. I spoke to the creator of the Penuma. I spoke to people doing more permanent dermal fillers. And all of them were reticent. You know, the way I make films is I embed for many years in these environments. When I made [the alt-right documentary] White Noise, I lived on the road with white nationalists for three or four years. And for this film, I lived in clinics for two years.

So I had to find a practitioner who was open. And finally I got to Bill Moore, this very classic American character. He’s a businessman, not a doctor, and he said, “Come on down to Dallas.” So I booked a one-way ticket, and I would just sit in the waiting room and introduce myself to different patients. With a story like this, it’s really the only way. These men are so ashamed, they’re not gonna open up to a random reporter who calls them. So I knew I would have to put in a lot of time. I would just sit there, usually with my camera in a different room, and introduce myself. Sometimes they’d say, “Come back,” some would say no, some would say yes.

On those first two shoots, I met a megachurch pastor getting his penis enlarged. He’s very famous, and I cannot say who it is. A border patrol agent in the film. A father of five, an OnlyFans star, someone with brain cancer.

Super hard, and I try to be very patient. You want to push your way in at the right times and with the right people, but this is not the kind of project where you want to be coercive in any way. The last thing you want is someone saying that they were forced to appear naked in a film. So all of these men consented in different forms. Some said, “Change my voice.” Some said, “Anonymize my face.” Some said, “Just shoot my dick.” Some said, “You can shoot my face, but not my dick. I can talk about having a small dick, but don’t show it.”

There was kind of every version and permutation. But when I started to look for the main characters who could carry a film, I needed someone who was comfortable with me filming their family. Usually I’m doing vérité, like direct cinema. Really in their lives for at least a year and a half. I feel like this is front of mind for everyone now because of the Lance Oppenheim Nathan Fielder movie [You Can See Everything]. But you need someone who’s willing to invite you into their home and play the game with you, and Bill was willing to do that from the beginning.

Ruben was the next person who signed on. He’s a father of five on his second marriage. And it doesn’t go the way he might have hoped. The hardest one, I think, which speaks to your question, was David Smith. David is a pseudonym. He’s an OnlyFans star, and he had never told his story before. You would not know this from watching the film, but it actually took the entire production to get him to show his face. It was such an incredible story. I’ve never heard someone talk so openly about their botched penis and growing up evangelical and the horrors of being a male porn star.

We had a very small budget, but we saved a tiny bit of money up until the SXSW deadline. We were about to work with a face replacement company in France because that was his wish, and we thought it spoke to the theme of shame. We were starting to explore, do we hire an actor? And around that time we said, “You know what?” I used to work at The New Yorker, where you don’t really screen things. But I said, “Let’s just take a chance.” So we flew David to New York. We said, “You have no editorial control.” None of the subjects in any of my work ever have any editorial control, including my grandmother. But let’s just show him the film and see what he thinks.

And he was so blown away, he cried in the room. He called his brother, and has since opened up to his family about everything. He’s touring with the film. He came to SXSW. That took until literally a week before the premiere at SXSW, and it’s an ongoing process. He continues to become more and more open.

Yeah. I mean, it’s funny. He was a porn star. You’d think that he had such a level of exposure that he would be comfortable with this. But I think this speaks to the film. Somehow talking about your body is easier than talking about your feelings. Having to talk about his shame, his insecurity, his issues with faith, and with his parents is super, super hard for him. He needed to see the final cut to decide to go forward with it. It was the biggest gamble of my career and, thank God, it paid off.

That’s a great point. So many of the men—this takes me back now—like, I was more nervous than them. I felt like I was being potentially intrusive. I didn’t want to appear coercive in any way, as I mentioned. I wanted them to feel comfortable. But many of them felt grateful to have what you might call a third space to talk about how they feel, because most of them are not opening up to their partners, believe it or not. I don’t know how they come home with a soup can and explain that. And many of them are paying cash. There’s no credit card transaction fee. Many of them are finding ways to anonymize what they’re doing.

But at the same time, they want to talk to someone about it, which is so strange. They just don’t want the people that are part of their daily life to know, but they want Bill to know, and I think Bill deserves a lotta credit for that. He’s a queer man treating these oftentimes right-wing Texans, holding their dicks and enlarging them and making them feel comfortable.

And they wanted to talk to me, and if they wanted it to be off record, that was fine. If they wanted to be on record, that was fine. I think for many of them that was a relief. It’s so common when you work on intense stories that people start to see you as a friend or a collaborator. People see you as someone who understands their plight, and I think whenever I felt like it was starting to get there, I would remind them I’m a journalist. The world is gonna see this. Anything that is private or uncomfortable, just make sure you’re comfortable sharing before it goes in front of the world.

These guys feel so alone. Going back to White Noise, my first film, the single biggest motivator for joining those white nationalist movements wasn’t ideological conviction. I mean, some of them are gnarly racists or antisemites, but a lot of them just, like, want to be part of a club. I saw that in a lot of these men too. They just feel isolated. They want someone to talk to, and felt relieved that Bill was there to listen and that I was there to listen.

I think men, and particularly straight men—I say this as a straight man who probably struggles with this myself—have an underdeveloped sense of self oftentimes.

I’ve done these types of stories for ten years now. When I’ve interviewed women or gay men, they’ve had to think about who they are and their place in the world from such a young age. Especially queer men, from their earliest memories or certainly when they started to understand their sexuality, have had to grapple with who they are and how they appear publicly. I think that because there’s this lack of communication or lack of internal dialogue in a lot of these men, they’re internalizing so much constantly, and they’re not reaching out to those around them.

The reason I got so excited about Tuben as a character is he felt emblematic of everything we were talking about during Trump’s last re-election. You have the. disaffected conservative man who maybe voted for Trump. He would never tell me. He wouldn’t say whether he did or he didn’t, but he thinks all politicians are corrupt, and he’s living in this world on his phone that goes from Andrew Tate to porn to Nick Fuentes.

And, then here comes along a doctor, or not even a doctor, that says, “All of the things that you’re feeling can be fixed with this shot.” If you’re Ruben and you’re already feeling so alone and you haven’t spent your life thinking about who you are and your place in the world, you see a chance to fix all of your problems.

And when Ruben and Lana, his partner, had deep conversations, or when Ruben is on stage doing comedy, connecting with an audience, he feels so much better about himself. But then when he’s back to his phone, he’s feeling horribly alone, like he needs to change something. I think that’s something we all feel.

When I’m talking to my fiancée about how I’m nervous about this or that, I feel great. I feel connected. But then I go back to my phone, and I feel like shit again. So yeah, the ones who have those conversations are in a much better place.

That was by design. Every kind of man is getting this. Anecdotally speaking, Bill says that about two-thirds of the patients are straight and one-third are queer, which is surprising. Sometimes he even says three-quarters are straight, and anecdotally from my experience, that’s accurate. I’ve seen patients as young as early 20s. I mean, David was in his late teens when he got botched, or maybe right around 20 years old. He’s 24 in the film.

Yeah. I also filmed with men in their 70s. I’ve spoken to practitioners who’ve done penis enlargements for men in their 90s.

Men have been trying to enlarge their penis all the way back to the days of the cavemen, as the movie says. But now there’s this extra layer of social pressure, and technology makes it possible. It doesn’t mean that it’s safe, but it makes it possible. Every kind of man is doing this, and I felt like I needed an avatar for both.

You have the guy who’s completely seduced by bullshit online. We all know that guy. I have friends I went to college with who are that guy now. Certainly people from high school who are that guy. And then David is a little bit more heartfelt coming from OnlyFans and dealing with the scars of his experience.

There’s always something bigger. No pun intended. I really tried not to be reductive. For Bill, it was a partner who called him a “little dick motherfucker” 15 or 20 years ago, and then he started changing every part of his body. He has fake balls. He has silicone balls. He has his [fake] pecs, all of it. For David, it was growing up evangelical. For Ruben, it was dealing with abuse and being Mexican-American and things like that.

But there are ordinary people. Believe it or not, the most ordinary person I met was the megachurch pastor. He claimed he was just doing it for his wife, who he loves very much. I hope that that’s true. But almost everyone else would start that way, and then you know how it goes. It’s the old Errol Morris trick: you just kind of stay quiet and let them continue. Then they’d be like, “Oh, and also it’s this, and that, and this kid who said this fucked up thing to me 15 years ago. And by the way, my wife and I don’t have sex anymore.”

Look at implants. Whenever Dolly Parton got hers, they were sort of the medical frontier. I’m sure whoever was the version of me and you at the time was dealing with the same sort of fun, gonzo stories.

And there was probably a Dr. Loria at that time [a penis enlargement provider in the film] who was botching breast implants. It’s a lot safer now, and we know how those work. This is a—maybe unregulated isn’t the right word—but under-regulated frontier. You have people like Dr. Loria operating with impunity in Florida.

This is a guy who designs his own proprietary blend of who knows what. He literally will not tell me. It’s some kind of silicone oil. He says he’s “a hobbyist pharmacist,” and he likes to come up with his own proprietary solutions which he creates in Florida at his office. And the results you see in the film are egregious. I have yet to talk to a Loria patient who has had a positive outcome, and he is still practicing in the state of Florida.

The movie intentionally tries to leave that in a gray zone. But even the better technologies like hyaluronic acid, which is lip filler, the FDA has never said that you can inject that into someone’s dick. [But] it hasn’t said you can’t. It’s fine for off-label use. It’s all sort of the Wild West right now, and I think people don’t realize that the American medical system has all these gray areas and openings.

Bill is not a doctor. He just has to be under the supervision of a doctor, meaning a doctor came to his facility at some point and sanctioned it. Where I see the trouble is that all of these urologists who are trained to do really important medical procedures, like someone struggling with ED or who has issues after prostate cancer, they see a way to make money doing this. I saw literally dozens of urologists flock to Bill because they realize they can make a few thousand dollars in twenty minutes doing penile enhancement. Is that what they should be doing with their time? Probably not. Is that a way that they can make a lot of money? Certainly.

Business looks good. And sorry, one last point is that the penis is different also because it’s invisible. Men already don’t talk about their feelings, as you and I know. But other types of female work are visible. The media has been objectifying women from the beginning of time.

This is something that almost feels personal to men. They’re not telling their partners. Many of them say they’re doing it for themselves. Some of them literally tell me they just want it to poke bigger through their pants at the gym, or they want to show it off in the locker room. So it’s a personal choice, I think, in a way that I’m skeptical of, that’s also different from other medical procedures or kinds of plastic surgery.

I don’t know if you can put “long breath” in the transcript, but… I believe in a kind of documentary filmmaking that doesn’t impose a takeaway. I think we now live in this streamer era where movies are designed to be “two screen” documentaries. It’s a Netflix term, where you can fold laundry [while watching], and they tell you every third of the movie what it’s about and what the takeaway is. The movie is not pro-penis enlargement. It’s not anti-penis enlargement. It’s using that as a canvas to explore all of these things and I think that’s where I like to start. That said, I would not recommend my friends do it. Bill tried to get me to do it, by the way.

Many times. And I am willing to do anything for my stories, like be in bed with Nazis for years or whatever the fuck. I was not willing to do that. The simple fact is that this is a medical gray area. No one knows how safe it is. Filler migrates, and the problem is in your penis.

Whoever that friend is, I would be like, “What issue are you having in your marriage, with your kids, with your self-esteem, with your body?” And I would really welcome the chance to get close to that friend again, you know? As you get older, people are around less, people have kids, people are also more isolated. They’re in their family. And those moments actually can lead to incredible breakthroughs when your friend is like, “I’m scared that my dick is not good enough.”

I would have just been gifted with the most exciting conversation that I’ve had in months, and I would welcome that. We would go on a hike, or have a beer, and talk about why he doesn’t like his dick. I think we as a society would be better if we did that more often.

#6599. 8 Great Airbnbs in Marfa to Book for a Design-Forward Vacation

If you’re a design and art lover, Marfa is one of those places you need to see at least once. With about 1,800 residents, it’s a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it town in the high desert of West Texas, put on the map by the minimalist artist Donald Judd. Judd left New York for Marfa in the 1970s, bought buildings downtown, and later took over a decommissioned army post outside of town. He filled it with permanent installations, turning the town into a creative hub that continues to attract a steady stream of art-devoted acolytes.

But even those who aren’t chasing the museums or the Prada Marfa store will get something out of the town to love; the nature-driven traveler, for example, can find some of the best stargazing in the country. So whether your itinerary is packed with gallery visits or you plan on doing little more than watching the sun set from a porch, kick things off by booking an Airbnb in Marfa.

These eight spots offer just as much inspirational design as the town itself; here’s where to stay in Marfa for a memorable desert getaway.

Quite naturally, this home takes its cues from Donald Judd, with clean lines and furniture that leaves plenty of space around it. It’s laid out as three separate studios, each with its own entrance, bath, and walled patio, so a group of friends can come together but still have a quiet place to retreat. The main studio is anchored by a fireplace with a low sofa and two lounge chairs—ideal for cozy nights in—while the library studio has a vintage wood-burning stove and worktable. Judd’s work at the Chinati Foundation is minutes away and the Marfa Lights viewing area is a short drive.

Amenities: Private soaking pool, fireplace, wood-burning stove, full kitchen plus two kitchenettes, Starlink WiFi, pet friendly

In this beautiful two-bedroom rental, a large tumbleweed hangs from the ceiling of the sunroom and the floor-to-ceiling glass doors open onto Southwestern-style gardens. The desert theme is not subtle, but it is done in an elevated, tasteful way—right down to the limewashed walls that echo the tones and textures of the West Texas landscape.

Head outside to the private courtyard to discover an oversized chiminea; stay inside, and you’ll find a fireplace and a hi-fi record player. It sleeps a small group or a couple of friends, and the detached casita next door can be booked for bigger groups.

Amenities: Fireplace, outdoor chiminea,WiFi, flat top grill and smoker, AC, dog friendly

Built in 1937 and carefully restored, this Spanish Revival home keeps its original wood beams and plaster walls, but has been warmed up with textiles and Western artwork. From the pink kitchen to the blue tile that outlines the television, this is definitely a house where style leads.

In fact, each of the four bedrooms in the main house has its own flavor: the Library Suite is lined with books, the Treetop Suite looks out over the desert. A detached casita with its own king bed and kitchen sits across the property with an expansive outdoor area. The whole place sleeps 10 adults, which makes it great for a group trip. The living room, with its fireplace and roomy sofa, is where everyone is likely to end up after a day at the galleries, which are a short walk away.

Amenities: Fireplace, detached casita with kitchen, WiFi, dedicated workspace, AC, outdoor backyard

This solar-powered house sits alone across 1,000 acres of ranch land, with the Rio Grande at the edge of the property and Mexico on the horizon. There is a modern wood-burning stove inside which heats the living room, and both bedrooms have their own tiled baths and windows framing the view. It’s a true escape for two couples; or perhaps a writer who needs a distraction-free setting from which to work (especially since there’s no cell service, only a landline and internet). Chinati Hot Springs is 20 minutes away for a soak, and Big Bend Ranch State Park is about an hour off for mountain biking.

Amenities: Solar powered, wood-burning stove, chef’s kitchen with gas stove, outdoor grill, washer, internet and landline, outdoor TV

Few houses in Marfa get photographed as often as this 320-square-foot box on the edge of town. It looks like one of Donald Judd’s sculptures turned into a place to live—to see the real things, Judd’s concrete and aluminum works at the Chinati Foundation are a short walk away.

Downstairs is an open kitchen with a dining area and a walk-in shower; two doors open from the kitchen straight onto a shaded patio with outdoor dining. A steep staircase leads up to the bedroom, which juts out over the first floor and faces the desert. You can watch the sunrise from the queen bed, and a heated mattress pad helps on cold fall nights.

Amenities: Fire pit, shaded patio with outdoor dining and loungers, heated bed pad, full kitchen, walk-in shower

Attention, green thumbs: The garden here is so stunning, it’s been featured in four books. The hosts co-wrote a field guide to Chihuahuan Desert plants and have filled all 1.25 acres of the property with native plantings and walking trails. The outdoors is very much the focus here: This casita is a 500-square-foot room, with a kitchenette and large covered porches that look out to the garden and mountains. Its al fresco appeal extends after hours, too. McDonald Observatory has certified the property as night-sky friendly, so after dark you can see even the Milky Way from the porch.

Amenities: Covered porch, native garden with walking trails, kitchenette (induction cooktop, convection toaster oven, microwave)

Most of the action at this Marfa adobe happens out back, under a big pergola with climbing vines, two long outdoor sofas, and many areas to sit and gather. Indoors, rooms are filled with bold paintings and modern furnishings like a low curved sofa in chocolate brown, worn leather armchairs, an iron chandelier that hangs over a white brick fireplace, and a cute checkerboard floor kitchen. Downtown is within walking distance, so you can stroll to galleries and dinner and come back to a fire.

Amenities: Fireplace, covered pergola patio with outdoor lounge and dining, dedicated workspace, WiFi, AC

If you’re coming to Marfa for a milestone birthday or special event, book this place for the barn alone. It’s a historic 1,250-square-foot space with room for a large dinner or party. The home itself was newly renovated to include a cook’s kitchen, a gym, and two king bedrooms—all set under 10-foot ceilings. Best of all, you’ll be just a short walk from downtown, and since dogs are welcome, you can extend the guest list to the whole family.

Amenities: AC, dedicated workspace, barn for events, gym, WiFi, pet-friendly

#6598. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6597. 8 Pantry Items Pro Organizers Say You Should Toss ASAP

Your expired spices and stale snacks are taking up prime shelf space.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

No one wants to waste perfectly good food—I’m more likely to eat something slightly past its expiration date than throw it out prematurely—but some pantry items are just taking up space.

Dusty canned foods, old spices, expired baking ingredients, and more past-their-prime goods serve little to no culinary value. Getting rid of them will actually help you identify the pantry items that you can still use before they go bad. But how can you keep your pantry organized more regularly, and what exactly should you throw away?

Go through every item in your pantry at least twice a year, recommends Nicole Gabai, professional organizer, founder of B. Organized, and author of The Art of Organizing: An Artful Guide to an Organized Life.

If a twice-yearly check-in feels too daunting, consider a weekly five-minute check-in to discard expired goods, says Shaniece Jones, professional organizer and founder of Closet Therapy. “Organize by accessibility and intention,” she says. “Keep your daily go-tos at eye level, heavy items like large cans of oil and bottled water on lower shelves, and seasonal or rarely used items up high.” Labels, Lazy Susans, and drawer dividers are some of her go-to tools for organizing the pantry.

As you start cleaning, check off the following items—these are some of the most common pantry items our organizing experts find past their prime.

While many shelf-stable foods, such as canned goods, are still safe to eat past their expiration date, you should still check for signs of spoilage. “You can tell canned goods have spoiled if they are rusted, or if you see the cans bulge or dent,” Gabai says.

Labeling pantry items helps you check how long they’ve been open. For opened packages and bulk goods you’ve decanted into containers, write the date on the label so you know when you opened them.

Spices that have lost their smell? Time to go. “If it smells flat or just not aromatic, then it needs to be replaced since it will add very little, if any, flavor to what you’re cooking,” Gabai says. She also notes that ground spices typically last one to two years, while dried herbs can last up to three years.

“Baking ingredients like flour, baking powder, and baking soda can lose their effectiveness over time,” says Meaghan Kessman, founder of Meaghan Kessman Home Organization.

Eventually, flour will go bad, but how long it takes to get rancid depends on how it’s stored and the type of flour. In general, Gabai says it will last at room temperature for six to eight months. She recommends storing it in an airtight container in the fridge or freezer.

“Check for expiration dates and any signs of spoilage, such as clumping or an off smell,” Kessman says. “If you’re unsure, test baking powder by adding a teaspoon to hot water—if it bubbles, it’s still good to use.”

We often buy cooking oils in bulk, but keep in mind that they eventually go bad. “Oils and fats, such as olive oil, vegetable oil, and shortening, can become rancid if stored for too long. Rancid oils have a sour or off smell,” Kessman says. “Always check the expiration date and store oils in a cool, dark place to keep them fresh longer.”

Gabai recommends storing oils in a cool, dark place and disposing of them properly; freeze in a zip-top bag, then toss in the trash (never pour down the drain).

These pantry staples are oil-rich, so they spoil faster than you might think. “They can last about 6 months at room temperature, but if you freeze them, they can last a year or more,” Gabai says.

“Snacks and cereals can go stale quickly once opened,” Kessman says. She recommends checking expiration dates and signs of staleness, like an unusual smell or texture.

According to Gabai, grains, rice, and beans can last about one to two years, but brown rice and other whole grains will not last as long because of their higher oil content.

“Condiments like ketchup, mustard, and salad dressings often get pushed to the back of the pantry and forgotten,” Kessman says. “Check for expiration dates and any signs of separation, discoloration, or off smells.”

Honey is the rare exception that probably isn't spoiled. The National Honey Board states that honey has a shelf life of approximately two years, although it can last much longer if stored correctly in a sealed container.

“Honey was found in the tombs of kings and royalty as far back as 3,000 years in Egypt—and it was still edible!” Gabai notes.

If you notice crystallization, Gabai recommends gently heating the honey container in a pot of water.

#6596. The USDA Thinks I Can Live on $65 a Week. Can I?

Welcome to The Receipt, a series documenting how Bon Appétit readers eat and what they spend doing it. Each food diary follows one reader’s week of expenses related to groceries, restaurant meals, coffee runs, and every bite in between. In this time of rising food costs, The Receipt reveals how folks—from different cities, with different incomes, on different schedules—are figuring out their food budgets.

In today’s special edition of The Receipt, we're unmasking the diarist and following James Beard Award-winning writer Paul Greenberg—a self-described cheapskate—on his quest to live on the USDA's Thrifty Food Plan.

My friends sometimes mistake me for a survivor of the Great Depression and not a Gen X-er raised in a household free from deprivation. I don't just bargain hunt. I bargain scour as if it were 1931.

This habit stays with me no matter if I’ve got a book on the bestseller list or if the stock market has just tanked. As a lifelong fisherman, I love angling for opportunities lolling in the currents of American commerce. I can’t stand the idea of buying a $5 gallon of milk when I know that the same milk from the same cows is lurking at a supermarket across the street for under three bucks.

With the inflationary surge of recent years, my friends have at last started to take a curiosity in the methods of my madness. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, the price of sirloin steak is up 21% since January 2024. Romaine lettuce? 27%. Even a gosh darn cup of coffee will cost you over 50% more in 2026 than it did when the Kansas City Chiefs last won the Superbowl. So when Bon Appétit asked my cheapskate self if I could get through a week of groceries for below what the USDA stipulates as its “thrifty food plan,” I smiled the knowing smile of an old-timer. Bon Appétit and USDA, I accept your challenge.

The USDA established the Thrifty Food Plan in 1975 and updated it in 2021 in an attempt to model a healthy diet that hits all the food groups. The TFP, as we’ll call it here forward (to economize on words in these lean times), proposes different shopping lists for different genders and age groups. I took those 2021 numbers and adjusted them for 2026 inflation. As a man in his 50s, I was given a total allotment of $64.90 per week, and recently, I took to the weird yet familiar corners all over New York City at which I procure my groceries. Using my usual regular shopping list, I mostly beat those numbers across the board—without, as US Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins recently suggested, resorting to a nutritionally suspect “$3 a meal for a piece of chicken, a piece of broccoli, you know, a corn tortilla and one other thing.”

However, the experiment raised a deeper question: Should I have to? But first, here’s how I did it.

Out of habit or laziness, many of us have a “favorite grocery store.” In an era of rapacious capitalism that has pushed so many Americans toward insolvency, there can be no favorites. Rather, it pays to seek out places where merciless competition drives major chains towards a common bargain basement. In Manhattan, where I live, I call these places “golden corners”—spots where Trader Joe’s, Target, and the rising star of discount grocery chains, Lidl, cluster together around a single intersection.

I’m able to easily deduce which place offers the lowest prices and run between them in a single shopping outing. While I’ll occasionally venture elsewhere for my meat and dairy (see: Chinatowns, featured later in this article), I find a good cutthroat corner serves me best when looking for animal protein.

Note: There is no beef on this list. For climate change reasons, I’ve never been a fan of the world’s most carbon-intensive protein, and to my mind, the three-dollars-cheaper-per-pound ground turkey works just fine in a Bolognese. Also note that neither the TFP nor I put any cheese on our lists either. I’m not sure why TFP refrained, but after beef, cheese is one of the most climate impactful animal proteins on the planet. The environmentalist in me also says cut the cheese.

Professional economizers often encourage us to choose vegetables and fruits with longer shelf lives that can bang around in our fridges until we’re ready to eat them. I’ve found picking the cheapest fruits and vegetables when they’re available is ultimately a better deal. For this, I turn to a staple of American urban street life: the fruit cart.

Fruit cart vendors, common in New York, Los Angeles, Miami, and Chicago, buy produce wholesale and offer deep discounts, especially when shelf life is short. My go-to cart-guy in Lower Manhattan nearly always has a $1 special (cauliflower, cucumbers, asparagus, berries of all kinds) and the relationship we’ve built means he steers me toward what’s good.

What if the nearly overripe berries go off? To this I say: There is no berry too off that can’t be made into jam (which saves you in the miscellaneous category at this article’s end). As for salad greens, while the mainstream shopping world wrings its hands over cyclosporiasis, I’ve found that joining a community garden circumvents the dreaded disease while also purging the scourge of inflation from your wallet. My community garden costs me about $50 a year in membership fees, seeds, and fertilizer, plus about an hour of my time a week in tending. The buy-in amounts to roughly $0.50 per salad.

Whatever fruit carts and my garden can’t supply, I usually find at great prices in Manhattan’s Chinatown, likely because vendors have connections to a handful of small farms and wholesalers that operate outside of most mainstream supermarkets. According to the California Migration Museum, there are roughly 50 Chinatowns across America in nearly every major American city, which is to say that a lot of the country should have access to one.

Note: Even with bargain basement shopping, I only barely hit USDA’s fruit mark. This was because nearly half of USDA’s fruit budget is juice, which, to my mind, is a bit like calling ketchup a vegetable.

The TFP drives a hard bargain on grains, expecting the home shopper to plunk down $3.76 for an entire week’s worth of “refined-grain staple grains," which include rice, pasta, bread, tortillas and the like. That’s tough when a loaf of Wonder Bread at Walmart costs you $2.47. Add a single box of one-pound pasta and it could send you over-budget.

There’s a bit more give in the "whole-grain staple grains" category, which allows $6.94. But even a whole-wheat loaf from Walmart (priced at $2.97) eats up just over half of my weekly allotment.

The only way I was able to snag the bread, rice, and pasta in my weekly shop and stay under budget was by leaning on another Asian country and by working hard on my home turf.

Patel Brothers, a national chain of Indian grocery stores, sells brown and white rice as well as beans of all flavors and provenances for prices that range from $0.80 to $2 per pound. As for bread, Target’s house brand of whole wheat flour is $2.69 for a five-pound bag. About a pound and a quarter of it makes a loaf. Weekly sandwich bread therefore costs out at $0.67 per loaf.

Last and actually also least: pasta. Nobody but nobody beats Trader Joe’s buck a pound.

Shopper beware—the last-minute, forgotten miscellaneous item is often the thing that stings you most at the register. Salt, sugar, cooking oil, and coffee purchased last minute, at even a cheap store, can be double what you’d pay if you are keeping careful track of who's charging what at your local golden corner. Keeping a passive list in your head of where the best buys on miscellany live helps these kinds of rookie mistakes from happening.

Additionally, as above, a little home elbow grease can be surprisingly effective in the condiment aisle. Fruit cart fruit made into jam and an immersion-blended home mayonnaise (a commitment of two minutes max) cost you pennies. And then there’s online. I have yet to find a better deal on coffee than on Amazon.

So I did it. I filled my fridge, stocked one shelf of my pantry, and even had a little left to treat myself to breakfast after this exhausting pan-city forage. Here’s what the final numbers looked like:

Does this mean the USDA’s stingy allowance is appropriate for these ever more expensive times? That anyone can be a successful cost-cutter like me?

Um, no. My kids are grown. I’m a freelance writer with weird hours. I live in a vast, quirky city with odd corners that can cost out cheaper than parts of the developing world. A busy working mom in a food desert who can’t commit to a community garden would find the ordeal a heavy lift.

Thank you for joining me on this ride through my own personal Great Depression. But as for you, USDA, I think it’s time you upped your budget. Stop cutting things like food stamps and healthcare. Perhaps the newest iteration of Congress will be more inclined to make this happen than its predecessor. We are, after all, among the wealthiest sovereign nations in the world.

C’mon, America! Don’t be such a cheapskate.

#6595. Joan Jett and Hannah Martin Are Bringing a “Bad Reputation” to Fine Jewelry

You’d never imagine being asked to pierce the ears of one of your teenage idols, but five years ago, renegade London jeweler Hannah Martin found herself in that exact, heart-racing predicament.

Pitched up at the Sunset Marquis hotel in West Hollywood—Martin’s self-described “home from home in Los Angeles”—she received a call from her close friend Maryam Malakpour, the stylist to rock legend Joan Jett, who just so happened to be staying at the same hotel. “I headed over to her villa feeling vaguely anxious because she’s my total hero,” Martin says, with a laugh. “In the end, it was more a case of forcefully pushing an earring through an existing piercing, rather than a totally new one…” (So far, so punk!)

Following that first encounter, Martin began loaning the “Bad Reputation” singer pieces of jewelry—her suitably subversive designs include hoop earrings punctured with malachite safety pins, rings resembling kinky harnesses, and razor-blade dog tags—before the pair decided to collaborate on something to mark the 45th anniversary of Jett’s version of “I Love Rock ’n’ Roll.” “The conversation was really organic,” Martin says. “We began talking about creating one piece, but there was such a wealth of inspiration that I got very overexcited.”

The resulting Hannah Martin London x Joan Jett collection comprises 14 pieces of jewelry and precious accessories, rendered in sterling silver, white, and yellow gold, that riff on the iconography of Jett’s legendary rock-star style. Think: high-waisted denim with zips secured by safety pins, battered leather jackets, Ramones tees, and a tangle of leather cords and chains strung with pendants.

“Hannah is the designer and I was really the muse,” Jett explains, “so a lot of it started with conversations about things I’ve worn, symbols that mean something to me, and pieces from my own jewelry and closet.”

The first piece—a pacifier pendant inspired by one Jett wore religiously in the ’80s, and her favorite of the collection—has been reimagined as a sculptural, geometric orb. “There’s something very punk about taking an object like that and turning it into fine jewelry. It has an edge to it, but Hannah made it feel elevated and beautiful,” Jett says. Elsewhere, DIY concert badges are reimagined in hand-painted enamel, leather lighter cases dangle from roadie-style lanyards, and leather cuffs are fastened with smooth sterling-silver buckles. The safety pin is reduced to its purest form, as a sculptural link in a chain, while Martin’s signature teardrop motif becomes a sleek heart, studded with spiky, reverse-set diamonds.

“It was really about stripping everything back,” Martin explains of her approach to the collection. “My design language is always about focusing on elemental forms.” And so, alongside pin-ups of Jett, Martin’s mood board also featured sculptures by Constantin Brancusi and works by Austrian designer and metalworker Carl Auböck. “It was a real mix of punk imagery and refined artistic forms.”

Martin can’t quite remember when she first heard Jett’s music, but suspects she absorbed it by osmosis from her dad’s record collection while growing up in the ’90s. “It was such a male-dominated universe and people like Joan, Courtney Love, and Patti Smith became part of my musical world,” she says. Now, one of her teenage heroines has made it into her fine-jewelry hall of fame.

#6593. Nara Smith’s Mom’s Pasta

In our Cooking With Friends series, friends of Delish visit the Test Kitchen to share their favorite recipes with you. Happy cooking!

This is my mom’s recipe, and it taught me what simple abundance really looks like. She’d grate tomatoes and spoon the sauce over her native South African pap (a dish made from cornmeal, similar to grits or polenta), rice, ground beef, or almost anything that needed a little love. I couldn’t believe something so good could come from a handful of ingredients, and she showed me that with this dish it’s not about adding more, but how you handle what you have.

The magic is in the grating. It separates the sweet tomato pulp and leaves the skins behind, giving you the pure heart of the fruit. Please don’t skip the beef bouillon—it gives the sauce its deeper savory backbone. I love this tossed with freshly made spaghetti or tagliatelle, though dried pasta works beautifully, too—exactly like my mom makes it. You can enjoy this year-round, but it’s especially delightful in summer, when tomatoes taste like the sun.

#6592. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6591. LuxExperience Reports 8.5% Sales Growth Amid Turnaround

LuxExperience — owner of Mytheresa, Net-a-Porter, Mr Porter, and Yoox — grew net sales 8.5% on a constant currency basis in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, generating €604.7 million. This marked the fourth consecutive quarter of growth since the group formed in April 2025 following Mytheresa’s acquisition of Yoox Net-a-Porter (YNAP) Group.

“[It was a] super quarter considering that it’s still a mixed picture out there for luxury,” group CEO Michael Kliger tells Vogue Business. “It shows there is demand in multi-brand and digital.

The group’s adjusted EBITDA improved year-on-year, climbing 590 basis points to 2.1%, up from -3.9%. LuxExperience also honed its outlook for fiscal 2027 to 6-9% growth, up from a mid-single-digit to high-single-digit range. The company increased its adjusted EBITDA margin to 2.5-3.5%, up from 2-3%.

Kliger described the quarter as the group’s strongest so far since the LuxExperience inception. “We are ahead of plan with these numbers. That’s why we upped the guidance,” he says.

By brand, Mytheresa’s sales grew 10%, generating €250.8 million, bolstered by a 9% climb in the US. Net-a-Porter and Mr Porter together grew 7.2%, generating €231 million, attributing this to a 24.3% jump in the US. Carried by strong performance in Europe (excluding the UK), Yoox — the group’s off-price retailer — also grew 8.2%, reporting €128.6 million in net sales.

Despite the group’s online foundation, each business invested in IRL events during the quarter. Mytheresa delivered 18 premium customer activations across Europe, the US, and Asia, continuing its one-of-a-kind VIC clienteling strategy. Net-a-Porter and Mr Porter also executed seven and 10 “extremely important person” (EIP) experiences, respectively, across the US and Europe. Yoox continued its focus in Europe, unveiling 14 community events in the region.

“This customer on the luxury side [Mytheresa and the Porter brands] is resilient,” says Kliger. “On the Yoox side, we see that in the lower and middle class, people prefer good offers, having not so much discretionary spend and still loving luxury. Whereas on the Mytheresa and the Net-a-Porter and Mr Porter side, we really speak to those that have the means to buy the latest [product] as soon as it hits the market.”

Mytheresa increased its adjusted EBITDA by 128.1%, while Net-a-Porter and Mr Porter upped theirs to 0.3%, marking the second quarter of profitability post-acquisition. Yoox remained unprofitable; however, it reduced its quarterly loss from €-19.1 million to €-6 million, taking adjusted EBITDA margin from -16.1% to -4.6%

Kliger says that Mytheresa is leveling out its marketing investment, shifting focus from digital to premium physical events, citing the two-week yacht voyage across Monte Carlo and St. Tropez, as well as upcoming pop-ups in the French Alps and Florida.

Both Net-a-Porter and Mytheresa will keep their focus on top spenders, Kliger affirms. What distinguishes Mytheresa and the Porter brands? “Mytheresa is very focused on the womenswear side,” Kliger says, noting that it only offers around 220 brands. “Net-a-Porter [offering around 500 brands] is broader and is for the customer that looks for editorial advice and brand discovery.”

For Net-a-Porter and Mr. Porter, the company is investing more in marketing and ramping up the editorial output and video production. “So we invest more to really inject energy into these brands,” Kliger adds.

Between Net-a-Porter and Mytheresa, customer overlap remained at 12%. (The figure has not changed in the last 18 months.) “The brands themselves have really carved out different personalities,” says Kliger. “If anything, we want that to become even sharper. The growth both businesses show does not come at the expense of one of the other. They’re growing into the market.”

Kliger attributes LuxExperience’s continued growth to a handful of core factors. First, the company is digital, and the digital market is expanding. Second, the group is positioned on both sides of the market, offering high-end and off-price. Lastly, the business isn’t heavily exposed to the luxury slowdown in China. “Our China business — we have good representation in APAC — but it was never oversized, and therefore we don’t suffer overly from the sluggish demand.”

Looking ahead, Kliger doesn’t foresee any major obstacles to the continued growth and predicted return to profit for Yoox, which he expects to realize between the last quarter of fiscal 2027 and the first quarter of 2028.

#6590. In Puerto Rico, It's Not Thanksgiving—It's Sanguiving

Puerto Rican Thanksgiving is an exhilarating holiday remix. Think turkey marinated in garlic, lime, and oregano, then stuffed with fried green plantains and chicharrón mofongo. Gravy is more likely to be made with guava than with giblets, and flan stands in for apple pie. “Pumpkin spice” is nowhere to be found; here, the local winter squash calabaza takes center stage. And in lieu of warm apple cider, sweet coconut water is sipped beachside straight from a coco.

Thanksgiving is just as cherished in Puerto Rico as it is on the mainland. Celebrated locally since the early 20th century, shortly after the United States invaded in 1898, it marks the beginning of the island’s rambunctious holiday season. It is also a favorite of chef and restaurateur Giovanna Huyke, who over four decades has become the feast’s culinary authority in Puerto Rico.

I meet with Huyke, widely considered the Puerto Rican answer to Julia Child, on a hot summer day at SatoFino, a neon-hued, woman-owned restaurant in San Juan. The bartender quickly spies her—Huyke is a regular, and her signature red hair makes her easy to spot—and prepares the chef ’s go-to drink, a stiff Manhattan. We settle into our barstools, readying to plan what will ultimately unfurl into an epic cooking adventure. Huyke has a propensity for them, she tells me. In the preceding days she traveled to Atlanta to cook for Ser Familia—a nonprofit that specializes in supporting Hispanic families—before she rushed back to Caguas, a city 20 miles south of San Juan, where she fed VIPs attending the Miss Universe Puerto Rico pageant. Then she raced across the island to teach a traditional-methods cooking class in San Germán, the second-oldest city in Puerto Rico. Now, she’ll show me how to prepare a Puerto Rican Thanksgiving feast.

A vueltita through the Plaza del Mercado de Río Piedras with a fresh haul of groceries, in preparation for Sanguiving.

“We have a rich and resilient food history—it came from necessity, lack, and a bounty from the land,” Huyke says. It’s a complex cuisine informed by both a deep agricultural heritage and a modern reliance on imported and shelf-stable ingredients, which, despite many obstacles, manages to emerge beautiful and full of flavor—the continuation of a culinary evolution ongoing for centuries. “Our food comes from Spain, Indigenous Taíno people, and [enslaved] West Africans,” Huyke continues. “But it grew from our land and from our history, mixing every influence in our pilónes and our cauldrons.”

Being around Huyke is a joy. A local TV personality, newspaper columnist, and cookbook writer since the late ’80s, Huyke has taught generations of Puerto Rican home cooks how to prepare the island’s most treasured dishes. Among them was my grandmother, Sara, who I call Tata. Like many members of the Puerto Rican diaspora, my family traveled back to the island for the festivities, alternating each year between Thanksgiving and Christmas. We’d enter Hartsfield- Jackson International Airport in Atlanta in heavy winter coats and leave San Juan’s Luis Muños Marín in shorts and tank tops.

Tata’s Thanksgiving table centered on the expected turkey, but her stuffing was exceedingly Puerto Rican. To a base of Pepperidge Farm stuffing mix, she added picadillo: ground beef cooked with sofrito—the fragrant blend of garlic, onions, peppers, and the punchy native herb culantro that is the cornerstone of the Puerto Rican palate—and pimiento-stuffed Manzanilla olives, all seasoned with the golden spice blend sazón. When Tata died I inherited a weathered copy of Huyke’s 2004 recipe booklet Celebraciones. Within it were recipes that clearly informed Tata’s tremendous Thanksgiving menu; it turned out Huyke had been influencing my holiday for even longer than I knew.

Although formally known in Puerto Rico as El Día de Acción de Gracias, in true Boricua fashion, Thanksgiving is often referred to as Sanguiving, a play on words that gestures to the Roman Catholicism that remains the region’s predominant religion. It’s also El Día del Pavo, which directly translates to “Turkey Day,” and Sangiving, spelled like it sounds. We islanders have a fondness for clever, shortened expressions, an example of our natural tendency toward Puertorriqueñizar—in English, “to make Puerto Rican.”

A stall brims with large slabs of local calabaza.

“Our adobo goes on the turkey, and all the sides have something to do with sofrito,” Huyke tells me, walking me through the standard Puerto Rican Thanksgiving table. In Puerto Rico, adobo takes two forms—one wet and one dry. Each is a spectacular blend of Spanish, African, and Indigenous ingredients and techniques—garlic, onion, peppers, and herbs pounded in a wooden mortar and pestle with Taíno roots called a pilón, binding the island’s ancestral and colonial cultures.

Puerto Ricans officially became American citizens (and draft eligible) in 1917, just weeks before the US entered World War I. As many as 20,000 locals served, and Puerto Rican soldiers have played a role in every US military conflict since. In many respects, Thanksgiving traditions rooted en la isla are part of a broader military promise: American soldiers always eat well on Thanksgiving Day. Puerto Rican soldiers brought many wartime foodways home with them, and this combined with government subsidies means that today staples can at times feel military-adjacent—especially given the reliance on shelf-stable foods required by a storm-prone island. Over time, the territory’s once agrarian economy (centered around sugar, coffee, and tobacco exports) was transformed into an industrial manufacturing system. Puerto Ricans still consume many foods like tinned corned beef, Vienna sausages, Spam, club soda crackers, and canned vegetables; roughly 85 percent of all food in Puerto Rico is imported.

When Huyke’s father, Hector, served in the Korean War, he encountered the military’s famously bland instant mashed potatoes. From then on, he flat-out refused the dish except during holidays, when Huyke’s mother, Alice (herself a trained cooking instructor), made an impossible-to-resist version: yellow potatoes slowly simmered in cream, enriched with chicken bouillon, then whipped until fluffy with butter. Today a garlicky variation features on Huyke’s Sanguiving table.

Huyke, for her part, wants to steer Puerto Rican cuisine away from processed ingredients and back toward fresh foods—not only because they’re healthier, but also because they are richer in flavor and better convey the layered story of the island’s culinary heritage. She favors from-scratch dishes that lean on regional bounty, from Indigenous staples like maize, peppers, yuca, and other root vegetables to later introductions like plantains and coconuts.

Ají dulce (sweet peppers) are essential to local cuisines across Latin America and the Caribbean—and Chef Giovanna's Sanguiving table.

The best way to explain, she tells me, is to cook together. A few weeks later Huyke joins me in my own kitchen in North Carolina. I quickly learn that cooking alongside her is a lot like having your own personal instructor. At each step she explains how she’s arrived at a certain preparation and why she uses specific ingredients over others. It’s clearly a familiar role: Education remains a central focus for Huyke, and she counts among her mentees young women like Natalia Vallejo, the island’s first James Beard Award–winning chef. She frequently enlists up-and-coming chefs to cook alongside her and makes herself available for mentoring phone calls. I now feel lucky that I can count myself among them.

Although Huyke auditions new Sanguiving dishes every year, Puerto Rican favorites are always on the menu, many of them influenced by her mother’s recipes. Key among them is yuca stuffing—or “estuffing,” as Puerto Ricans commonly pronounce it. Huyke’s family version, Agüeybaná stuffing, is named for the island’s powerful Taíno chief who led the local people at the time of the Spanish invasion in 1493. Huyke peels and then grates fresh yuca before grinding it to a paste in the food processor. Meanwhile, she instructs me to sauté sofrito in olive oil before adding ground and salt pork, annatto, herbs, and aromatics. It’s all piled into a high-walled dish and baked.

Next we turn our attention to pastelón, a lasagna-like layered casserole of fried sweet plantains and creamy queso fresco. The dish was likely born in New York City, where Puerto Rican and Italian communities converged, before finding its way to the island.

“The Puerto Rican and Italian diasporas were physically close in New York during the ’50s—they were exposed to lasagna and mozzarella,” she explains.

Then come more sides. Gandules, or pigeon peas, are a treasured crop. Though they’re frequently served with rice at Sanguiving and other times of year—arroz con gandules is Puerto Rico’s national dish— Huyke instead opts for an escabèche-style salad that marries gandules with tomatoes, avocado, and herbs in a tangy vinaigrette. Another island staple, canned beets, gets a fresh reinterpretation as Huyke roasts a local-grown variety and tops them with crumbled queso fresco.

Huyke’s Sanguiving turkey rests on a banana leaf bed and is adorned with freshly picked wildflowers from the rainforest.

Many Puerto Rican families choose pernil, or roast pork shoulder, as their Sanguiving centerpiece. It is typically marinated overnight in an adobo of minced garlic, sour orange juice, olive oil, oregano, salt, and pepper. But Huyke sticks to turkey, brining it first in a mixture of salt, brown sugar, dried bay leaves, fresh herbs, and peppercorns before pushing butter under the skin and brushing the bird with a blend of rum, melted butter, and guava jelly. Huyke preserves the drippings for a tangy-sweet guava-infused gravy. She also shows me how to make ajilímojilí, a highly adaptable, herbaceous sauce of garlic, ají dulce peppers (similar to bell but fruitier and more delicate), culantro, cilantro, olive oil, vinegar, and her own signature addition: a copious amount of capers. Guests will drizzle it over nearly every dish on her Sanguiving table, she tells me.

After hours of cooking and using every imaginable tool, from a traditional pilón to a modern Vitamix blender, we sit down to enjoy the fruits of our frying, molding, steaming, sautéing, and roasting. The result is unmistakably an American Thanksgiving spread, refracted kaleidoscopically through a fresh, colorful Puerto Rican lens.

Puerto Ricans have both embraced and resisted US imperialism at various points. There always lingers the question of statehood, which exists alongside the island’s long-standing and active independence movement. As Huyke’s cooking demonstrates, this push-pull relationship only continues to play out in all sorts of dynamic ways.

“I believe every cuisine evolves,” she says. “But traditions should be kept and taught. So we do not lose the roots that make us unique.”

#6588. David Corenswet Wore a Cult-Favorite Seiko on the Red Carpet

Superman actor David Corenswet, who’s set to reprise his Man of Steel role in Man of Tomorrow next year, just wore a way-out-of-left-field watch with a tuxedo during the 17th Governors Awards last night. There was no mistaking the glint of its dial from across the step-and-repeat: a Seiko ref. 6139 "Pogue" automatic chronograph. The bulky sport watch looked totally out of place in the restrained, elegant atmosphere of the awards ceremony…and absolutely perfect.

The “Pogue,” as the yellow-dial variant is known, is a wildly cool and beloved watch, and Corenswet smartly took advantage of the way it pops against the black-and-white of a classic tux. Plus, it doesn’t hurt that among Seiko collectors, the Pogue is a cult classic, often ranking towards the top of best-Seiko-ever lists. Not only is it an aesthetic swerve on the red carpet, but it’s the type of relatively affordable oddball celebrities rarely reach for.

What’s so special about the 6139, and why is it called the “Pogue,” you might ask? The 6139 was among the very first batch of automatic chronographs. A group of brands—Seiko; a consortium of Hamilton-Büren, Heuer-Leonaids, Breitling, and Dubois Dépraz; and Zenith-Movado—raced to be the first to debut the mechanical innovation. Who won the race is still a matter of debate, but one thing is for certain: when the 6139 hit the Japanese market in 1969, it featured an integrated design, a column wheel, and a vertical clutch. Meshing hallmarks of classic chronograph construction with the convenience of automatic winding at a relatively affordable price, it was paired with a wide variety of colorful dials and funky cases and produced for roughly a decade.

One of these designs, the ref. 6139-6002, is particularly eye-catching thanks to its bright-yellow dial with a contrasting blue-and-red tachymeter bezel, a 30-minute chronograph register, and a day-date display. American astronaut Col. William R. famously wore the Pogue during the Skylab 4 mission from November 1973 to February 1974. Subsequently, the 6139-6002 took on Pogue’s name, and is now one of the most collectible vintage Seiko references.

The best part? Though there’s unfortunately no magic bullet to make you 6’4” and handsome as Superman, you can snag a pretty good “Pogue” for under $2,000. It may not take you into space, but as Corenswet has proven, it sure livens up your average black-tie outfit.

#6587. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

#6584. Cranberry Cream Cheese Spread

Of all the incredible dips we’ve created over the years, our cranberry whipped feta dip is an internet and personal favorite—so much so that I just had to come back with an equally luxurious variation: this cranberry-topped whipped cream cheese spread. With the holiday party season just around the corner, this spread is begging to be included in your party spread. Plus, it's as easy to make as it is delicious—a tangy, sweet cranberry sauce gets finished with brandy, then is spooned atop a lemony whipped cream cheese for a guaranteed winning combo.

Fresh Or Frozen Cranberries? I used both while testing, and they both work interchangeably. I found the fresh cranberries broke down a little more than frozen, so it depends on whether or not you’re looking for more or less texture in your sauce.

What temperature should the cream cheese be? Make sure the cream cheese is chilled and softened but not super cold. It should be somewhat pliable when whipping to avoid lumps; this will ensure the mixture is light and airy. A little heavy cream will loosen the mixture if it's too thick.

The lemon zest: I found that the cream cheese layer needed a little more oomph. If you get a bite of cream cheese on a cracker, it shouldn’t be one-dimensional. Adding a touch of lemon zest makes it more palatable.

Storage:Store the cream cheese spread, with or without cranberry sauce, in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days.

#6583. Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup

Chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a new personality. Unlike plain noodles, which quickly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

#6580. Mashed Potatoes

No holiday table—or really any dinner table, for that matter—is truly complete without a substantial side of creamy, buttery mashed potatoes. While it may seem like simple, classic comfort food, there are a few ways to take mashed potatoes from good to great. That's why we retested this recipe again and again until we achieved potato perfection.

What People Are Saying:"So good! I don’t typically like sour cream on its own but it was a huge improvement for basic mashed potatoes. Will definitely be making this again." – PurpleStrawberry

"Easily my go-to mashed potato recipe. I've made it for Thanksgiving, and got requests to make it again. It's so good, doesn't even need gravy." – kitkat123

Really, the only chopping you'll have to do is cut up the potatoes. I do suggest peeling them (more on that later), and be sure to try to cut the potatoes into equal-sized pieces so they cook evenly. Around 1" chunks are ideal. Time to cook 'em! In testing, I found that covering the potatoes with cold water first yields the best consistency and ensures the potatoes don't become too mushy. Don't forget to add a pinch of salt to the water! Let the potatoes cook until softened—the best way to test is to use a paring knife and make sure it can be inserted with no resistance. This should take about 20 minutes. Make sure to drain when they're done so they don't overcook.

Now comes the fun part: Mashing the potatoes until smooth. You can use a masher, a ricer, or even a handheld mixer for this step. I think the smoother, the better, but you do you, of course.

On to what makes these potatoes the best ever: Heat up some whole milk and butter until the butter is melted in a pot.

Then, pour over the still-warm potatoes and mix to combine. Then add the sour cream, some salt, and pepper, and you're basically good to go! Mix everything well, transfer to your prettiest serving bowl, and proceed with the finishing touches: a couple of pieces of butter to melt into the potatoes, plus fresh parsley for some color and brightness. Brace yourself for the compliments.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

If you have any leftovers, store them in an airtight container in the fridge for a max of 3 to 4 days. With all of our recipes to transform your creamy leftover mashed potatoes—like fried mashed potato balls, potato rolls, waffles... we doubt they'll even last that long.
